When Britain declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939 following the [invasion of Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invasion_of_Poland "Invasion of Poland"), Southern Rhodesia issued its own declaration of war almost immediately, before any of the dominions did.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWood20059-13) Huggins backed full military mobilisation and "a war to the finish", telling parliament that the conflict was one of national survival for Southern Rhodesia as well as for Britain; the mother country's defeat would leave little hope for the colony in the post-war world, he said.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGannGelfand1964149-14)[\[d\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-16) This stand was almost unanimously supported by the white populace, as well as most of the coloured community, though with World War I a recent memory this was more out of a sense of patriotic duty than enthusiasm for war in itself.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald194514-17)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKillingray201266%E2%80%9367-18) The majority of the black population paid little attention to the outbreak of war.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVickery1989427-19)

The British had expected [Fascist Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fascist_Italy_/(1922-1943/) "Fascist Italy (1922-1943)")—with its African possessions—to join the war on Germany's side as soon as it began, but fortunately for the [Allies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II "Allies of World War II") this did not immediately occur.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald194721%E2%80%9322-20) No. 1 Squadron SRAF was already in northern [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Colony "Kenya Colony"), having been posted to the [Italian East African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_East_Africa "Italian East Africa") frontier at Britain's request in late August.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald194716-21) The first Southern Rhodesian ground forces to be deployed abroad during World War II were 50 [Territorial troops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territorial_Army_/(United_Kingdom/) "Territorial Army (United Kingdom)") under Captain T G Standing, who were posted to [Nyasaland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyasaland "Nyasaland") in September at the request of the colonial authorities there to guard against a possible uprising by German expatriates. They returned home after a month, having seen little action.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald194517%E2%80%9319-22) White Rhodesian officers and [non-commissioned officers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-commissioned_officer "Non-commissioned officer") left the colony in September and October 1939 to command units of black Africans in the west and east of the continent, with most joining the [Royal West African Frontier Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_West_African_Frontier_Force "Royal West African Frontier Force") (RWAFF) in the [Colony of Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colony_and_Protectorate_of_Nigeria "Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria"), the [Gold Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Coast_/(British_colony/) "Gold Coast (British colony)") and neighbouring colonies.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald194517%E2%80%9319-22) The deployment of white Rhodesian officers and NCOs to command black troops from elsewhere in Africa met with favour from the military leadership and became very prevalent.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBinda201247-23)

> "All I wish to say to you is this: we know that you will carry on the traditions that this young colony established in the last war."[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald194584-24)

Huggins to a draft of 700 Rhodesians bound for the Middle East, 14 April 1940

As in World War I, white Rhodesians volunteered for the forces readily and in large numbers. Over 2,700 had come forward before the war was three weeks old.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald194720-25) Somewhat ironically, the Southern Rhodesian recruiters' main problem was not sourcing manpower but rather persuading men in strategically important occupations such as mining to stay home. Manpower controls were introduced to keep certain men in their civilian jobs.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGann1965-6) The SRAF accepted 500 recruits in the days following the outbreak of war, prompting its commander Group Captain [Charles Meredith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Warburton_Meredith "Charles Warburton Meredith") to contact the [Air Ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Ministry "Air Ministry") in London with an offer to run a flying school and train three squadrons.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald194720-25) This was accepted. In January 1940 the Southern Rhodesian government announced the establishment of an independent Air Ministry to oversee the [Rhodesian Air Training Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Air_Training_Group "Rhodesian Air Training Group"), Southern Rhodesia's contribution to the [Empire Air Training Scheme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Commonwealth_Air_Training_Plan "British Commonwealth Air Training Plan") (EATS).[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald194733-26)

Huggins set up a Defence Committee within the Cabinet to co-ordinate the colony's war effort in early 1940. This body comprised the Prime Minister, Tredgold and Lieutenant-Colonel [Ernest Lucas Guest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Lucas_Guest "Ernest Lucas Guest"), the Minister of Mines and Public Works, who was put in charge of the new Air Ministry.[\[e\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-27) About 1,600 of the colony's whites were serving overseas by May 1940 when, during the [Battle of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_France "Battle of France"), Salisbury passed legislation allowing the authorities to call up any male [British subject](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_subject "British subject") of European ancestry aged between 19 and a half and 25 who had lived in the colony for at least six months. The minimum age was reduced to 18 in 1942.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGann1965-6) Part-time training was compulsory for all white males between 18 and 55, with a small number of exceptions for those in reserved occupations.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald194749-28) On 25 May 1940 Southern Rhodesia, the last country to join the EATS, became the first to start operating an air school under it, beating Canada by a week.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald194747-29)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950608-30) The SRAF was absorbed into the British [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force") in April 1940, with No. 1 Squadron becoming [No. 237 Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._237_Squadron_RAF "No. 237 Squadron RAF").[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPetter-Bowyer200515%E2%80%9316-7) The RAF subsequently designated two more Rhodesian squadrons, namely [No. 266 Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._266_Squadron_RAF "No. 266 Squadron RAF") in 1940 and [No. 44 Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._44_Squadron_RAF "No. 44 Squadron RAF") in 1941, in a manner similar to the [Article XV squadrons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Article_XV_squadrons "Article XV squadrons") from Australia, Canada and New Zealand.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald19479-31)

Africa and the Mediterranean
----------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Africa and the Mediterranean")\]

[![Image 3: Soldiers in colonial-era military uniform march with rifles shouldered.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/Coloured_Mechanical_Transport_Coy_in_Salisbury%2C_1940.jpg/250px-Coloured_Mechanical_Transport_Coy_in_Salisbury%2C_1940.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Coloured_Mechanical_Transport_Coy_in_Salisbury,_1940.jpg)

[Coloured](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloured "Coloured") and [Indian-Rhodesian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indians_in_Zimbabwe "Indians in Zimbabwe") drivers parading in Salisbury before going to East Africa, 1940

No. 237 Squadron, based in Kenya since before the start of the war, had expanded to 28 officers and 209 other ranks by March 1940.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald194733%E2%80%9335-32) By mid-1940, most of the officers and men Southern Rhodesia had sent overseas were in Kenya, attached to various East African formations, the [King's African Rifles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King%27s_African_Rifles "King's African Rifles") (KAR), the RWAFF, or to the colony's own Medical Corps or Survey Unit. The Southern Rhodesian surveyors charted the previously unmapped area bordering Abyssinia and Italian Somaliland between March and June 1940, and the Medical Corps operated No. 2 General Hospital in [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi") from July.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald194787%E2%80%9391-33) A company of coloured and Indian-Rhodesian transport drivers was also in the country, having arrived in January.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald194733%E2%80%9335-32)

The first Southern Rhodesian contingent despatched to North Africa and the Middle East was a draft of 700 from the Rhodesia Regiment who left in April 1940. No white Rhodesian force of this size had ever left the territory before.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald194751-34) They were posted to a variety of British units across Egypt and Palestine.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald194752%E2%80%9354-35) The largest concentration of Rhodesian soldiers in North Africa belonged to the [King's Royal Rifle Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King%27s_Royal_Rifle_Corps "King's Royal Rifle Corps") (KRRC), whose connections with the colony dated back to World War I. Several Rhodesian platoons were formed in the KRRC's 1st Battalion in the Western Desert.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947278%E2%80%93282-36) A company of men from the Southern Rhodesian Signal Corps was also present, operating in tandem with the British [Royal Corps of Signals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Corps_of_Signals "Royal Corps of Signals").[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947117%E2%80%93120-37)

Italy joined the war on Germany's side on 10 June 1940, opening the [East African Campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_African_Campaign_/(World_War_II/) "East African Campaign (World War II)") and the [Desert War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Desert_Campaign "Western Desert Campaign") in North Africa.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947102%E2%80%93103-38) A Rhodesian-led force of irregulars from the [Somaliland Camel Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somaliland_Camel_Corps "Somaliland Camel Corps")—based in [British Somaliland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Somaliland "British Somaliland"), on the [Horn of Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horn_of_Africa "Horn of Africa")'s north coast—took part in one of the first clashes between British and Italian forces when it exchanged fire with an Italian _[banda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bands_/(Italian_Army_irregulars/) "Bands (Italian Army irregulars)")_ (irregular company) around dawn on 11 June.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald194775-39) Two days later three [Caproni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caproni "Caproni") bombers of the _[Regia Aeronautica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regia_Aeronautica "Regia Aeronautica")_ attacked [Wajir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wajir "Wajir"), one of No. 237 Squadron's forward airstrips, damaging two Rhodesian aircraft.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947102%E2%80%93103-38)

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Italian_East_Africa_%281938%E2%80%931941%29.svg/330px-Italian_East_Africa_%281938%E2%80%931941%29.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Italian_East_Africa_/(1938%E2%80%931941/).svg)

[Italian East Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_East_Africa "Italian East Africa") was bordered by [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Colony "Kenya Colony") to the south, [British Somaliland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Somaliland "British Somaliland") to the north-east, and the [Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Egyptian_Sudan "Anglo-Egyptian Sudan") to the west

[Italian forces entered British Somaliland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_conquest_of_British_Somaliland "Italian conquest of British Somaliland") from Abyssinia on 4 August 1940, overcame the garrison at [Hargeisa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hargeisa "Hargeisa"), and advanced north-east towards the capital [Berbera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berbera "Berbera"). The British force, including a platoon of 43 Rhodesians in the 2nd Battalion of the [Black Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Watch "Black Watch"), took up positions on six hills overlooking the only road towards Berbera and engaged the Italians at the [Battle of Tug Argan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tug_Argan "Battle of Tug Argan"). Amid heavy fighting, the Italians gradually made gains and by 14 August had almost pocketed the Commonwealth forces. The British retreated to Berbera between 15 and 17 August, the Rhodesians making up the left flank of the [rearguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rearguard "Rearguard"), and by 18 August had evacuated by sea. The Italians took the city and completed their conquest of British Somaliland a day later.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald194774%E2%80%9387-40)

No. 237 Squadron embarked on reconnaissance flights and supported ground assaults on Italian desert outposts during July and August 1940. Two British brigades from West Africa arrived to reinforce Kenya's northern frontier in early July—the partly Rhodesian-officered [Nigeria Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigeria_Regiment "Nigeria Regiment") joined the front at [Malindi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi "Malindi") and [Garissa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garissa "Garissa"), while a battalion of the [Gold Coast Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Coast_Regiment "Gold Coast Regiment"), also with Rhodesian commanders attached, relieved the KAR at Wajir. The British forces in East Africa adopted the doctrine of "mobile defence" that was already being used in the [Western Desert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Desert_/(North_Africa/) "Western Desert (North Africa)") in North Africa—units embarked on long, constant patrols to guard wells and deny water supplies to the Italians. The British evacuated their north forward position at Buna in September 1940, and expected an attack on Wajir soon after, but the Italians never attempted an assault. Boosted considerably by the arrival of three South African brigades during the last months of 1940, the Commonwealth forces in Kenya had expanded to three divisions by the end of the year. No. 237 Squadron was relieved by South African airmen and redeployed to the [Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Egyptian_Sudan "Anglo-Egyptian Sudan") in September.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947101%E2%80%93115-41)

Rebasing at [Khartoum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khartoum "Khartoum"), No. 237 Squadron undertook regular reconnaissance, dive-bombing and [strafing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strafing "Strafing") sorties during October and November 1940.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947115-42) Meanwhile, the Southern Rhodesian Anti-Tank Battery arrived in Kenya in October and, following a period of training, received [2-pounder guns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_QF_2-pounder "Ordnance QF 2-pounder") and joined the front at Garissa around the turn of the new year.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947157-43) No. 237 Squadron was partially re-equipped during January 1941, receiving some [Westland Lysander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westland_Lysander "Westland Lysander") Mk IIs, but most of the squadron continued operating Hardys.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947144%E2%80%93148-44)

The British forces in Kenya under General [Alan Cunningham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Cunningham "Alan Cunningham"), including Rhodesian officers and NCOs in the King's African Rifles and the Nigeria and Gold Coast Regiments, as well as the South African [1st South African Infantry Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Infantry_Division_/(South_Africa/) "1st Infantry Division (South Africa)"), advanced into Abyssinia and [Italian Somaliland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Somaliland "Italian Somaliland") during late January and February 1941, starting with the occupation of the ports of [Kismayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kismayo "Kismayo") and [Mogadishu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mogadishu "Mogadishu"). The Italians retreated to the interior.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947157%E2%80%93163-45) No. 237 Squadron meanwhile provided air support to the [4th Indian Infantry Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4th_Infantry_Division_/(India/) "4th Infantry Division (India)") and [5th Indian Infantry Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5th_Infantry_Division_/(India/) "5th Infantry Division (India)") during Lieutenant-General [William Platt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Platt "William Platt")'s offensive into [Eritrea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Eritrea "Italian Eritrea") from the Sudan, attacking ground targets and engaging Italian fighters. One of the Rhodesian Hardys was shot down near [Keren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keren,_Eritrea "Keren, Eritrea") on 7 February with the loss of both occupants. Two days later, five Italian fighters attacked a group of grounded Rhodesian aircraft at [Agordat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agordat "Agordat") in western Eritrea, and wrecked two Hardys and two Lysanders.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947144%E2%80%93148-44)

Platt's advance into Eritrea was checked during the seven-week [Battle of Keren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Keren "Battle of Keren") (February–April 1941), during which No. 237 Squadron observed Italian positions and took part in bombing raids. After the Italians retreated and surrendered, the Rhodesian squadron moved forward to [Asmara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asmara "Asmara") on 6 April, whence it embarked on bombing sorties on the port of [Massawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massawa "Massawa").[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947178%E2%80%93182-46) The same day, the Italian garrison in the Abyssinian capital [Addis Ababa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addis_Ababa "Addis Ababa") surrendered to the [11th (East Africa) Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/11th_/(East_Africa/)_Division "11th (East Africa) Division"), including many Rhodesians.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947199-47) During the [Battle of Amba Alagi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Amba_Alagi_/(1941/) "Battle of Amba Alagi (1941)"), Platt and Cunningham's forces converged and surrounded the remainder of the Italians, who were commanded by the [Duke of Aosta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Amedeo,_Duke_of_Aosta "Prince Amedeo, Duke of Aosta") at the mountainous stronghold of [Amba Alagi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amba_Alagi "Amba Alagi"). The viceroy surrendered on 18 May 1941, effectively ending the war in East Africa.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947184-48) No. 237 Squadron and the Rhodesian Anti-Tank Battery thereupon moved up to Egypt to join the war in the Western Desert.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947216-49) Some Italian garrisons continued to fight—the last surrendered only following the [Battle of Gondar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Gondar "Battle of Gondar") in November 1941.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947253-50) Until this time the partly Rhodesian-commanded Nigeria and Gold Coast Regiments remained in Abyssinia, patrolling and rounding up scattered Italian units.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947246%E2%80%93255-51) Around 250 officers and 1,000 other ranks from Southern Rhodesia remained in Kenya until mid-1943.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947252-52)

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/AfricaMap1.jpg/500px-AfricaMap1.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:AfricaMap1.jpg)

The progress of [Operation Compass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Compass "Operation Compass") and strategic locations. [Benghazi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benghazi "Benghazi") is to the north-west, [Tobruk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobruk "Tobruk") is on the coast near the map's centre, and [El Alamein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Alamein "El Alamein") is to the east.

In North Africa, Rhodesians in the [11th Hussars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/11th_Hussars "11th Hussars"), [2nd Leicesters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Leicestershire_Regiment "Royal Leicestershire Regiment"), [1st Cheshires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheshire_Regiment "Cheshire Regiment") and other regiments contributed to [Operation Compass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Compass "Operation Compass") between December 1940 and February 1941 as part of the [Western Desert Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Desert_Force "Western Desert Force") under Major-General [Richard O'Connor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_O%27Connor "Richard O'Connor"), fighting at [Sidi Barrani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sidi_Barrani "Battle of Sidi Barrani"), [Bardia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Bardia "Battle of Bardia"), [Beda Fomm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beda_Fomm "Beda Fomm") and elsewhere.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947125%E2%80%93128,_148%E2%80%93155-53) This offensive was extremely successful, with the Allies suffering very few casualties—around 700 killed and 2,300 wounded and missing—while capturing the strategic port [Tobruk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobruk "Tobruk"), over 100,000 Italian soldiers and most of [Cyrenaica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrenaica "Cyrenaica").[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947152-54) The Germans reacted by despatching the _[Afrika Korps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrika_Korps "Afrika Korps")_ under [Erwin Rommel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erwin_Rommel "Erwin Rommel") to shore up the Italian forces. Rommel led a strong counter-offensive in March–April 1941 that forced a general Allied withdrawal towards Egypt. German and Italian forces surrounded Tobruk but failed to take the largely Australian-garrisoned city, leading to the lengthy [Siege of Tobruk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Tobruk "Siege of Tobruk").[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947215%E2%80%93216,_273-55)

The Rhodesian contingents in the 11th Hussars, Leicesters, [Buffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffs_/(Royal_East_Kent_Regiment/) "Buffs (Royal East Kent Regiment)"), [Argylls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argyll_and_Sutherland_Highlanders "Argyll and Sutherland Highlanders"), [Royal Northumberland Fusiliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Northumberland_Fusiliers "Royal Northumberland Fusiliers"), [Durham Light Infantry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham_Light_Infantry "Durham Light Infantry") and [Sherwood Foresters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherwood_Foresters "Sherwood Foresters") were transferred _en masse_ to Kenya in February 1941 to join the new [Southern Rhodesian Reconnaissance Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Armoured_Corps "Rhodesian Armoured Corps"), which served in East Africa over the following year.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947155,_253%E2%80%93254-56) The Rhodesians in the 1st Cheshires moved with that regiment to Malta the same month.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947224%E2%80%93225-57) The Rhodesian Signallers were withdrawn to Cairo to form a section handling high-speed communications between Middle East Command and General Headquarters in England.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947153%E2%80%93154-58) The 2nd Black Watch, with its Rhodesian contingent, took part in the unsuccessful Allied [defence of Crete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Crete "Battle of Crete") in May–June 1941, then joined the garrison at Tobruk in August 1941.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947217%E2%80%93223,_274%E2%80%93275-59) No. 237 (Rhodesia) Squadron was re-equipped with [Hawker Hurricanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawker_Hurricane "Hawker Hurricane") the following month.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947273-60)

[![Image 6: A military vehicle in the desert with five soldiers aboard.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/Rhodesians_of_60th_KRRC_in_North_Africa%2C_1942.jpg/250px-Rhodesians_of_60th_KRRC_in_North_Africa%2C_1942.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rhodesians_of_60th_KRRC_in_North_Africa,_1942.jpg)

Southern Rhodesians with the [King's Royal Rifle Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King%27s_Royal_Rifle_Corps "King's Royal Rifle Corps") in North Africa, 1942

Rhodesians made up an integral component of the [Long Range Desert Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Range_Desert_Group "Long Range Desert Group") (LRDG), a mechanised reconnaissance and raiding unit formed in North Africa in 1940 to operate behind enemy lines. Initially made up of New Zealanders, the unit's first British and Rhodesian members joined in November 1940.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMolinari200716%E2%80%9317-61) It was reorganised several times over the next year as it expanded and by the end of 1941 there were two Rhodesian patrols: S1 and S2 Patrols, B Squadron. Each vehicle bore a Rhodesian place-name starting with "S" on the bonnet, such as "Salisbury" or "[Sabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Save_River_/(Africa/) "Save River (Africa)")".[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947267-62) From April 1941 the LRDG was based at [Kufra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kufra "Kufra") in south-eastern Libya. The Rhodesians were posted to Bir Harash, about 160 kilometres (99 mi) to the north-east of Kufra, to patrol, hold the Zighen Gap and guard against a possible Axis attack from the north. For the next four months they lived in near-total isolation from the outside world, an exception coming in July 1941 when they and a group of airmen from No. 237 Squadron celebrated [Rhodes Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes_Day "Rhodes Day") together in the middle of the Cyrenaican desert.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947267%E2%80%93270-63)

In November 1941 the British [Eighth Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighth_Army_/(United_Kingdom/) "Eighth Army (United Kingdom)"), commanded by General Cunningham, launched [Operation Crusader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Crusader "Operation Crusader") in an attempt to relieve Tobruk. The British [XXX Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XXX_Corps_/(United_Kingdom/) "XXX Corps (United Kingdom)"), led by the [7th Armoured Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7th_Armoured_Division_/(United_Kingdom/) "7th Armoured Division (United Kingdom)") ("the Desert Rats") with its Rhodesian platoons, would form the main body of attack, advancing west from [Mersa Matruh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mersa_Matruh "Mersa Matruh"), then sweeping around in a north-westerly direction towards Tobruk. The [XIII Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XIII_Corps_/(United_Kingdom/) "XIII Corps (United Kingdom)") would concurrently advance north-west and cut off Axis forces on the coast at [Sollum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sollum "Sollum") and Bardia. When signalled the Tobruk garrison would [break out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakout_/(military/) "Breakout (military)") and move south-east towards the advancing Allied forces.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947277-64) The operation was largely successful for the Allies, and the siege was broken. The Rhodesians of the LRDG took part in raids on Axis rear areas during the operation, ambushing Axis convoys, destroying Axis aircraft and pulling down telegraph poles and wires.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947267%E2%80%93270-63)

> My bloody Rhodesians were often scruffy—but clean—and they were sometimes late for briefings, but they were always swift into action and their gunnery was without equal.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBinda201273-65)

Brigadier C.E. Lucas-Phillips, reflecting on Rhodesians he commanded in the Western Desert

From late 1941 the LRDG co-operated closely with the newly formed [Special Air Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Air_Service "Special Air Service") (SAS), which also included some Rhodesians. The Rhodesian LRDG patrols transported and supported SAS troops during operations behind Axis lines. The LRDG also maintained a constant "Road Watch" along the _[Via Balbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libyan_Coastal_Highway "Libyan Coastal Highway")_ on the north coast of Libya, along which almost all Axis road traffic from [Tripoli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tripoli,_Libya "Tripoli, Libya"), the main Libyan port, had to travel east. The LRDG set up a watch post about 8 kilometres (5.0 mi) east of the Italian [Marble Arch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marble_Arch_/(Libya/) "Marble Arch (Libya)") monument, and teams of two men each recorded Axis vehicle and troop movements in shifts throughout the day and night. This information was relayed back to the British commanders in Cairo.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947267%E2%80%93270-63)

Rommel advanced east from January 1942, and won a major victory over the Eighth Army, commanded by Lieutenant-General [Neil Ritchie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Ritchie "Neil Ritchie"), at the [Battle of Gazala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Gazala "Battle of Gazala") in May–June 1942. The Axis soon thereafter captured Tobruk.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947326%E2%80%93331,_334%E2%80%93343-66) During the Axis victory at the "Retma Box"—part of the British-devised system whereby isolated, strongly fortified "boxes", each manned by a brigade group, formed the front line—and the subsequent Allied retreat, the Southern Rhodesian Anti-Tank Battery lost five men killed, nine wounded and two missing; 37 were captured.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBinda201279-67) Rommel's advance was stalled in July by the Eighth Army, now headed by General [Claude Auchinleck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Auchinleck "Claude Auchinleck"), at the [First Battle of El Alamein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Battle_of_El_Alamein "First Battle of El Alamein") in western Egypt. Two months later the Rhodesians of the LRDG took part in [Operation Bigamy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Bigamy "Operation Bigamy") (aka Operation Snowdrop), an unsuccessful attempt by the SAS and LRDG to raid [Benghazi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benghazi "Benghazi") harbour.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950356%E2%80%93357-68) The SAS raiding force, headed by Lieutenant-Colonel [David Stirling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Stirling "David Stirling"), was discovered by an Italian reconnaissance unit, prompting Stirling to turn back to Kufra.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMolinari200770%E2%80%9371-69) The Rhodesians, meanwhile, were led into impassable country by a local guide, and swiftly retreated after being attacked by German bombers.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950356%E2%80%93357-68)

Southern Rhodesian pilots played a part in the [siege of Malta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Malta_/(World_War_II/) "Siege of Malta (World War II)") during 1942. [John Plagis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Plagis "John Plagis"), a Rhodesian airman of [Greek ancestry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greeks_in_Zimbabwe "Greeks in Zimbabwe"), joined the multinational group of Allied airmen defending the strategically important island in late March and on 1 April achieved four aerial victories in an afternoon, thereby becoming the siege's first [Spitfire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supermarine_Spitfire "Supermarine Spitfire") [flying ace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_ace "Flying ace"). By the time of his withdrawal in July he had been awarded the [Distinguished Flying Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distinguished_Flying_Cross_/(United_Kingdom/) "Distinguished Flying Cross (United Kingdom)") twice.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTENichols200892-70) The British finally delivered vital supplies to Malta on 15 August with [Operation Pedestal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Pedestal "Operation Pedestal").[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTELatimer200287-71)

Back in Salisbury, the Southern Rhodesian government was coming under pressure from Britain to put its armed forces under the purview of a regional command. Huggins decided in late October 1942 to join a unified Southern African Command headed by South Africa's [Jan Smuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Smuts "Jan Smuts"). This choice was motivated by a combination of strategic concerns and geopolitical manoeuvring. Apart from considering South Africa a more appropriate partner in geographical, logistical and cultural terms, Huggins feared that the alternative—joining the British [East Africa Command](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Africa_Command "East Africa Command")—might detract from the autonomous nature of Southern Rhodesia's war effort, with possible constitutional implications. A shift in the deployment of the colony's troops duly occurred. For the rest of the war the majority of Rhodesian servicemen went into the field integrated into South African formations, prominently the [6th Armoured Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/6th_Armoured_Division_/(South_Africa/) "6th Armoured Division (South Africa)").[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlake1977234%E2%80%93235-72)

[![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/78/Rhodesians_of_60th_KRRC_in_North_Africa_fire_Bren_gun%2C_1942.jpg/330px-Rhodesians_of_60th_KRRC_in_North_Africa_fire_Bren_gun%2C_1942.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rhodesians_of_60th_KRRC_in_North_Africa_fire_Bren_gun,_1942.jpg)

A Rhodesian [Bren light machine gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bren_light_machine_gun "Bren light machine gun") team with the King's Royal Rifle Corps in the Western Desert, 1942

The decisive victory of Lieutenant-General [Bernard Montgomery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Montgomery,_1st_Viscount_Montgomery_of_Alamein "Bernard Montgomery, 1st Viscount Montgomery of Alamein")'s Eighth Army over the Germans and Italians at the [Second Battle of El Alamein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Battle_of_El_Alamein "Second Battle of El Alamein") in October–November 1942 turned the tide of the North African war strongly in favour of the Allies, and did much to revive Allied morale. The Rhodesians of the KRRC took part in the battle as part of the 7th Armoured Division under the XIII Corps, forming part of the initial thrust in the southern sector.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950359%E2%80%93367-73)

The Rhodesian Anti-Tank Battery under Major Guy Savory also fought at El Alamein, supporting the Australian [9th Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9th_Division_/(Australia/) "9th Division (Australia)") as part of the XXX Corps. The fighting around "Thompson's Post" between 1 and 3 November was some of the fiercest Rhodesians took part in during the war. Hoping to knock out the Allied anti-tank guns before counter-attacking, the Germans concentrated intense artillery fire on the Australian and Rhodesian guns before advancing 12 [Panzer IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panzer_IV "Panzer IV") tanks towards the weakest point of the Australian line. The Australian [six-pounders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_QF_6-pounder "Ordnance QF 6-pounder") had been largely disabled by the bombardment but most of the Rhodesian guns remained operational. The Rhodesian gunners disabled two Panzers and seriously damaged two more, compelling an Axis retreat, and held their position until being relieved on 3 November. One Rhodesian officer and seven other ranks were killed and more than double that number were wounded. For his actions at Thompson's Post, Sergeant J A Hotchin received the [Distinguished Conduct Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distinguished_Conduct_Medal "Distinguished Conduct Medal"); Lieutenants R J Bawden and H R C Callon won the [Military Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_Cross "Military Cross") and Trooper P Vorster the [Military Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_Medal "Military Medal").[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950363%E2%80%93367-74)

The KRRC Rhodesians were in the forefront of the Allied column pursuing the retreating Axis forces after El Alamein, advancing through Tobruk, Gazala and Benghazi before reaching [El Agheila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Agheila "El Agheila") on 24 November 1942. They patrolled around the Axis right flank until being withdrawn to [Timimi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timimi "Timimi") in December.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950366-75) [Tripoli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tripoli,_Libya "Tripoli, Libya") fell to the Eighth Army on 23 January 1943, and six days later Allied forces reached Tunisia's south-eastern frontier, where Italian and German forces manned the [Mareth Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mareth_Line "Mareth Line"), a series of fortifications built by the French in the 1930s.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950395-76)

[![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a1/Tunisia1942-1943.svg/500px-Tunisia1942-1943.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tunisia1942-1943.svg)

Strategic locations in Tunisia and Algeria

The Mareth Line constituted one of two fronts in the [Tunisia Campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunisia_Campaign "Tunisia Campaign"), the second being to the north-west, where the British [First Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Army_/(United_Kingdom/) "First Army (United Kingdom)") and American [II Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/II_Corps_/(United_States/) "II Corps (United States)"), firmly established in formerly [Vichy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vichy_France "Vichy France")\-held Morocco and Algeria following [Operation Torch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Torch "Operation Torch") in November 1942, were gradually pushing the Axis forces under [Hans-Jürgen von Arnim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans-J%C3%BCrgen_von_Arnim "Hans-Jürgen von Arnim") back towards [Tunis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunis "Tunis"). After von Arnim won a decisive victory over the Americans at the [Battle of Sidi Bou Zid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sidi_Bou_Zid "Battle of Sidi Bou Zid") in mid-February 1943, destroying over 100 US tanks, the [Eighteenth Army Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/18th_Army_Group "18th Army Group") was formed under the British General [Harold Alexander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Alexander,_1st_Earl_Alexander_of_Tunis "Harold Alexander, 1st Earl Alexander of Tunis") to co-ordinate the actions of the Allied forces on both Tunisian fronts.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950395%E2%80%93396-77)

The Eighth Army under Montgomery spent February at [Medinine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medinine "Medinine") in south-eastern Tunisia. Expecting an imminent attack by the Axis, the Eighth Army mustered every anti-tank gun it could from Egypt and Libya. The [102nd (Northumberland Hussars) Anti-Tank Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northumberland_Hussars "Northumberland Hussars"), including the Rhodesian Anti-Tank Battery under Major Savory, duly advanced west from Benghazi and reached the front on 5 March 1943. The Germans and Italians [assaulted Medinine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Medenine "Battle of Medenine") the next day, but failed to make much progress and abandoned their attack by the evening. The Rhodesian gunners, held in reserve, did not take part in the engagement but were attacked from the air. The Rhodesians of the KRRC, now under the [7th Motor Brigade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7th_Motor_Brigade_/(United_Kingdom/) "7th Motor Brigade (United Kingdom)"), moved up from Libya during early March.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950399%E2%80%93401-78) No. 237 (Rhodesia) Squadron, which had spent 1942 and the first months of 1943 in Iran and Iraq, returned to North Africa the same month, with the future Prime Minister [Ian Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Smith "Ian Smith") [in its ranks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_service_of_Ian_Smith "Military service of Ian Smith") as a Hurricane pilot.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBerlyn197850%E2%80%9354-79)

Montgomery launched his major assault on the Mareth Line, [Operation Pugilist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Mareth_Line "Battle of the Mareth Line"), on 16 March. The Rhodesian Anti-Tank Battery, operating with the [50th (Northumbrian) Infantry Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/50th_/(Northumbrian/)_Infantry_Division "50th (Northumbrian) Infantry Division"), took part. The Allies advanced at first but the weather and terrain prevented the tanks and guns from moving forward, allowing the [15th Panzer Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15th_Panzer_Division_/(Wehrmacht/) "15th Panzer Division (Wehrmacht)") to counter-attack successfully. A flanking movement by the [2nd New Zealand Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2nd_New_Zealand_Division "2nd New Zealand Division") around the right of the German forces, through the [Tebaga Gap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tebaga_Gap "Tebaga Gap"), compelled an Axis withdrawal on 27 March. The Rhodesian anti-tank gunners fought their last action in Africa at [Enfidaville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enfidha "Enfidha"), 50 kilometres (31 mi) south of Tunis, on 20 April. The KRRC Rhodesians meanwhile took part in a long outflanking march which brought them to El Arousse, 65 kilometres (40 mi) south-west of Tunis, the next day. British armour entered Tunis on 7 May 1943. The Axis forces in North Africa—over 220,000 Germans and Italians, including 26 generals—surrendered a week later.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950401%E2%80%93405-80)

By time Tunis had fallen, few Rhodesians remained with the First or Eighth Armies; most were transferring to the South African 6th Armoured Division, then in Egypt, or making their way home on leave. Out of the 300 Southern Rhodesians who had joined the KRRC in Egypt, only three officers and 109 other ranks remained at the end of the Tunisian Campaign. The Rhodesian Anti-Tank Battery retraced many of the movements it had taken during the campaign as it returned to Egypt. "Left for Matruh at 0830 hours today," one Rhodesian gunner wrote. "Camped at night on the identical spot where we camped in June 1941. It gave me a queer feeling to look back and think how many of us are missing."[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950405%E2%80%93406-81)

[![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/86/Nomos_Dodekanisou.png/250px-Nomos_Dodekanisou.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nomos_Dodekanisou.png)

[Dodecanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dodecanese "Dodecanese") islands in red

Southern Rhodesia was represented in the [Dodecanese Campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dodecanese_Campaign "Dodecanese Campaign") of September–November 1943 by the Long Range Desert Group, which was withdrawn from the North African front in March 1943. After retraining for mountain operations in Lebanon, the LRDG moved in late September to the [Dodecanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dodecanese "Dodecanese") island of [Kalymnos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalymnos "Kalymnos"), north-west of [Kos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kos "Kos") and south-east of [Leros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leros "Leros"), off the coast of south-west Turkey. In the fall-out from the [Armistice of Cassibile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armistice_of_Cassibile "Armistice of Cassibile") between Italy and the Allies, which had been concluded in the first week of September, the Allies were attempting to capture the Dodecanese so the islands could be used as bases against the German-occupied [Balkans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balkans "Balkans"). Most of the Italian forces had changed sides; the LRDG found itself in an infantry role, acting as a mobile reserve for Italian troops.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950428%E2%80%93429-82)

The Germans swiftly mobilised to expel the Allied forces and launched heavy air assaults on Kos and Leros. Without fighter support, the islands' defence was soon precarious; the LRDG and the rest of the troops on Kalymnos were withdrawn to Leros on 4 October after the Germans won the [Battle of Kos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Kos_/(1943/) "Battle of Kos (1943)"). German air assaults on Leros intensified during late October, and at dawn on 12 November 1943 the Germans attacked Leros by sea and air. During the ensuing [Battle of Leros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Leros "Battle of Leros"), the LRDG Rhodesians at Point 320, commanded by Rhodesian Captain J R Olivey, [spiked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Touch_hole "Touch hole") their position's guns and withdrew before counter-attacking and retaking the point the next day. They held that position for three more days, during which they learned that the Germans were winning the battle. On 16 November, Olivey decided that holding the point any longer was pointless and ordered his men to split up, escape by any means possible and re-assemble in Cairo. Over half of the unit reached Egypt.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950429%E2%80%93436-83)

[![Image 10](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/Rhodesian_Sherman_tank_in_Rome%2C_June_1944.jpg/250px-Rhodesian_Sherman_tank_in_Rome%2C_June_1944.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rhodesian_Sherman_tank_in_Rome,_June_1944.jpg)

A Rhodesian [Sherman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M4_Sherman "M4 Sherman") tank on the [River Tiber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/River_Tiber "River Tiber") in Rome, June 1944

The largest concentration of Southern Rhodesian troops in the [Italian Campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Campaign_/(World_War_II/) "Italian Campaign (World War II)") of 1943–45 was the group of about 1,400, mainly from the Southern Rhodesian Reconnaissance Regiment, spread across the South African 6th Armoured Division. The 11th South African Armoured Brigade, one of the 6th Division's two main components, was made up of [Prince Alfred's Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Alfred%27s_Guard "Prince Alfred's Guard"), the [Pretoria Regiment (Princess Alice's Own)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pretoria_Regiment "Pretoria Regiment") and the [Special Service Battalion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Service_Battalion "Special Service Battalion"), each of which had a Rhodesian squadron of [Sherman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M4_Sherman "M4 Sherman") tanks. The other, the 12th South African Motorised Brigade, comprised infantry—the [Witwatersrand Rifles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witwatersrand_Rifles_Regiment "Witwatersrand Rifles Regiment"), the [Natal Carbineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natal_Carbineers "Natal Carbineers") and the [Cape Town Highlanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Town_Highlanders_Regiment "Cape Town Highlanders Regiment"), the last of which had a large Rhodesian contingent. There were also two Rhodesian artillery batteries—the original Rhodesian Anti-Tank Battery and a newer unit of Rhodesian field gunners.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950474%E2%80%93478-84) After a year's training in Egypt, the division sailed to Italy in April 1944, landing towards the end of the month at [Taranto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taranto "Taranto").[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950474%E2%80%93478-84) No. 237 Squadron, now flying Spitfires, rebased to [Corsica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corsica "Corsica") the same month to operate over Italy and southern France.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950471-85)

The 6th Division moved north-west from Taranto to take its place as part of the Eighth Army alongside the [US Fifth Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_North "United States Army North"). It took part in the fourth and final Allied [assault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Diadem "Operation Diadem") of the [Battle of Monte Cassino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Monte_Cassino "Battle of Monte Cassino") in the second and third weeks of May 1944, helping to force the Germans out, and thereafter advanced north-west up the [Liri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liri "Liri") valley to join the Allied [forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Shingle "Operation Shingle") at [Anzio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anzio "Anzio") and advance onwards to Rome.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950478%E2%80%93489-86) After wiping out a small German force about 50 km (31 mi) east of the Italian capital on 3 June, the 6th Division advanced north and captured the town of [Paliano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paliano "Paliano"), then doubled back to the south-west and moved on Rome, which was reached on the morning of 6 June.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950531%E2%80%93532-87) A Squadron, Pretoria Regiment—that unit's squadron of Rhodesian tanks—entered the city as part of the division's [vanguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanguard "Vanguard").[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950532-88)

The German commander [Albert Kesselring](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Kesselring "Albert Kesselring") fought a stubborn delaying action, gradually withdrawing his armies north with three Allied columns in pursuit, the 6th Armoured Division leading the most westerly spearhead of the Eighth Army in the centre. The mountainous terrain and the effective use of anti-tank weapons by the retreating Germans made the Allies' superiority in armour less decisive and slowed the Allied advance north to the banks of the [Arno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arno "Arno") between June and August 1944, during which time the Rhodesian tank squadrons took part in Allied victories at [Castellana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civita_Castellana "Civita Castellana"), [Bagnoregio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civita_di_Bagnoregio "Civita di Bagnoregio") and [Chiusi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiusi "Chiusi").[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950532%E2%80%93561-89)

[![Image 11](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/25pounderripoli.jpg/330px-25pounderripoli.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:25pounderripoli.jpg)

A Rhodesian [25-pounder gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_QF_25-pounder "Ordnance QF 25-pounder") in action at [Ripoli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bagno_a_Ripoli "Bagno a Ripoli"), late 1944

By the end of August 1944 the German forces in Italy had formed the [Gothic Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_Line "Gothic Line") along the [Apennine Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apennine_Mountains "Apennine Mountains"), and the 6th Division had come under the command of the US Fifth Army. The difficulty of using tanks in the mountains led to the Rhodesians of Prince Alfred's Guard temporarily adopting an infantry role, using dismounted tank machine-guns to support the Natal Carabineers during the fighting for [Pistoia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pistoia "Pistoia") during early September. The Southern Rhodesian Anti-Tank Battery meanwhile converted partially from guns to [4.2-inch mortars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_ML_4.2_inch_Mortar "Ordnance ML 4.2 inch Mortar"). The South Africans and Rhodesians met with fierce resistance from the [16th SS Panzer Grenadier Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/16th_SS_Panzergrenadier_Division_Reichsf%C3%BChrer-SS "16th SS Panzergrenadier Division Reichsführer-SS"), but helped push the Germans northwards towards the [Reno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reno_/(river/) "Reno (river)") river.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950587%E2%80%93592-90)

Hoping to repel Allied advances towards [Bologna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bologna "Bologna"), the Germans took up positions on Monte Stanco overlooking the main roads towards the city. Two Allied assaults on the mountain—one by an Indian battalion, the other by the Royal Natal Carabineers—were repulsed. A third, larger attack at dawn on 13 October provided the Rhodesian Company of the Cape Town Highlanders with some of the fiercest combat they encountered in Italy. Advancing up the slope on the Allied right flank while being fired on from two directions, they suffered heavy casualties but achieved their objective and held it. Both Rhodesian artillery batteries provided support during the assault.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950592%E2%80%93597-91)

When the line stabilised in November 1944, the portion occupied by the 6th Armoured Division extended for 16 kilometres (9.9 mi) along the heights over the Reno River. The Rhodesians of the Cape Town Highlanders patrolled nightly around the village of Casigno for the next three months.[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950601-92) Some of the tank crews, including the Rhodesians of the Special Service Battalion, were temporarily reassigned to infantry duties to assist in these patrols.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950621-93) Many of the Rhodesians had never seen snow before, but on the whole they adapted well, taking up winter sports such as skiing during time off duty.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950622-94) The Rhodesians of the Special Service Battalion received new, more heavily armed tanks in November–December 1944. In February 1945 the 6th Division was relieved by the American [1st Armoured Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Armored_Division_/(United_States/) "1st Armored Division (United States)") and moved to [Lucca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucca "Lucca"), 15 kilometres (9.3 mi) north of [Pisa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pisa "Pisa"), for rest and reorganisation.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950624%E2%80%93625-95) The Rhodesian Anti-Tank Battery was refitted with [M10 tank destroyers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M10_tank_destroyer "M10 tank destroyer").[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950636%E2%80%93637-96) The Spitfires of No. 237 Squadron, meanwhile, took part in assaults on German transport in the [Po Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Po_Valley "Po Valley") around [Parma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parma "Parma") and [Modena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modena "Modena").[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950633%E2%80%93634-97)

After the Battle of Leros, New Zealand withdrew its squadron from the Long Range Desert Group, compelling the LRDG to reorganise itself into two squadrons of eight patrols each. A Squadron was composed of Rhodesians and B Squadron comprised British troops and a squadron of signallers; around 80 of the officers and men were from Southern Rhodesia. The group was reassigned from the Middle East Command to the Central Mediterranean Force in early 1944, and deployed to the [Gargano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gargano "Gargano") peninsula in south-eastern Italy, where a new LRDG headquarters was set up near the seaside town of [Rodi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodi_Garganico "Rodi Garganico"). Britain hoped to compel the Germans to commit as many divisions as possible to south-eastern Europe so they could not be used on the more important fronts closer to Germany. In June 1944 the LRDG was assigned to operate on the coast of [Yugoslavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yugoslavia "Yugoslavia"), with orders to set up observation posts, report the movements of German ships and undertake minor raids.[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950526%E2%80%93527-98)

[![Image 12](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/Axis_occupation_of_Yugoslavia_1943-44.png/330px-Axis_occupation_of_Yugoslavia_1943-44.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Axis_occupation_of_Yugoslavia_1943-44.png)

[Yugoslavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yugoslavia "Yugoslavia") partitioned under Axis occupation, 1943–44

The successes of [Josip Broz Tito](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josip_Broz_Tito "Josip Broz Tito")'s [Yugoslav partisans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yugoslav_partisans "Yugoslav partisans") in [Dalmatia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dalmatia "Dalmatia") led the Allies to despatch small patrols into Yugoslavia and Albania to contact partisan leaders and arrange co-operation with the Allied air forces. Several Rhodesian patrols from the LRDG were selected to undertake such missions during August and September 1944. Yugoslav partisans subsequently indicated targets for Allied bombing missions, with some success.[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950527%E2%80%93531-99) From September, members of the LRDG's Rhodesian squadron under Captain Olivey undertook advanced reconnaissance in the [Peloponnese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peloponnese "Peloponnese") peninsula of southern Greece. Landing at [Katakolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katakolo "Katakolo"), they made their way inland to [Corinth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corinth "Corinth") and, along with the British [4th Parachute Battalion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4th_Battalion,_Parachute_Regiment "4th Battalion, Parachute Regiment"), entered [Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens "Athens") as the Germans departed in November. The Rhodesians of the LRDG spent November and December helping Greek forces to garrison an Athens orphanage against supporters of the communist [Greek People's Liberation Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_People%27s_Liberation_Army "Greek People's Liberation Army"). Four Rhodesians were killed.[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950627-100)

The LRDG returned to Yugoslavia in February 1945, operating around [Istria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istria "Istria") and Dalmatia, where Germany still held portions of the mainland and certain strategic islands. The Germans had heavily mined the southern Adriatic and were attempting to cover their shipping by moving only by night, close to shore, and heaving to during the day under camouflage nets. The LRDG was tasked to patrol the coast, find the ships and report their locations to the air force for bombing. This it did with success. It remained in Yugoslavia for the rest of the war.[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950627%E2%80%93629-101)

The heightened vigilance of the German garrison as the war entered its final phase made these operations especially hazardous, particularly as they were often attempted at extremely close quarters. On several occasions Rhodesian patrols only narrowly escaped discovery. During one action, two Rhodesian patrols catered for the possibility that Germans might be listening to their transmissions by communicating in [Shona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shona_language "Shona language"), an African language.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950629%E2%80%93631-102) The LRDG's last actions of the war, in April and May 1945, were to help Tito's partisans capture German-held islands off Dalmatia.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950632-103)

### Spring 1945 offensive in Italy

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Spring 1945 offensive in Italy")\]

Kesselring's forces in Italy retained their formidable defensive positions in the northern Apennines in March 1945. The 6th Division rejoined the line in early April, shortly before the Allies launched their [spring 1945 offensive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spring_1945_offensive_in_Italy "Spring 1945 offensive in Italy"), Operation Grapeshot. The units including Rhodesians took up positions opposite Monte Sole, Monte Abelle and Monte Caprara. The Rhodesian [25-pounder guns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_QF_25-pounder "Ordnance QF 25-pounder") were posted slightly forward of their former positions, and B (Rhodesia) Squadron, Prince Alfred's Guard, moved to [Grizzana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grizzana_Morandi "Grizzana Morandi"). The Special Service Battalion provided armoured support to the 13th South African Motorised Brigade.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950636%E2%80%93637-96)

The South Africans and Rhodesians launched a two-pronged assault on the German positions over the road to [Bologna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bologna "Bologna") at 22:30 on 15 April 1945. The Cape Town Highlanders' advance up the steep cliffs of Monte Sole was obstructed by a German minefield that guarded the peak. The Rhodesian officer commanding the leading platoon, Second Lieutenant G B Mollett, took a section of men and dashed through the minefield to the summit; for this he later received the [Distinguished Service Order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distinguished_Service_Order "Distinguished Service Order"). Hand-to-hand fighting on Monte Sole continued until dawn, when the Germans withdrew. The Witwatersrand Rifles meanwhile took Monte Caprara. The Cape Town Highlanders took Monte Abelle late on 16 April, advancing under heavy artillery fire to the summit before clearing it of Germans. The regiment lost 31 killed and 76 wounded during these actions, including three Rhodesians killed and three wounded.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950638%E2%80%93640-104)

This victory contributed to a general Allied breakthrough in the area, and by 19 April, the 6th Division's armour was moving towards [Lombardy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lombardy "Lombardy") and [Venetia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veneto "Veneto") as part of the Fifth Army's vanguard. American and Polish troops entered Bologna on 21 April. The South Africans and Rhodesians advanced north-west towards the [Panaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panaro_/(river/) "Panaro (river)") river. The Special Service Battalion's Rhodesian squadron, moving forward alongside the Cape Town Highlanders, and the Rhodesians of Prince Alfred's Guard took part in numerous engagements with the retreating German [rearguard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rearguard "Rearguard"), and suffered several fatalities.[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950640%E2%80%93644-105)

The 6th Division crossed the [Po](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Po_/(river/) "Po (river)") near [Ostiglia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ostiglia "Ostiglia") on 25 April and, after resupplying for a week, began a speedy advance towards [Venice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice "Venice"), aiming to cut off the retreat of elements of the German [Fourteenth Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/14th_Army_/(Wehrmacht/) "14th Army (Wehrmacht)"). The South Africans and Rhodesians advanced through [Nogara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nogara "Nogara") and [Cerea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerea "Cerea"), crossed the [Adige](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adige "Adige") early on 29 April, and then made for [Treviso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treviso "Treviso"), 19 kilometres (12 mi) north of Venice. The retreating German forces were by this time in such disarray that, during its advance from the Po, the 11th South African Armoured Brigade took prisoners from eight German divisions. On 30 April, the 6th Division joined up with British and American forces south of Treviso, and cut off the Germans' last escape route from Italy.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950643%E2%80%93645-106)

The German forces in Italy surrendered unconditionally on 2 May 1945, while the 6th Division was moving north-west; at the time of the announcement it was near [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan "Milan"). Twelve days later the 6th Division held a victory parade of its 1,200 guns, tanks and other vehicles at [Monza racetrack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autodromo_Nazionale_Monza "Autodromo Nazionale Monza"), 16 kilometres (9.9 mi) north of Milan. The Rhodesians separated from their vehicles after the parade, then spent May and June 1945 as occupation troops in Lombardy before returning home.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947643%E2%80%93645-107)[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOrpen1975309-108)

Britain, Norway and western Europe
----------------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Britain, Norway and western Europe")\]

[![Image 13](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f5/The_Royal_Air_Force_in_Britain%2C_29_September_1942_TR197.jpg/330px-The_Royal_Air_Force_in_Britain%2C_29_September_1942_TR197.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Royal_Air_Force_in_Britain,_29_September_1942_TR197.jpg)

[Lancaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avro_Lancaster "Avro Lancaster") bombers of [No. 44 (Rhodesia) Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._44_Squadron_RAF "No. 44 Squadron RAF"), based on the east coast of England, September 1942

Southern Rhodesia's fighting contributions in Britain and western Europe were primarily in the air, as part of the much larger Allied forces. Rhodesian pilots and Allied airmen trained in the colony's flying schools participated in the defence of Britain throughout the war, as well as in the [strategic bombing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_bombing_during_World_War_II "Strategic bombing during World War II") of Germany and other operations. Rhodesia provided the only RAF flying ace of the [Norwegian Campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwegian_Campaign "Norwegian Campaign") of April–June 1940, Squadron Leader [Caesar Hull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caesar_Hull "Caesar Hull").[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEThomas200229,_32-109) Later that year "[The Few](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Few "The Few")", the Allied airmen of the [Battle of Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Britain "Battle of Britain"), included three pilots of Southern Rhodesian birth—Hull, Pilot Officer John Chomley and Flight Lieutenant John Holderness[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTESalt2001187-110)—of whom two, Hull and Chomley, lost their lives.[\[f\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-113)

Two of the RAF's three Rhodesian squadrons, Nos. 44 and 266, operated from England during the war. No. 266 (Rhodesia) Squadron, a fighter squadron based in [Cambridgeshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridgeshire "Cambridgeshire") for most of the duration, was initially only nominally Rhodesian, being manned by a mixture of British and Commonwealth personnel, but it received more airmen from the colony gradually and was virtually all Rhodesian by August 1941.[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947230%E2%80%93231-114) Initially flying Spitfires, it switched to [Typhoons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawker_Typhoon "Hawker Typhoon") in early 1942.[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947312-115) It took as its motto the [Sindebele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ndebele_language "Northern Ndebele language") word _Hlabezulu_ ("Stabber of Skies") and first went into action over [Dunkirk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dunkirk "Dunkirk") on 2 June 1940,[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald194760-116) after which it fought in the Battle of Britain. The squadron's duties thereafter included patrolling, protecting convoys, sweeping around northern France and the Belgian and Dutch coasts, and escorting bombing raids over France and the [Rhine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhine "Rhine").[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947312-115)

No. 44 (Rhodesia) Squadron, based in [Lincolnshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lincolnshire "Lincolnshire") on the east coast, was a heavy bomber unit, and part of No. 5 Group in [RAF Bomber Command](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Bomber_Command "RAF Bomber Command")'s front line.[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTELake200281-117) Unlike the other two squadrons designated as "Rhodesian", No. 44 Squadron never had a Rhodesian majority, despite efforts to so populate it.[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTELake200282-118) Initially equipped with [Hampdens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Handley_Page_Hampden "Handley Page Hampden"), it became the first RAF squadron to convert to [Lancasters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avro_Lancaster "Avro Lancaster") at the end of 1941. It played a prominent part in the [attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombing_of_Augsburg_in_World_War_II "Bombing of Augsburg in World War II") on the [MAN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MAN_SE "MAN SE") diesel factory at [Augsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augsburg "Augsburg") in April 1942.[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTELake200282-118) In March 1943 No. 44 Squadron took part in the Allied bombing of cities in northern Italy, including [Genoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genoa "Genoa") and Milan, as well as targets in Germany such as [Wilhelmshaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelmshaven "Wilhelmshaven"), [Cologne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cologne "Cologne") and [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin").[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950386%E2%80%93391-119)

[![Image 14: Three men stand next to a fighter aircraft and look at it.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/Huggins_visits_No._266_%28Rhodesia%29_Squadron%2C_May_1944_b.jpg/250px-Huggins_visits_No._266_%28Rhodesia%29_Squadron%2C_May_1944_b.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Huggins_visits_No._266_/(Rhodesia/)_Squadron,_May_1944_b.jpg)

Huggins _(right)_ inspecting a Typhoon of [No. 266 (Rhodesia) Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._266_Squadron_RAF "No. 266 Squadron RAF") in England, 1944

From early 1944, No. 266 Squadron took part in ground attack operations over the Channel and northern France, operating from [RAF Harrowbeer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Harrowbeer "RAF Harrowbeer") in Devon. The squadron also escorted Allied bombers embarking on or returning from raids, protecting them from German fighters. Larger petrol tanks were fitted to the Typhoons to increase their range. In May 1944 the squadron was visited by the Prime Minister, who had been knighted and was now Sir Godfrey Huggins.[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950453%E2%80%93459-120) Over the next month, in preparation for the imminent Allied [invasion of Normandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invasion_of_Normandy "Invasion of Normandy"), the Rhodesian aircraft took on a fighter-bomber role, flying sorties across the channel twice a day and participating in the bombing of bridges, roads, railways and the like.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950517%E2%80%93519-121)

Apart from the Southern Rhodesian airmen serving with the RAF in Britain, the colony was sparsely represented in the [Normandy landings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normandy_landings "Normandy landings") of 6 June 1944 ("D-Day"). Several men from the colony served aboard cruisers and destroyers that engaged the German shore batteries. A small number of Southern Rhodesians parachuted into Normandy with the [6th Airborne Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/6th_Airborne_Division_/(United_Kingdom/) "6th Airborne Division (United Kingdom)") during [Operation Tonga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Tonga "Operation Tonga"), and some took part in the amphibious landings. No. 266 Squadron was part of the Allied force that flew over the beaches during the first landings, supporting the infantry. Later that day it took part in sorties to assist the paratroopers holding the bridgeheads north of [Caen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caen "Caen").[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950519%E2%80%93521-122)
