No. 266 Squadron, which remained 95% Rhodesian at the start of 1945,[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950612-123) thereafter provided air support to the advancing Allied armies through France, the [Low Countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Countries "Low Countries") and finally Germany. Through most of the European winter months it was based in [Antwerp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antwerp "Antwerp"). In late March 1945 the Rhodesian fighters formed part of the force tasked with protecting the descending Allied paratroopers during Field-Marshal Montgomery's crossing of the Rhine. During April the squadron operated over [Hanover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanover "Hanover") and the northern Netherlands.[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950611%E2%80%93614-124) No. 44 Squadron, meanwhile, embarked on bombing raids on targets as far away as [Gdynia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gdynia "Gdynia") and [Königsberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6nigsberg "Königsberg") in [East Prussia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Prussia "East Prussia"), as well as towns and cities closer to Berlin such as [Dresden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dresden "Dresden"), [Emden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emden "Emden") and [Leipzig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leipzig "Leipzig"). Its last bombing operation was a raid on the [Berghof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berghof_/(residence/) "Berghof (residence)"), Hitler's residence, near [Berchtesgaden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berchtesgaden "Berchtesgaden") in Bavaria on 25 April 1945. After [Germany surrendered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_instrument_of_surrender "German instrument of surrender") on 7 May, [ending the war in Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End_of_World_War_II_in_Europe "End of World War II in Europe"), No. 44 Squadron was one of many units selected to evacuate British prisoners of war home from the continent.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950614%E2%80%93620-125)

[![Image 15: A raft on a river. A man with a rifle stands in the centre, surrounded by other men kneeling on one knee.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f6/RAR_Burma_1.jpg/500px-RAR_Burma_1.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:RAR_Burma_1.jpg)

A [Rhodesian African Rifles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_African_Rifles "Rhodesian African Rifles") river patrol in [Burma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burma_Campaign "Burma Campaign"), 1945

Southern Rhodesia's main contribution to the [Burma Campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burma_Campaign "Burma Campaign") in terms of manpower was made by the [Rhodesian African Rifles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_African_Rifles "Rhodesian African Rifles") (RAR), a regiment of black troops led by white officers that joined the front at the end of 1944. The colony also made a significant contribution to the Commonwealth forces' command element in Burma, providing white officers and NCOs to the [81st (West Africa)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/81st_/(West_Africa/)_Division "81st (West Africa) Division"), [82nd (West Africa)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_/(West_Africa/)_Division "82nd (West Africa) Division") and 11th (East Africa) Divisions, made up of units from Nigeria, the Gold Coast, the Gambia, Sierra Leone, Kenya, Uganda, Tanganyika, Nyasaland, Northern Rhodesia and the Congo.[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950570-126) Almost every African battalion in Burma had white Rhodesian officers and NCOs attached; some were over 70% Rhodesian-led.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBinda201247-23)

Modelled on the Rhodesia Native Regiment of World War I, the RAR was formed in May 1940 under the command of Lieutenant-Colonel F J Wane, who the black soldiers nicknamed _msoro-we-gomo_ ("top of the mountain"). Most volunteers for the regiment came from [Mashonaland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mashonaland "Mashonaland"), much to the surprise of the white recruiters, who had expected [Matabeleland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matabeleland "Matabeleland"), with stronger martial traditions, to provide more men.[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBinda200741%E2%80%9345-127)[\[g\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-129) Originally comprising one battalion, the RAR expanded to two battalions in late 1943 to accommodate a rush of new recruits following the news that the 1st Battalion was being deployed overseas.[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBinda200748-130) Steps to organise two further battalions of black Southern Rhodesians were abandoned because of the conviction of the colony's overall military commander, Brigadier E R Day, that it was important "to preserve a fair balance" between black and white troops, and that raising the men would take too long in any case.[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950442%E2%80%93443-131)[\[h\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-133)

[![Image 16: Men sit against a wall, clearly tired. Some are sleeping.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ed/RAR_Burma_2.jpg/500px-RAR_Burma_2.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:RAR_Burma_2.jpg)

1RAR troops in Burma, resting in a dugout

1RAR trained in Kenya from December 1943 to September 1944, when it transferred to [Ceylon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceylon "Ceylon") and became part of the 22nd (East Africa) Infantry Brigade alongside the 1st KAR and the 3rd [Northern Rhodesia Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Rhodesia_Regiment "Northern Rhodesia Regiment"). In December 1944, after three months' training for jungle warfare, 1RAR and the other two components of the brigade joined the Burma Campaign at [Chittagong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chittagong "Chittagong") under the command of the [15th Indian Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XV_Corps_/(India/) "XV Corps (India)").[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBinda200748%E2%80%9349,_59-134) The brigade spent about three months supporting the [25th Indian Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/25th_Infantry_Division_/(India/) "25th Infantry Division (India)") in north-western Burma, advancing through the Mayu peninsula during January 1945 and taking part in the latter stages of the [Battle of Ramree Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Ramree_Island "Battle of Ramree Island"), landing on the island on 14 February. 1RAR fortified positions at Myinbin, Kyaukkale and Mayin but did not contact Japanese forces.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBinda200759-135)

A widespread belief developed among Japanese troops in Burma that the British Army's African soldiers were cannibals,[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBinda200773-136) partly because of deliberate disinformation spread by the black troops themselves as they travelled around the country.[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStapleton2011188-137) While entirely unfounded, the notion "that we Africans eat people", as one RAR soldier put it,[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStapleton2011188-137) had a fearsome psychological effect; men of 1RAR reported Japanese soldiers picking up their comrades' bodies in the midst of battle and running away.[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStapleton2011188-137)

In March 1945 the 22nd Brigade was ordered south to Dalaba where it became part of the 82nd (West Africa) Division, which had been tasked with clearing the Taungup area of Japanese troops. The 22nd Brigade was deployed as a flank guard, sweeping down the Tanlwe Chaung before hooking around to the Taungup Chaung and ultimately the road to [Prome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyay "Pyay"); this move was intended to cut Japanese units to the north off from the [Irrawaddy Delta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irrawaddy_Delta "Irrawaddy Delta") to the south, where most of the key battles were being fought. 1RAR patrolled the area during March and April 1945 and was involved in several contacts. On 20 April it assembled at a point overlooking Tanlwe Chaung, where it was shelled by Japanese artillery and mortars dug in atop two high features to the south.[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBinda200760%E2%80%9365-138) On the morning of 26 April, after a few days of patrols, 1RAR took the lead in what became the [Battle of Tanlwe Chaung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tanlwe_Chaung "Battle of Tanlwe Chaung"); after about half an hour of bombing, strafing and artillery bombardment of the Japanese positions, elements of A and D Companies, 1RAR charged up the slopes and routed much of the Japanese garrison before taking both hills. Seven RAR men were killed in the action and 22 were wounded, mostly from D Company; an officer was also injured.[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBinda200765%E2%80%9368-139)[\[i\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-141) An officer of the RAR recalled the battles of April 1945 around Taungup and Tanlwe Chaung as extremely intense:

> The way our fellows charged their way along these paths, yelling, makes a lump come into my throat when I think of it even now. It was sheer suicide for the leading group and the whole force faced machine guns up the sides of the slopes above them, on the sides of the features behind them, and even up the trees above them, with snipers behind who let them pass before opening fire. For sheer cold-blooded bravery, I can't believe it has ever been beaten in any other theatre of war; and this went on for three weeks solid.[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStapleton2011190-142)

1RAR spent most of May 1945 building quarters and training before marching the 110 km (68 mi) to Prome in late June; from here they went another 25 km (16 mi) by truck to [Gyobingauk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyobingauk "Gyobingauk"). The [monsoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monsoon "Monsoon") conditions took a dreadful toll on operations, making logistics particularly difficult and slow—men found themselves either found themselves knee-deep in mud or slipping around on the surface. From early July 1945 1RAR patrolled around Gyobingauk, repeatedly engaging parties of Japanese and forcing them into the hills. Even after the Japanese commanders in Burma surrendered unconditionally, the Allied troops had to continue patrolling to handle Japanese stragglers who either did know of this or did not believe it. After the Japanese forces in South-East Asia formally surrendered at Singapore on 12 September 1945, active Allied operations in the region were greatly diminished.[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBinda200771%E2%80%9373-143) 1RAR spent about half a year guarding Japanese prisoners in Burma before leaving for home in March 1946. They arrived back in Salisbury on 10 May.[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBinda200773%E2%80%9377-144)

Southern Rhodesians in other theatres
-------------------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Southern Rhodesians in other theatres")\]

In addition to the main deployments, Southern Rhodesian servicemen served in other theatres of the war. Rhodesian sailors in the [Royal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy"), [South African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_Navy "South African Navy") and [Merchant Navies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merchant_Navy_/(United_Kingdom/) "Merchant Navy (United Kingdom)") crewed ships in many parts of the world, including the [Indian Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Ocean_in_World_War_II "Indian Ocean in World War II"), the [Arctic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arctic_convoys_of_World_War_II "Arctic convoys of World War II") and the [Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_War "Pacific War").[\[136\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947289%E2%80%93297-145)[\[137\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950391%E2%80%93395-146) No. 237 (Rhodesia) Squadron operated in Iran and Iraq in 1942–43, guarding oil wells and pipelines and supporting the British [Tenth Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenth_Army_/(United_Kingdom/) "Tenth Army (United Kingdom)").[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBerlyn197850%E2%80%9354-79)

Closer to home, Southern Rhodesian military surveyors contributed to the preliminary planning work for the Allied [invasion of Madagascar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Madagascar "Battle of Madagascar") in May 1942, and landed at [Diego Suarez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antsiranana "Antsiranana") with the invading forces. They remained there long after the Vichy French garrison agreed to an armistice at [Ambalavao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambalavao "Ambalavao") on 6 November 1942—the last Rhodesian left the island in October 1943.[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947298%E2%80%93299-147)

### Rhodesian Air Training Group

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Rhodesian Air Training Group")\]

[![Image 17](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7b/Commonwealth_Joint_Air_Training_Plan%2C_No_20_Service_Flying_Training_School%2C_Cranborne%2C_Near_Salisbury%2C_Rhodesia%2C_January_1943_TR1265.jpg/250px-Commonwealth_Joint_Air_Training_Plan%2C_No_20_Service_Flying_Training_School%2C_Cranborne%2C_Near_Salisbury%2C_Rhodesia%2C_January_1943_TR1265.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Commonwealth_Joint_Air_Training_Plan,_No_20_Service_Flying_Training_School,_Cranborne,_Near_Salisbury,_Rhodesia,_January_1943_TR1265.jpg)

A trainee pilot climbing into a [Harvard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_American_T-6_Texan "North American T-6 Texan") at No. 20 Service Flying Training School near Salisbury, 1943

The colony's participation in the Empire Air Training Scheme is described in J F MacDonald's _War History of Southern Rhodesia_ as "undoubtedly Southern Rhodesia's greatest single contribution to the Allied victory",[\[139\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950607-148) an assertion corroborated by [Robert Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Blake,_Baron_Blake "Robert Blake, Baron Blake") in his 1977 _History of Rhodesia_.[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlake1977234-149) The Rhodesian Air Training Group (RATG) under Air Vice-Marshal Sir C W Meredith eventually operated [11 aerodromes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_British_Commonwealth_Air_Training_Plan_facilities_in_Southern_Rhodesia "List of British Commonwealth Air Training Plan facilities in Southern Rhodesia"), requiring a huge national effort to build, maintain and staff—at the scheme's peak more than a fifth of the white population was involved.[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlake1977234-149) This judicious management of skills and resources allowed the territory to make a much larger contribution to the Allied war effort than if it had simply sent all its manpower into the field.[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947172-150)

Southern Rhodesia was regarded as an ideal location for air training for a number of reasons. It was far from the hostilities, firmly pro-British and had excellent weather throughout the year.[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlake1977234-149) The British Air Ministry resolved to outsource training to the colony amid some urgency in late 1939 after EATS took a long time to get going in Canada.[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith1973-151) The RATG was the last EATS group to be formed, but the first to start training airmen; it also turned out fully qualified pilots before any of the others, doing so for the first time in November 1940.[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947172-150)

The programme originally called only for an initial training wing and six schools, but this was expanded to eight flying schools and a school for bomb aimers, navigators and air gunners. There were two air firing and bombing ranges. Six reserve landing grounds were constructed for landing and take-off instruction to prevent congestion on the main airstrips. Later in the war, a dedicated air station was designated for the training of instructors. Small administrative units were established in South Africa at [Cape Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Town "Cape Town"), [Durban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durban "Durban") and [Port Elizabeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Elizabeth "Port Elizabeth") to handle incoming equipment and arrivals and departures of personnel.[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith1973-151)

The complete pilot's course initially lasted six months, split into two months each of elementary, intermediate and advanced instruction. Ground subjects were also taught and each trainee had to fly at least 150 hours to qualify. By the end of the war each period had been shortened by a week to speed up the output of trained pilots.[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald194792%E2%80%9393-152)

The trainees were mostly British, but came from all over the world. "The diversity of nationalities under training was surprising and impressive," reported one officer. "British, South African, New Zealand, Australian, Canadian, American, men from Yugoslavia, Greece, Free France, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Kenya, Uganda, Tanganyika, Fiji Isles, Malta."[\[144\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947173-153) "\[Southern Rhodesia's\] part in the Commonwealth Air Training Scheme has been outstandingly fine," Sir James Ross of the British Air Ministry reported in 1942. "I say this from knowledge and without qualification. ... I know how gratefully the Air Staff in London reckon on the unfailingly regular flow of well-trained pilots and observers, course after course, month after month."[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950367-154)

[![Image 18](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Rhodesian_African_Rifles_Salisbury_1941.jpg/500px-Rhodesian_African_Rifles_Salisbury_1941.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rhodesian_African_Rifles_Salisbury_1941.jpg)

The 1st Battalion, RAR parades in Salisbury for [Armistice Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armistice_Day "Armistice Day"), 1941

The Rhodesian African Rifles were based at [Borrowdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borrowdale,_Harare "Borrowdale, Harare") in north-east Salisbury between 1940 and 1943.[\[146\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStapleton201196%E2%80%9397-155) Apart from a contingent sent south to Durban to guard Italian prisoners on their way to Rhodesia, the regiment's main role was garrison duties within the colony.[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKillingray201266-128) The Rhodesian Air Askari Corps, a unit of black volunteer troops under white command, guarded the air bases and also provided manpower for non-armed labour.[\[j\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-157) The perceived possibility that Japan might attempt an invasion of southern Africa via Madagascar led to the consolidation of a few hundred rural whites into the Southern Rhodesia Commando, a part-time cadre intended as the basis for a guerrilla-style resistance movement, from 1942.[\[148\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTERadford199482-158)

The mobilisation of white British South Africa Police officers for military service led to black male and white female constables taking on higher responsibilities.[\[k\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-160) The BSAP recruited more black patrolmen to accommodate the growth of the urban black population during the war, going from 1,067 black and 547 white personnel in 1937 to 1,572 blacks and 401 whites in 1945.[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStapleton20115,_39-161) This "[Africanisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africanisation "Africanisation")" led to higher appreciation for black constables among senior policemen and the public. The police remained rigidly segregated, but black constables received uniforms more similar to those of their white counterparts,[\[151\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStapleton2011156-162) and the nominal distinction between the BSAP "proper" and the British South Africa Native Police—the "force within the force" black personnel were traditionally regarded as members of—was abolished.[\[152\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStapleton20116-163)

White Southern Rhodesian women served in the war with auxiliary female units, in far greater numbers than in World War I. The Southern Rhodesian government set up the Women's Auxilitary Volunteers (WAV), the Women's Auxiliary Air Service (WAAS), the Women's Auxiliary Military Service (WAMS) and the Women's Auxiliary Police Service (WAPS).[\[153\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947240%E2%80%93242-164) Most Southern Rhodesian servicewomen served domestically within these organisations, while some went to East Africa with the [First Aid Nursing Yeomanry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Aid_Nursing_Yeomanry "First Aid Nursing Yeomanry").[\[154\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947135-165)

[![Image 19](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3a/Rhodesian_Women%27s_Auxiliary_Air_Service%2C_folding_parachute.jpg/250px-Rhodesian_Women%27s_Auxiliary_Air_Service%2C_folding_parachute.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rhodesian_Women%27s_Auxiliary_Air_Service,_folding_parachute.jpg)

A Rhodesian servicewoman folding and packing a parachute

[![Image 20](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/Rhodesian_Women%27s_Military_Auxiliary_Service%2C_December_1941.jpg/250px-Rhodesian_Women%27s_Military_Auxiliary_Service%2C_December_1941.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rhodesian_Women%27s_Military_Auxiliary_Service,_December_1941.jpg)

The Rhodesian Women's Military Auxiliary Service on parade in Salisbury in December 1941

The WAV, run by the Ministry of Defence, recruited and trained female personnel for the WAAS and the WAMS, which respectively came under the Air and Defence Ministries. According to the official statement announcing their formation, the services' purpose was "to substitute women for men wherever necessary and practicable throughout the military and air forces within Southern Rhodesia."[\[153\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947240%E2%80%93242-164)

Recruitment for the women's services began in June 1941. Most volunteers were married women, many of them the wives of military men. The air and military services both offered a wide variety of positions. In addition to jobs as typists, clerks, caterers and the like, women served as drivers and in the stores and workshops. Many of the women in the air service did skilled work, checking flying instruments, testing parts and doing minor repairs. The women of the Auxiliary Police Service served as BSAP officers both in stations and on the streets.[\[155\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947240%E2%80%93241-166)

Members of Southern Rhodesia's white female population who did not join the forces still contributed to the war in various ways. Women worked in munitions factories and engineering workshops in Salisbury and [Bulawayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulawayo "Bulawayo").[\[156\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947242-167) The Women's National Service League, which thousands of women joined before the war even started, revived the role white Rhodesian women had played in World War I, sending the colony's servicemen overseas parcels containing warm clothes, newspapers, razor blades, soap, food and minor luxuries such as sweets, tobacco and novels. Efforts such as these did much to keep the troops' morale up.[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1947100-168)

On the outbreak of war, Huggins invited the leader of the opposition [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Labour_Party "Rhodesian Labour Party"), [Harry Davies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Davies_/(politician/) "Harry Davies (politician)"), to join a [coalition government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coalition_government "Coalition government"). Davies accepted without consulting his party caucus, much to the indignation of many of his contemporaries; Labour promptly split. The two Labour factions reconciled in 1943 and briefly threatened Huggins's premiership until a heated dispute over whether Labour should become multiracial led to the party's disintegration in 1944.[\[158\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlake1977235%E2%80%93237-169)

### Economic impact; conscripted labour

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Economic impact; conscripted labour")\]

> The enemy wants _you_ to slacken off ... _You_ have a responsibility ... Southern Rhodesia's war effort may be small in comparison with that of Russia, Britain, the United States and the big dominions, but its value is none the less real.[\[159\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950447%E2%80%93448-170)

Extract from an Office of Information newsletter, late 1943

The Southern Rhodesian economy grew considerably during the war despite the concurrent rise of war expenditure to pay for the expansion of the military and the air training scheme. Expenditure on the war grew from £1,793,367 in the financial year 1940–41 to £5,334,701 in 1943–44[\[160\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950379-171)—total Southern Rhodesian expenditure on the air training scheme was £11,215,522.[\[l\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-172) These sums, while tiny compared to those incurred by larger nations, were enormous when scaled against the white population of less than 70,000 that accounted for most of the colony's economic output.[\[160\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950379-171) Annual costs for the air training scheme alone far exceeded the pre-war national budget.[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith1973-151)

Southern Rhodesia was then the second largest gold producer in the world, after South Africa.[\[161\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDumett1985398%E2%80%93399-173) The colony's gold output had expanded greatly during the 1930s, and it remained the territory's main source of income during the war, though many extracting operations were diverted towards strategic minerals, most prominently [chrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium "Chromium") and [asbestos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asbestos "Asbestos"). Southern Rhodesia became one of the two main sources of chrome for the Allies (South Africa was the other) and the world's third largest producer of asbestos after Canada and the Soviet Union.[\[161\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDumett1985398%E2%80%93399-173) By the end of the war the mines at [Shabani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zvishavane "Zvishavane") and [Mashaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mashava "Mashava") were turning out 1.5 million tonnes of asbestos a year, in addition to 600,000 tonnes of chrome.[\[162\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950379%E2%80%93380,_604%E2%80%93605-174) Gold output reached peak levels in 1941–42 and thereafter subsided.[\[161\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDumett1985398%E2%80%93399-173) Southern Rhodesia also exported [tungsten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tungsten "Tungsten"), [mica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mica "Mica") and [tin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tin "Tin"), and provided coal for the copper mines of Northern Rhodesia and the Congo.[\[162\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950379%E2%80%93380,_604%E2%80%93605-174) The Southern Rhodesian government encouraged private enterprise to form [secondary industries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secondary_sector_of_the_economy "Secondary sector of the economy") to exploit the colony's natural resources and increase production, but also set up some state industries in an attempt to spark growth.[\[163\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950382-175) The establishment of the RATG prompted a minor economic boom, and also caused the primary direct demand placed on Southern Rhodesia's black population during the early stages of the war—a programme of [conscripted labour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_conscription "Civil conscription") to build the aerodromes.[\[164\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVickery1989425-176)

The government assigned labour quotas for each district to native commissioners across the territory who in turn called on local chiefs and headmen to provide workers. The tribal leaders decided who was required at the [kraal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kraal "Kraal") and who would report to the district native commissioner for work.[\[165\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVickery1989425%E2%80%93426-177) This system, known locally as the _chibaro_, _cibbalo_, _isibalo_ or _chipara_—according to [Charles van Onselen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_van_Onselen "Charles van Onselen"), synonymous etymologically with concepts ranging from contract labour to slavery—had been relatively widespread during [Company rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Company_rule_in_Rhodesia "Company rule in Rhodesia") (1890–1923), but had fallen out of use by the 1930s.[\[166\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVickery1989424-178) Some tribal communities were resettled to make room for the airstrips.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVickery1989427-19)

The _chibaro_ workers received pay and provisions, but the salary of 15[s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shilling "Shilling")/- per month compared unfavourably with the 17s/6[d](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_/(British_pre-decimal_coin/) "Penny (British pre-decimal coin)") generally received on white-owned farms. It met with widespread opposition, with many men electing to run away rather than join the work parties. "Hundreds if not thousands", according to Kenneth Vickery, crossed into [Bechuanaland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bechuanaland_Protectorate "Bechuanaland Protectorate") or South Africa to avoid the call-up.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVickery1989427-19) Some suspected that after finishing the conscripted aerodrome work, they might be drafted to fight overseas. Rumours to this effect abounded enough that the chief native commissioner, H H D Simmonds, distributed a circular in November 1940 instructing the commissioners to make clear that the drafted men were required for labour only.[\[m\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-180)

Voluntary employment increased sharply during 1940 and 1941, both among indigenous blacks and migrant labourers, but many white farmers still complained about a lack of manpower.[\[168\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVickery1989427%E2%80%93428-181) A severe drought during the 1941–42 season led to a food shortage in the colony, prompting the passing in June 1942 of the Compulsory Native Labour Act, under which unemployed black males between 18 and 45 years of age could be conscripted for work on white-owned farms. Announcing the act, Tredgold—by now Minister of Native Affairs in addition to Defence and Justice—commented that its "principle ... would be intolerable under ordinary circumstances", but that the war made it necessary.[\[169\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVickery1989428-182) The act required each draftee to work at least three months at 15s/- per month; the pay rose to 17s/6 if he agreed to stay a further three months.[\[n\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-183) This conscription of labour contributed to the rise in the country's overall agricultural yield, but had a negative impact on the localised production of many kraals, either because too many men had been drafted for work elsewhere or because they had fled to avoid it. The scheme continued until the act's repeal in 1946.[\[170\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVickery1989428%E2%80%93431-184)

A central Food Production Committee, set up in early 1942, organised the conscripted labourers and attempted to help the white farmers to grow all the crops they could.[\[170\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVickery1989428%E2%80%93431-184) Maize production grew by 40% between 1942 and 1944, the potato harvest doubled and the onion crop grew sixfold by the end of the war. Production of the colony's most important cash crop, tobacco, was high throughout the war, averaging about 40 million pounds (18 million kg) annually.[\[171\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950380%E2%80%93381,_604%E2%80%93605-185) The number of cattle slaughtered by the beef industry increased by 134%, from 71,000 head in 1937 to 160,000 head in 1945.[\[172\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTESamasuwo2003494-186) [Vegetable dehydration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drying_/(food/) "Drying (food)"), one of the Food Production Committee's main initiatives, proved a great success, allowing Rhodesia to export many products to the UK that would previously have spoiled in transit.[\[171\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950380%E2%80%93381,_604%E2%80%93605-185) Southern Rhodesia also provided goods to the [Eastern Group Supply Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Group_Supply_Council "Eastern Group Supply Council"), a body set up in 1940 to co-ordinate the build-up of war materiel in India and other British colonies and dominions east of Suez, with the goal of reducing the amount of supplies shipped from the UK. A Rhodesian officer, Brigadier E G Cook, was the group's deputy controller general. Between 1941 and 1945 Southern Rhodesia contributed large quantities of timber, leather goods, soap and building materials.[\[173\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950605%E2%80%93606-187)

### Internment camps and Polish refugees

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Internment camps and Polish refugees")\]

Thousands of Axis POWs and people described as "enemy aliens" were held in Southern Rhodesia during the conflict. These were mainly Italians and Germans, but there were also a handful from Iraq and the Levant; the colony furthermore hosted nearly 7,000 refugees from Poland.[\[174\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950380%E2%80%93383-188) Britain delegated responsibility for co-ordinating investigation into enemy aliens in central Africa to the Southern Rhodesian government, which set up a system whereby the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) identified potential detainees while a body called the Internment Camps Corps oversaw the camps. Many of those held in Southern Rhodesia were sent there by Britain or authorities elsewhere in the Empire.[\[175\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTERupiah1995-189)

Five internment camps were set up in two waves. No. 1 (General) Internment Camp opened to the north-east of Salisbury in October 1939 and No. 2 (Tanganyika) Internment Camp, just south of the city, opened the following year, mostly housing Germans formerly resident in Tanganyika.[\[175\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTERupiah1995-189) The first two camps together had less than 800 inmates.[\[174\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950380%E2%80%93383-188) The third, fourth and fifth camps were set up near [Gatooma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kadoma,_Zimbabwe "Kadoma, Zimbabwe"), [Umvuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mvuma "Mvuma") and [Fort Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masvingo "Masvingo") in 1941–42 to accommodate roughly 5,000 Italians from Somaliland and Abyssinia. The Internment Camps Corps' reliance on the elderly, the infirm and so-called "friendly aliens" to staff the three new camps led to indiscipline, poor living conditions and dozens of escapes. A 1943 government commission into the quality of the internment camps reported the second wave camps to be of far worse quality than those of the first wave.[\[175\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTERupiah1995-189)

Polish refugees were housed at dedicated [settlements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_civilian_camps_in_World_War_II "Polish civilian camps in World War II") set up at [Marandellas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marondera "Marondera") and [Rusape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rusape "Rusape"), two towns about 40 km (25 mi) apart to the south-east of Salisbury, from 1943.[\[o\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-190) There were similar camps in Kenya, Nyasaland, Tanganyika, Northern Rhodesia and South Africa. The Polish settlements in Southern Rhodesia were run jointly by local authorities and the Polish consulate in Salisbury; the [Polish government-in-exile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_government-in-exile "Polish government-in-exile") in London provided funding. Transport back to Europe picked up sharply as the war came to a close, and by October 1945 less than 2,000 Polish refugees remained.[\[175\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTERupiah1995-189) Colonial officials were reluctant to let the Poles stay indefinitely, asserting that they were not culturally British enough and might have communist connections or sympathies,[\[176\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTETavuyanagoaMugutiaHlongwana2012-191) but most of those who remained showed little inclination to leave. Southern Rhodesia ultimately allowed around 726 Polish refugees to settle permanently after the war.[\[175\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTERupiah1995-189)

[![Image 21](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fe/Allied_Victory_Parade_in_London%2C_1946_H42784.jpg/330px-Allied_Victory_Parade_in_London%2C_1946_H42784.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Allied_Victory_Parade_in_London,_1946_H42784.jpg)

South African and Southern Rhodesian contingents marching in the London [Victory Parade of 1946](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victory_Celebrations_of_1946 "London Victory Celebrations of 1946")

Along with most of the Commonwealth and Allied nations, Southern Rhodesia sent a delegation of soldiers, airmen and seamen to London to take part in the grand [Victory Parade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Victory_Celebrations_of_1946 "London Victory Celebrations of 1946") of 8 June 1946. The colony's contingent, led by Colonel R E B Long,[\[177\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBinda200781-192) marched after South Africa and before Newfoundland. The Southern Rhodesian [colour guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_guard "Color guard") comprised a white officer and two black sergeants of the Rhodesian African Rifles.[\[178\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBinda200789-193) During the royal visit to Southern Rhodesia in April 1947, [King George VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_VI "George VI") accorded the prefix "Royal" to the Rhodesia Regiment in recognition of its contributions to the two World Wars, and agreed to be its [Colonel-in-Chief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonel-in-Chief "Colonel-in-Chief").[\[179\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBinda2012119-194)

Southern Rhodesia had contributed more manpower to the Allied cause in World War II, proportional to white population, than any other British dominion or colony, and more than the UK itself.[\[180\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMoorcraft1990-195) According to figures compiled by MacDonald for his _War History of Southern Rhodesia_, 26,121 Southern Rhodesians served in the armed forces during the conflict, of whom 2,758 were commissioned officers. Broken down by race and gender, there were 15,153 black men, 9,187 white men, 1,510 white women and 271 coloured and Indian men. Of the 8,390 who served outside the territory, 1,505 were black men, 6,520 were white men, 137 were white women and 228 were coloured or Indian men.[\[181\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950appx._p._i-196)

According to official figures, 33,145 black Southern Rhodesians were conscripted for labour between 1943 and 1945; Vickery estimates that between 15,000 and 60,000 more may have worked on the aerodromes.[\[182\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVickery1989431-197) According to Ashley Jackson's work _The British Empire and the Second World War_, the Rhodesian Air Training Group instructed 8,235 Allied pilots, navigators, gunners, ground crew and others—about 5% of overall EATS output.[\[p\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-199)

A total of 2,409 Southern Rhodesians (977 officers and 1,432 other ranks) served in the RAF during the war, 373 (86 officers and 287 ratings) joined the Royal Navy, and 13 officers and 36 ratings from Southern Rhodesia mustered into the South African Navy. The vast majority of the rest served in either the Southern Rhodesian territorial forces or the British or [South African Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_Army "South African Army"). The colony's men and women received 698 decorations during the war; whites received 689 while black troops won nine. No coloured or Indian serviceman was decorated. Army officers won 269 decorations while the other ranks received 158; the air force officers and other ranks respectively won 184 and 72 decorations. All eight decorated Southern Rhodesian naval personnel were officers. Of the seven decorated women, all but one held commissioned rank.[\[181\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950appx._p._i-196) Two hundred and fifty-three Southern Rhodesians were [mentioned in despatches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mentioned_in_despatches "Mentioned in despatches") during the war.[\[184\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950appx._p._viii-200)

MacDonald records 916 Southern Rhodesian fatalities from enemy action during World War II—498 airmen, 407 ground troops, eight seamen and three female personnel—and 483 wounded, of whom 434 were soldiers, 47 were airmen and two were sailors.[\[181\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMacDonald1950appx._p._i-196)

The Rhodesian Air Training Group, widely accepted as the colony's main contribution to World War II, proved to be "one of the most important happenings in Rhodesian history", in the words of its commander Air Vice-Marshal Sir C W Meredith, as it led to great economic development and a large wave of immigration after the war by former instructors, trainees and other staff.[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith1973-151) This contributed to the swelling of Southern Rhodesia's white population to 135,596, over double its pre-war size, by 1951.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWeinrich197315-4)[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeredith1973-151) RAF training operations in the country were stepped down considerably after the war, and the project formally ended in March 1954.[\[185\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTESalt2001309-201)

The strengthening of ties with South Africa continued following the war as both countries underwent considerable industrialisation. Between 1948 and 1953 Southern Rhodesia and South Africa operated a customs agreement under which most export and import duties were waived.[\[186\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPhimister1991430%E2%80%93440-202) The decade immediately following 1945 has been called "the moment when Southern Rhodesia's economy 'took off'".[\[187\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPhimister1991430-203) Huggins, secure in office at the end of the war, remained Prime Minister for another decade afterwards, and oversaw the colony's [Federation with Northern Rhodesia and Nyasaland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland "Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland") in 1953. He retired in 1956.[\[188\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlake1977269,_294-204) Southern Rhodesia [contributed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesian_military_involvement_in_the_Malayan_Emergency "Southern Rhodesian military involvement in the Malayan Emergency") to several Commonwealth counter-insurgency operations during the 1950s and early 1960s, including the [Malayan Emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malayan_Emergency "Malayan Emergency"),[\[189\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBinda2007127%E2%80%93140,_404-205) similar actions in [Aden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colony_of_Aden "Colony of Aden") and Cyprus, and [Operation Vantage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Vantage "Operation Vantage") in Kuwait.[\[190\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTECorum2008172-206)

[![Image 22](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Montgomery_inspects_Royal_Rhodesia_Regiment_guard_of_honour%2C_1947.jpg/500px-Montgomery_inspects_Royal_Rhodesia_Regiment_guard_of_honour%2C_1947.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Montgomery_inspects_Royal_Rhodesia_Regiment_guard_of_honour,_1947.jpg)

Field Marshal [Bernard Montgomery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Montgomery "Bernard Montgomery") inspects a [Royal Rhodesia Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia_Regiment "Rhodesia Regiment") guard of honour, 1947

Amid [decolonisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decolonisation_of_Africa "Decolonisation of Africa") and the [Wind of Change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_of_Change_/(speech/) "Wind of Change (speech)"), the Federation failed to become a [Commonwealth realm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_realm "Commonwealth realm") and collapsed in 1963.[\[188\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBlake1977269,_294-204) Two years later, following prolonged dispute with Britain over the terms for full sovereignty, the mostly white government in Southern Rhodesia (or Rhodesia, following Northern Rhodesia's independence as Zambia) issued a [Unilateral Declaration of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence "Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence") (UDI). The Rhodesian government, which had in it World War II veterans including the Prime Minister Ian Smith, attempted to emphasise Rhodesians' prior war record on Britain's behalf by declaring independence on [Armistice Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armistice_Day "Armistice Day"), 11 November, at 11:00 [local time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Africa_Time "Central Africa Time").[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMcLaughlin1980141-1)[\[191\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWood2005463,_471-207) As part of its subsequent isolation of Rhodesia, the UK government banned the post-UDI authorities from taking part in the annual Armistice Day service at [the Cenotaph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cenotaph,_Whitehall "The Cenotaph, Whitehall") in London. Smith's government organised its own Rhodesian wreath-laying ceremony there.[\[192\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYoung1969448-208) Veterans of World War II and Malaya held many key positions in the [Rhodesian Security Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Security_Forces "Rhodesian Security Forces") during the [Bush War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Bush_War "Rhodesian Bush War") of the 1970s.[\[193\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTECilliers198476-209)

After the country's reconstitution and recognised independence as Zimbabwe in 1980, [Robert Mugabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe "Robert Mugabe")'s administration pulled down many monuments and plaques making reference to the dead of the First and Second World Wars, perceiving them as reminders of white minority rule and colonialism that went against what the modern state stood for. This view was partly rooted in the association of these memorials with those commemorating the [British South Africa Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_South_Africa_Company "British South Africa Company")'s dead of the Matabele Wars, as well as those memorialising Rhodesian servicemen killed during the Bush War. Many Zimbabweans saw their nation's involvement in the World Wars as a consequence of colonial rule that had more to do with the white community than the black majority.[\[194\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStapleton20061%E2%80%935-210)

[The Cenotaph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cenotaph,_Bulawayo "The Cenotaph, Bulawayo") in Bulawayo commemorates Southern Rhodesians who served in the world wars and later conflicts, including the Bush War.[\[195\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-211)[\[196\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-212) A number of other memorials in Zimbabwe are maintained by the [Commonwealth War Graves Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_War_Graves_Commission "Commonwealth War Graves Commission").[\[197\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_II#cite_note-213)

| | Today part of | [Malawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malawi "Malawi") [Zambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambia "Zambia") [Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe "Zimbabwe") | [![Image 10](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b0/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland.png) Administrative divisions of the federation The **Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland**, also known as the **Central African Federation** (**CAF**), was a colonial [federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation "Federation") that consisted of three southern African territories: the [self-governing British colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-governing_colony "Self-governing colony") of [Southern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia "Southern Rhodesia") and the [British protectorates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_protectorate "British protectorate") of [Northern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Rhodesia "Northern Rhodesia") and [Nyasaland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyasaland "Nyasaland"). It existed between 1953 and 1963. Rhodesia and Nyasaland bordered [Angola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Angola "Portuguese Angola") (Portuguese province), [Bechuanaland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bechuanaland_Protectorate "Bechuanaland Protectorate") (British protectorate), [Congo-Léopoldville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo_/(L%C3%A9opoldville/) "Republic of the Congo (Léopoldville)") ([Belgian colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgian_Congo "Belgian Congo") before 1960), [Mozambique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Mozambique "Portuguese Mozambique") (Portuguese province), [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa"), [South West Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_West_Africa "South West Africa") (South African mandate) and [Tanganyika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanganyika_/(1961%E2%80%931964/) "Tanganyika (1961–1964)") ([British mandate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanganyika_Territory "Tanganyika Territory") before 1961). The Federation was established on 1 August 1953,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-2) with a [Governor-General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor-General_of_the_Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland "Governor-General of the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland") as the Queen's representative at the centre. The constitutional status of the three territories – a self-governing Colony and two Protectorates – was not affected, though certain enactments applied to the Federation as a whole as if it were part of Her Majesty's dominions and a Colony.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-CnC-3) A novel feature was the African Affairs Board, set up to safeguard the interests of Africans and endowed with statutory powers for that purpose, particularly in regard to discriminatory legislation.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-CnC-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-Somerville-4) The economic advantages to the Federation were never seriously called into question, and the causes of the Federation's failure were purely political: the strong and growing opposition of the African inhabitants.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-CnC-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-Somerville-4): 393  The rulers of the new black African states were united in wanting to end colonialism in Africa. With most of the world moving away from colonialism during the late 1950s and early 1960s, the United Kingdom was subjected to pressure to decolonise from both the United Nations and the [Organisation of African Unity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organisation_of_African_Unity "Organisation of African Unity") (OAU). These groups supported the aspirations of the black [African nationalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_nationalism "African nationalism") and accepted their claims to speak on behalf of the people. The federation ended on 31 December 1963.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-6) In 1964, shortly after the dissolution, Northern Rhodesia and Nyasaland became independent under the names [Zambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambia "Zambia") and [Malawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malawi "Malawi"), respectively. In November 1965, Southern Rhodesia [unilaterally declared independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence "Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence") from the United Kingdom as the state of [Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia "Rhodesia"). ### Central African Council \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland&action=edit§ion=2 "Edit section: Central African Council")\] In 1929, the [Hilton Young Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilton_Young_Commission "Hilton Young Commission") concluded that "in the present state of communications the main interests of Nyasaland and Northern Rhodesia, economic and political, lie not in association with the Eastern African Territories, but rather one another and with the self-governing Colony of Southern Rhodesia". In 1938, the [Bledisloe Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bledisloe_Commission "Bledisloe Commission") concluded that the territories would become interdependent in all their activities, but stopped short of recommending federation. Instead, it advised the creation of an inter-territorial council to coordinate government services and survey the development needs of the region. The [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War") delayed the creation of this institution until 1945, when the Central African Council was established to promote coordination of policy and action between the territories. The [Governor of Southern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Southern_Rhodesia "Governor of Southern Rhodesia") presided over the council and was joined by the leaders of the other two territories. The Council only had consultative, and not binding, powers.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-:0-7): 591 In November 1950, [Jim Griffiths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Griffiths "Jim Griffiths"), the [Secretary of State for the Colonies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_the_Colonies "Secretary of State for the Colonies"), informed the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom "House of Commons of the United Kingdom") that the government had decided that there should be another examination of the possibility of a closer union between the Central African territories, and that a conference of the respective governments and the Central African Council was being arranged for March 1951. While many points of contention were worked out in the conferences that followed, several proved to be acute, and some, seemingly insurmountable. The negotiations and conferences were arduous. Southern Rhodesia and the Northern Territories had very different traditions for the 'Native Question' (black Africans) and the roles they were designed to play in civil society.\[[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-8) An agreement would likely not have been reached without [Sir Andrew Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Cohen_/(statesman/) "Andrew Cohen (statesman)"), CO Assistant Undersecretary for African Affairs (and a later [Governor of Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Uganda "Governor of Uganda")). He became one of the central architects and driving forces behind the creation of the Federation, often seemingly singlehandedly untangling deadlocks and outright walkouts on the part of the respective parties. Cohen, who was [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jew "Jew") and traumatised by [The Holocaust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Holocaust "The Holocaust"), was an anti-racialist and an advocate of African rights. But he compromised his ideals to avoid what he saw as an even greater risk than the continuation of the paternalistic white ascendancy system of Southern Rhodesia – its becoming an even less flexible, radical [white supremacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_supremacy "White supremacy"), like the [National Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Party_/(South_Africa/) "National Party (South Africa)") government in South Africa. [Lord Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Blake,_Baron_Blake "Robert Blake, Baron Blake"), the [Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_University "Oxford University")\-based historian, wrote: "In that sense, [Apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartheid "Apartheid") can be regarded as the father of Federation".[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-9) The Commons approved the conferences' proposals on 24 March 1953, and in April passed motions in favour of federating the territories of Northern Rhodesia and Nyasaland. A [referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Referendum "Referendum") was held in Southern Rhodesia on 9 April.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-:0-7): 592  Following the insistence and reassurances of the Southern Rhodesian prime minister, [Sir Godfrey Huggins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Godfrey_Martin_Huggins,_1st_Viscount_Malvern "Godfrey Martin Huggins, 1st Viscount Malvern"), a little more than 25,000 [white Southern Rhodesians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_people_in_Zimbabwe "White people in Zimbabwe") voted in the referendum for a federal government, versus nearly 15,000 against.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-10) A majority of [Afrikaners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrikaner "Afrikaner") and black Africans in all three territories were resolutely against it.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-Farmers1-11)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-Shaw-12) The Federation came into being when the [Parliament of the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_the_United_Kingdom "Parliament of the United Kingdom") enacted the Rhodesia and Nyasaland Federation Act, 1953. The Act authorised [the Queen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_of_the_United_Kingdom "Queen of the United Kingdom"), by way of an [Order in Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_in_Council "Order in Council"), to provide for the federation of the three constituent territories. This order was made on 1 August 1953, bringing certain provisions of the Constitution into operation. The first Governor-General, [Lord Llewellin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Llewellin,_1st_Baron_Llewellin "John Llewellin, 1st Baron Llewellin"), assumed office on 4 September. On 23 October 1953, Llewellin issued a proclamation bringing the remainder of the provisions of the Constitution into operation.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-:0-7): 591 The semi-independent federation was finally established, with five branches of government: one Federal, three Territorial, and one British. This often translated into confusion and jurisdictional rivalry among various levels of government. According to Lord Blake, it proved to be "one of the most elaborately governed countries in the world."[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-13) The Constitution provided for a federal government with enumerated powers, consisting of an executive government, a unicameral Federal Assembly (which included a standing committee known as the African Affairs Board), and a Supreme Court, among other authorities. Provision was made for the division of powers and duties between the federal and territorial governments. Article 97 of the Constitution empowered the Federal Assembly to amend the Constitution, which included a power to establish a second legislative chamber.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-14) The Governor-General would be the representative of the Queen in the Federation. Federal authority extended only to those powers assigned to the federal government and to matters incidental to them. The enumerated federal powers were divided into a "Federal Legislative List" for which the federal legislature could make laws, and a "Concurrent Legislative List" for which both the federal and territorial legislatures could make law.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-:0-7): 593  Federal laws prevailed over territorial laws in all cases where the federal legislature was empowered to legislate, including the concurrent list. The executive government consisted of the [Governor-General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor-General_of_the_Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland "Governor-General of the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland"), who would represent the Queen, an Executive Council consisting of the [prime minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_the_Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland "Prime Minister of the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland") and nine other ministers appointed by the Governor-General on recommendation from the Prime Minister, and a Cabinet of ministers appointed by the Prime Minister. The judiciary consisted of a Supreme Court, later regulated by the Federal Supreme Court Act, 1955, which consisted of the Chief Justice, two federal justices, and the chief justices of each of the three constituent territories of the Federation. The court was inaugurated on 1 July 1955, when the Governor-General swore in the Chief Justice and the other judges. The ceremony was also attended by the [Lord High Chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Chancellor "Lord Chancellor") and the [Chief Justice of the Union of South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Justice_of_South_Africa "Chief Justice of South Africa").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-:0-7): 595  The Chief Justices were [Sir Robert Tredgold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Tredgold "Robert Tredgold"), previously [Chief Justice of Southern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_Justice_of_Southern_Rhodesia "Chief Justice of Southern Rhodesia"), who was Chief Justice of the Federation from 1953 to 1961, and [Sir John Clayden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Clayden "John Clayden"), from 1961 to 1963. The Supreme Court's jurisdiction was limited chiefly to hearing appeals from the high courts of the constituent territories. The court, however, had original jurisdiction over the following: * Disputes between the federal government and territorial governments, or between territorial governments _inter se_, if such disputes involved questions (of law or fact) on which the existence or extent of a legal right depended; * Matters affecting vacancies in the Federal Assembly and election petitions; and * Matters in which a writ or order of [mandamus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandamus "Mandamus"), or prohibition or an [injunction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Injunction "Injunction"), is sought against an officer or authority of the federal government.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-:0-7): 596  In 1958, the Prime Minister established an Office of Race Affairs which reviewed policies, practices and activities which may have hampered or adversely affected a climate favourable to the federal government's equal "partnership" policy. On 1 April 1959, the Prime Minister appointed the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Home Affairs, who held the status of a full minister, to assume responsibility for racial affairs. [![Image 11](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/74/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland_map_1960.jpg/250px-Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland_map_1960.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland_map_1960.jpg) A map of the Federation, with the [Southern Rhodesian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia "Southern Rhodesia") capital of [Salisbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harare "Harare") doubled as the federal capital It was commonly understood that Southern Rhodesia would be the dominant territory in the federation – economically, electorally, and militarily. How much so defined much of the lengthy constitutional negotiations and modifications that followed. African political opposition and [nationalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_nationalism "African nationalism") aspirations, for the time, were moot.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-auto-15) Decisive factors in both the creation and dissolution of the Federation were the significant difference between the number of Africans and Europeans in the Federation, and the difference between the number of Europeans in Southern Rhodesia compared to the Northern Protectorates. Compounding this was the significant growth in Southern Rhodesia's European settler population (overwhelmingly British migrants), unlike in the Northern Protectorates. This was to greatly shape future developments in the Federation. In 1939, approximately 60,000 Europeans resided in Southern Rhodesia; shortly before the Federation was established there were 135,000; by the time the Federation was dissolved they had reached 223,000 (though newcomers could only vote after three years of residency). Nyasaland showed the least European and greatest African population growth.\[[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-16) The dominant role played by the Southern Rhodesian European population within the CAF is reflected in that played by its first leader, Sir Godfrey Huggins (created [Viscount Malvern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viscount_Malvern "Viscount Malvern") in February 1955), Prime Minister of the Federation for its first three years and, before that, [Prime Minister of Southern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Southern_Rhodesia "Prime Minister of Southern Rhodesia") for an uninterrupted 23 years. Huggins resigned the premiership of Southern Rhodesia to take office as the federal prime minister, and was joined by most [United Rhodesia Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Rhodesia_Party "United Rhodesia Party") cabinet members. There was a marked exodus to the more prestigious realm of federal politics. The position of Prime Minister of Southern Rhodesia was once again, as under Britain's Ministerial Titles Act of 1933, reduced to a Premier and taken by [The Rev.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Reverend "The Reverend") [Garfield Todd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garfield_Todd "Garfield Todd"), the soon-to-be controversial [centre-left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre-left "Centre-left") politician. It was considered that Todd's position and territorial politics in general had become relatively unimportant, a place for the less ambitious politician. In fact, it was to prove decisive both to the future demise of the CAF, and to the later rise of the [Rhodesian Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Front "Rhodesian Front").\[[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-auto-15) Rather than a federation, Prime Minister Huggins favoured an amalgamation, creating a unitary state. However, after the Second World War, Britain opposed this because Southern Rhodesia would dominate the property and income franchise (which excluded the vast majority of Africans) owing to its much larger European population. A federation was intended to curtail this.\[[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-17) Huggins was thus the first prime minister from 1953 to 1956, and was followed by [Sir Roy Welensky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Welensky "Roy Welensky"), a prominent Northern Rhodesian politician, from 1956 to the Federation's dissolution in December 1963. The fate of the Federation was contested within the [British Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Government "British Government") by two principal [Ministries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_/(government_department/) "Ministry (government department)") of [the Crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Crown "British Crown") in deep ideological, personal and professional rivalry – the [Colonial Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonial_Office "Colonial Office") (CO) and the [Commonwealth Relations Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Relations_Office "Commonwealth Relations Office") (CRO) (and previously with it the [Dominion Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominion_Office "Dominion Office"), abolished in 1947). The CO ruled the northern territories of Nyasaland and Northern Rhodesia, while the CRO was formally but indirectly in charge of Southern Rhodesia. The northern territories opposed a Southern Rhodesian hegemony, one that the CRO promoted. Significantly, the CO tended to be more sympathetic to African rights than the CRO, which tended to promote the interests of the Southern Rhodesian (and to a lesser extent, Northern Rhodesian) European settler populations.\[[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-18) In 1957, this led to calls by Welensky for the creation of a single department with responsibility for all three territories, with Macmillan also favouring the CRO assuming sole responsibility for them, but was persuaded by the Cabinet Secretary that this would face opposition from both Africans and members of the colonial service in the northern territories.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-19) Consequently, in 1962, the Federation's affairs were transferred to a new department, known as the Central Africa Office, with [Rab Butler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rab_Butler "Rab Butler") the minister responsible.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-20) However, this was to be short lived, as following the succession of Macmillan as prime minister by [Alec Douglas-Home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alec_Douglas-Home "Alec Douglas-Home"), responsibility for the Federation was returned to the CRO and CO, with [Duncan Sandys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duncan_Sandys "Duncan Sandys") responsible for both.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-21) It was convenient to have all three territories colonised by [Cecil Rhodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Rhodes "Cecil Rhodes") under one constitution. But, for Huggins and the Rhodesian establishment, the central economic motive behind the CAF (or amalgamation) was the abundant copper deposits of Northern Rhodesia. Unlike [the Rhodesias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rhodesias "The Rhodesias"), Nyasaland had no sizeable deposits of minerals and its tiny community of Europeans, largely [Scottish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_people "Scottish people"), was relatively sympathetic to African aspirations. Its inclusion in the Federation was more a symbolic gesture than a practical necessity. This inclusion would eventually work against the CAF: Nyasaland and its African population was where the impetus for destabilisation of the CAF arose, leading to its dissolution.\[[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Rhodesia_and_Nyasaland#cite_note-22)
