election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1962_Southern_Rhodesian_general_election "1962 Southern Rhodesian general election").[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-rowe52-49) However, much of the white community saw Whitehead as too radical, and soft on what they saw as black extremism. As a result, the UFP was soundly defeated in the primarily white seats by the [Rhodesian Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Front "Rhodesian Front") (RF), a newly formed alliance of conservative voices headed by [Winston Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Field "Winston Field") and Ian Smith, in what was widely considered a shock result.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood97101-50) Field became Prime Minister, with Smith as his deputy.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood119122-51)

### Federal dissolution; the roots of mistrust

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Federal dissolution; the roots of mistrust")\]

Meanwhile, secessionist black Rhodesian parties won electoral victories in Northern Rhodesia and Nyasaland,[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood119122-51) and [Harold Macmillan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Macmillan "Harold Macmillan")'s [Conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_/(UK/) "Conservative Party (UK)") administration in Britain moved towards breaking up the Federation, resolving that it had become untenable. In February 1962, the British [Secretary of State for Commonwealth Relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Commonwealth_Relations "Secretary of State for Commonwealth Relations"), [Duncan Sandys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duncan_Sandys "Duncan Sandys"), secretly informed the Nyasaland nationalist leader [Hastings Banda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hastings_Banda "Hastings Banda") that secession would be allowed. A few days later, he horrified Welensky by telling him that "we British have lost the will to govern".[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-52) "But we haven't", retorted [Julian Greenfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_Greenfield "Julian Greenfield"), Welensky's Law Minister.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-53)[\[n 7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-vomited-55) Macmillan's [Deputy Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Prime_Minister_of_the_United_Kingdom "Deputy Prime Minister of the United Kingdom") and [First Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Secretary_of_State "First Secretary of State"), [R. A. Butler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rab_Butler "Rab Butler"), who headed British oversight of the Federation,[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-56) officially announced Nyasaland's right to secede in December 1962.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood123-24) Four months later, he informed the three territories that he was going to convene a conference to decide the Federation's future.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood133135-57)

As Southern Rhodesia had been the UK's legislative partner in forming the Federation in 1953, it would be impossible (or at least very difficult) for Britain to dissolve the union without Southern Rhodesia's co-operation. Field could therefore potentially hamstring the British by refusing to attend the conference until they pledged to grant his country full independence.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood133135-57) According to Field, Smith and other RF politicians, Butler made several such guarantees orally to ensure their co-operation at the conference, but repeatedly refused to give anything on paper.[\[n 8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-promise-59) The Southern Rhodesians claimed that Butler justified his refusal to give a written promise by saying that binding Whitehall to a document rather than his word would be against the Commonwealth's "spirit of trust"—an argument that Field eventually accepted.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-butlerpromise-58) "Let's remember the trust you emphasised", Smith warned, according to Field's account wagging his finger at Butler; "if you break that you will live to regret it."[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood167-60) Southern Rhodesia attended the conference, which was held at Victoria Falls over a week starting from 28 June 1963, and among other things it was agreed to formally liquidate the Federation at the end of the year.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood169172-61) In the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom "House of Commons of the United Kingdom") afterwards, Butler flatly denied suggestions that he had "oiled the wheels" of Federal dissolution with secret promises to the Southern Rhodesians.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-butlerpromise-58)

Field's government was startled by Britain's announcement in October 1963 that Nyasaland would become fully independent on 6 July 1964. While no date was set for Northern Rhodesian statehood, it was generally surmised that it was going to follow shortly thereafter. Smith was promptly sent to London, where he held a round of inconclusive Southern Rhodesian independence talks with the new British Prime Minister, Sir [Alec Douglas-Home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alec_Douglas-Home "Alec Douglas-Home").[\[n 9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-douglashome-63) Around the same time, the presence and significance of Section 111 of the 1961 constitution emerged in Southern Rhodesia, prompting speculation in political circles that a future British government might, if it were so inclined, go against previous conventions by legislating for Salisbury without its consent, withdrawing devolved powers or otherwise altering the Southern Rhodesian constitution. Fearing what the [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_/(UK/) "Labour Party (UK)") might do if it won the next British general election (which was projected for late 1964), the Southern Rhodesians stepped up their efforts, hoping to win independence before Britain went to the polls, and preferably not after Nyasaland.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood186190-64) The Federation dissolved as scheduled at the end of 1963.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood186190-64)

Positions and motivations
-------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Positions and motivations")\]

### British government stance

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: British government stance")\]

The British government's refusal to grant independence to Southern Rhodesia under the 1961 constitution was largely the result of the geopolitical and moral shifts associated with the [Wind of Change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wind_of_Change_/(speech/) "Wind of Change (speech)"), coupled with the UK's wish to avoid opprobrium and loss of prestige in the United Nations (UN) and the Commonwealth.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-mcwilliam-65) The issue gained international attention in Africa and worldwide as a flashpoint for questions of decolonisation and racism.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-66) By the early 1960s, general consensus in the post-colonial UN—particularly the [General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly "United Nations General Assembly"), where the [communist bloc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Bloc "Eastern Bloc") and the [Afro-Asian lobby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian%E2%80%93African_Conference "Asian–African Conference") were collectively very strong—roundly denounced all forms of colonialism, and supported communist-backed black nationalist insurgencies across southern Africa, regarding them as racial liberation movements. Amid the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War"), Britain opposed the spread of [Soviet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") and Chinese influence into Africa, but knew it would become an international pariah if it publicly expressed reservations or backed down on NIBMAR in the Southern Rhodesia question.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-67) Once the topic of Southern Rhodesia came to the fore in the UN and other bodies, particularly the [Organisation of African Unity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organisation_of_African_Unity "Organisation of African Unity") (OAU), even maintaining the _status quo_ became regarded as unacceptable internationally, causing the UK government a great deal of embarrassment.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-68)

In the Commonwealth context, too, Britain knew that simply granting independence to Southern Rhodesia was out of the question as many of the Afro-Asian countries were also Commonwealth members. Statehood for Salisbury without majority rule would split the Commonwealth and perhaps cause it to break up, a disastrous prospect for British foreign policy.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-mcwilliam-65) The Commonwealth repeatedly called on Britain to intervene directly should Southern Rhodesian defiance continue,[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-69) while liberals in Britain worried that if left unchecked Salisbury might drift towards South African-style [apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartheid_in_South_Africa "Apartheid in South Africa").[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-cunningham-70) Anxious to avoid having to choose between Southern Rhodesia and the Commonwealth, Whitehall attempted to negotiate a middle way between the two, but ultimately put international considerations first, regarding them as more important.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-mcwilliam-65)

At party level, the Labour Party, in opposition until October 1964, was overtly against Southern Rhodesian independence under the 1961 constitution and supportive of the black Rhodesian movement on ideological and moral grounds. The [Liberal Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_/(UK/) "Liberal Party (UK)"), holding a handful of parliament seats, took a similar stance. The Conservative Party, while also following a policy of decolonisation, was more sympathetic to the Southern Rhodesian government's position, and included members who openly supported it.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-71)[\[n 10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-lobby-74)

### Southern Rhodesian government view

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Southern Rhodesian government view")\]

The Southern Rhodesian government found it bizarre that Britain was making independent states out of Northern Rhodesia and Nyasaland, which the Rhodesians considered to be less developed territories with little experience of self-rule, while withholding sovereign statehood from Southern Rhodesia, the Federation's senior partner, which had already been self-governing for four decades and which was one of the most prosperous and developed countries in Africa. The principle of majority rule, the basis for this apparent inconsistency, was considered irrelevant by the Southern Rhodesians.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-75) They had presumed that in the event of Federal dissolution they would be first in line for independence without major adjustments to the 1961 constitution, an impression confirmed to them by prior intergovernmental correspondence, particularly the oral promises they claimed to have received from Butler. When it did not prove forthcoming they felt cheated.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood371-76) Salisbury contended that its predominantly white legislature was more deserving of independence than the untried black Rhodesian leaders as it had proven its competence over decades of self-rule.[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-77)

The RF claimed that the bloody civil wars, military coups and other disasters that plagued the new majority-ruled African states to the north, many of which had become corrupt, autocratic or communist one-party states very soon after independence,[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-78) showed that black Rhodesian leaders were not ready to govern. Influenced strongly by the white refugees who had fled south from the [Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congo_Crisis "Congo Crisis"), it presented chaotic doomsday scenarios of what black Rhodesian rule in Southern Rhodesia might mean, particularly for the white community.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-79) Proponents of the RF stand downplayed black Rhodesian grievances regarding land ownership and segregation, and argued that despite the racial imbalance in domestic politics—whites made up 5% of the population, but over 90% of registered voters—the electoral system was not racist as the franchise was based on financial and educational qualifications rather than ethnicity.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-80) They emphasised the colony's proud war record on Britain's behalf,[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-moorcraft1990-81) and expressed a wish in the Cold War context to form an anti-communist, pro-[Western](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Bloc "Western Bloc") front in Africa alongside South Africa and [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Empire "Portuguese Empire").[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-olsonshadle10291030-82)

These factors combined with what RF politicians and supporters saw as British decadence, chicanery and betrayal to create the case they put forward that UDI, while dubious legally and likely to provoke international uproar, might nevertheless be in their eyes justifiable and necessary for the good of the country and region if an accommodation could not be found with Whitehall.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood190-83)

### First steps, under Field

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: First steps, under Field")\]

Field's failure to secure independence concurrently with the end of the Federation caused his Cabinet's support for him to waver during late 1963 and early 1964.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood186190-64) The RF [caucus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caucus "Caucus") in January 1964 revealed widespread dissatisfaction with him on the grounds that the British seemed to be outwitting him. The Prime Minister was put under immense pressure to win the colony's independence.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood190-83) Field travelled to England later that month to press Douglas-Home and Sandys for independence, and raised the possibility of UDI on a few occasions, but returned empty-handed on 2 February.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-84)

The RF united behind Field after Sandys wrote him a terse letter warning him of the likely Commonwealth reaction to a declaration of independence, but the Prime Minister then lost his party's confidence by failing to pursue a possible route to at least _de facto_ independence devised by [Desmond Lardner-Burke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Lardner-Burke "Desmond Lardner-Burke"), a lawyer and RF MP for [Gwelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gweru "Gweru"). During March 1964, the Legislative Assembly in Salisbury considered and passed Lardner-Burke's motion that the Governor, Sir [Humphrey Gibbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humphrey_Gibbs "Humphrey Gibbs"), should submit a petition to the Queen requesting alteration of Section 111 of the 1961 constitution so that the [Royal Assent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Assent "Royal Assent") described therein would be exercised at the request of the Southern Rhodesian government rather than that of its British counterpart. This would both remove the possibility of British legislative interference and pave the way for an attempted assumption of independence by [Order in Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_in_Council "Order in Council").[\[n 11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-harper-87)

The RF's intention was partly to test whether or not the British would attempt to block this bill after Gibbs had granted Royal Assent to it,[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-88) but this issue never came to a head because Sandys persuaded Field not to forward it to Gibbs for ratification on the grounds that it had not been unanimously passed.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-89) [Lord Salisbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Gascoyne-Cecil,_5th_Marquess_of_Salisbury "Robert Gascoyne-Cecil, 5th Marquess of Salisbury"), one of Southern Rhodesia's main supporters in Britain, despaired at Field's lack of action, telling Welensky that as he saw it "the simple time to have declared independence, whether right or wrong, would have been when the Federation came to an end".[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood204207-86) The RF hierarchy interpreted this latest backtrack by Field as evidence that he would not seriously challenge the British on the independence issue, and forced his resignation on 13 April 1964.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood204207-86) Smith accepted the Cabinet's nomination to take his place.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-fieldtosmith-90)

### Smith replaces Field; talks with Douglas-Home

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Smith replaces Field; talks with Douglas-Home")\]

[![Image 5: A portrait photograph of Ian Smith](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/Ian_Smith_1950s.jpg/250px-Ian_Smith_1950s.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ian_Smith_1950s.jpg)

[Ian Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Smith "Ian Smith") replaced [Winston Field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Field "Winston Field") as Southern Rhodesian Prime Minister in April 1964, and pledged to challenge Britain on independence.

Smith, a farmer from the [Midlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midlands_Province "Midlands Province") town of [Selukwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shurugwi "Shurugwi") who had been seriously wounded while [serving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_service_of_Ian_Smith "Military service of Ian Smith") in the British [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force") during the Second World War, was Southern Rhodesia's first native-born Prime Minister.[\[n 12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-nativeborn-94) Regarded in British political circles as a "raw colonial"—when he took over, Smith's personal experience of the UK comprised four brief visits—he promised a harder line than Field in independence talks.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-fieldtosmith-90) The RF's replacement of Field drew criticism from the British Labour Party, whose leader [Harold Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Wilson "Harold Wilson") called it "brutal",[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-95) while Nkomo described the new Smith Cabinet as "a suicide squad ... not interested in the welfare of all the people but only in their own".[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-96) Smith said he was pursuing a middle course between black Rhodesian rule and apartheid so that there would still be "a place for the white man" in Southern Rhodesia;[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-97) this would benefit the blacks too, he claimed.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-hall22-98) He held that the government should be based "on merit, not on colour or nationalism",[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-hall22-98) and insisted that there would be "no African nationalist government here in my lifetime".[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-99)

Salisbury's blunt refusal to be part of the Wind of Change caused the [Southern Rhodesian military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Security_Forces "Rhodesian Security Forces")'s traditional British and American suppliers to impose an informal embargo,[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood319-100) and prompted Whitehall and Washington to stop sending Southern Rhodesia financial aid around the same time.[\[n 13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-102) In June 1964, Douglas-Home informed Smith that Southern Rhodesia would not be represented at the year's [Commonwealth Prime Ministers' Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Prime_Ministers%27_Conference "Commonwealth Prime Ministers' Conference"), despite Salisbury's record of attendance going back to 1932,[\[n 14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-conference-104) because of a change in policy to only include representatives from fully independent states. This decision, taken by Britain to preempt the possibility of open confrontation with Asian and black African leaders at the conference, deeply insulted Smith.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-105) Lord Malvern equated Britain's removal of Southern Rhodesia's conference seat with "kicking us out of the Commonwealth",[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-106) while Welensky expressed horror at what he described as "this cavalier treatment of a country which has, since its creation, staunchly supported, in every possible way, Britain and the Commonwealth".[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-welenskyspeech-103)

[![Image 6: A photograph of Sir Alec Douglas-Home](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Alec_Douglas-Home_%28c1963%29.jpg/250px-Alec_Douglas-Home_%28c1963%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alec_Douglas-Home_/(c1963/).jpg)

UK Prime Minister Sir [Alec Douglas-Home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alec_Douglas-Home "Alec Douglas-Home") met Smith in London in September 1964.

At [10 Downing Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10_Downing_Street "10 Downing Street") in early September 1964, impasse developed between Douglas-Home and Smith over the best way to measure black public opinion in Southern Rhodesia. A key plank of Britain's Southern Rhodesia policy was that the terms for independence had to be "acceptable to the people of the country as a whole"—agreeing to this, Smith suggested that white and urban black opinion could be gauged through a general referendum of registered voters, and that rural black views could be obtained at a national _[indaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indaba "Indaba")_ (tribal conference) of chiefs and headmen. Douglas-Home told Smith that although this proposal satisfied him personally, he could not accept it as he did not believe the Commonwealth, the United Nations or the Labour Party would also do so. He stressed that such a move towards accommodation with Smith might hurt the Conservatives' chances in the British general election the next month, and suggested that it might be in Smith's best interests to wait until after the election to continue negotiations. Smith accepted this argument. Douglas-Home assured Smith that a Conservative government would settle with him and grant independence within a year.[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-107)

Attempting to form a viable white opposition to the Rhodesian Front, the UFP resurrected itself around Welensky, renamed itself the Rhodesia Party, and entered the Arundel and Avondale by-elections that had been called for 1 October 1964. Perturbed by the prospect of having to face the political heavyweight Welensky in parliament at the head of the opposition, the RF poured huge resources into winning both of these former UFP safe seats, and fielded [Clifford Dupont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_Dupont "Clifford Dupont"), Smith's deputy, against Welensky in Arundel.[\[n 15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-campaign64-111) The RF won both seats comfortably, and the Rhodesia Party soon faded away. Spurred on by this success, Smith organised the _indaba_ for 22 October, and called a general [independence referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Southern_Rhodesian_independence_referendum "1964 Southern Rhodesian independence referendum") for 5 November 1964.[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-byelection-108) Meanwhile, Wilson wrote a number of letters to black Southern Rhodesians, assuring them that "the Labour Party is totally opposed to granting independence to Southern Rhodesia so long as the government of that country remains under the control of the white minority".[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-berlyn157-112)

### Wilson's Labour government; Salisbury's tests of opinion

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Wilson's Labour government; Salisbury's tests of opinion")\]

[![Image 7: A portrait photograph of Harold Wilson](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Harold_Wilson.jpg/250px-Harold_Wilson.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Harold_Wilson.jpg)

[Harold Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Wilson "Harold Wilson") replaced Douglas-Home in October 1964, and proved a formidable opponent of Smith.

Labour defeated the Conservatives by four seats in the British [general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_United_Kingdom_general_election "1964 United Kingdom general election") on 15 October 1964, and formed a government the next day. Both Labour and the Conservatives told Smith that a positive result at the _indaba_ would not be recognised by Britain as representative of the people, and the Conservatives turned down Salisbury's invitation to send observers. Smith pressed on, telling parliament that he would ask the tribal chiefs and headmen "to consult their people in the traditional manner", then hold the _indaba_ as planned.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-113) On 22 October 196 chiefs and 426 headmen from across the country gathered at [Domboshawa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domboshawa "Domboshawa"), just north-east of Salisbury, and began their deliberations. Smith hoped that Britain, having taken part in such _indabas_ in the past, might send a delegation at the last minute, but none arrived, much to his annoyance, particularly as the British government's Commonwealth Secretary [Arthur Bottomley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Bottomley "Arthur Bottomley") was only across the [Zambezi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambezi "Zambezi") in [Lusaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lusaka "Lusaka") at the time.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood242243-114)[\[n 16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-observers-115)

While the chiefs conferred, Northern Rhodesia became independent Zambia on 24 October 1964, emulating Nyasaland, which had achieved statehood as Malawi three months earlier. Reasoning that it was no longer necessary to refer to itself as "Southern" in the absence of a northern counterpart, Southern Rhodesia began calling itself simply Rhodesia.[\[n 17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-name2-117) The same day, the commander of the [Rhodesian Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Army "Rhodesian Army"), Major-General John "Jock" Anderson, resigned,[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-118) announcing publicly that he was forced to do so because of his opposition to UDI, which he said he could not go along with because of his oath of allegiance to the Queen. Interpreting this as a sign that Smith intended to declare independence if a majority backed it in the referendum, Wilson wrote a stiff letter to Smith on 25 October, warning him of the consequences of UDI, and demanding "a categorical assurance forthwith that no attempt at a unilateral declaration of independence on your part will be made".[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood243246-119) Smith expressed confusion as to what he had done to provoke this, and ignored it.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood243246-119)

When the _indaba_ ended on 26 October, the chiefs and headmen returned a unanimous decision to support the government's stand for independence under the 1961 constitution, attesting in their report that "people who live far away do not understand the problems of our country".[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood243246-119) This verdict was rejected by the nationalist movement on the grounds that the chiefs received governmental salaries; the chiefs countered that the black MPs in parliamentary opposition also received such salaries, but still opposed the government.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood243246-119) Malvern, who was becoming perturbed by the RF's actions, dismissed the _indaba_ as a "swindle", asserting that the chiefs no longer had any real power; the British simply ignored the whole exercise.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood250-120) On 27 October, Wilson released a firm statement regarding Britain's intended response to UDI, warning that Rhodesia's economic and political ties with Britain, the Commonwealth and most of the world would be immediately severed amid a campaign of sanctions if Smith's government went ahead with UDI.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood243246-119) This was intended to discourage white Rhodesians from voting for independence in the referendum,[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood247-121) for which the RF campaign slogan was "Yes means Unity, not UDI".[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-122) Wilson was pleased when Douglas-Home, his leading opponent in the House of Commons, praised the statement as "rough but right".[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-123) On 5 November 1964, Rhodesia's mostly white electorate [voted "yes" to independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Rhodesian_independence_referendum "1964 Rhodesian independence referendum") under the 1961 constitution by a margin of 89%,[\[n 18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-vote-125) prompting Smith to declare that the British condition of acceptability to the people as a whole had been met.[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood251-126)

### Stalemate develops between Smith and Wilson

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Stalemate develops between Smith and Wilson")\]

Smith wrote to Wilson the day after the referendum, asking him to send Bottomley to Salisbury for talks. Wilson replied that Smith should instead come to London.[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood251-126) The British and Rhodesians exchanged often confrontational letters for the next few months. Alluding to the British financial aid pledged to Salisbury as part of the Federal dissolution arrangements, Wilson's High Commissioner in Salisbury, [J B Johnston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Baines_Johnston "John Baines Johnston"), wrote to the Rhodesian Cabinet Secretary [Gerald B. Clarke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_B._Clarke "Gerald B. Clarke") on 23 December that "talk of a unilateral declaration of independence is bound to throw a shadow of uncertainty on the future financial relations between the two governments".[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-127) Smith was furious, seeing this as blackmail, and on 13 January 1965 wrote to Wilson: "I am so incensed at the line of your High Commissioner's letter that I am replying directly to you ... It would appear that any undertakings given by the British government are worthless ... such immoral behaviour on the part of the British government makes it impossible for me to continue negotiations with you with any confidence that our standards of fair play, honesty and decency will prevail."[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-smith85-128)

[![Image 8: A wide shot of Downing Street](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/10_Downing_Street_2010.jpg/250px-10_Downing_Street_2010.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:10_Downing_Street_2010.jpg)

[10 Downing Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10_Downing_Street "10 Downing Street"), where Wilson received Smith in January 1965

The two premiers were brought together in person in late January 1965, when Smith travelled to London for Sir [Winston Churchill's funeral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_and_state_funeral_of_Winston_Churchill "Death and state funeral of Winston Churchill"). Following an episode concerning Smith's non-invitation to a luncheon at [Buckingham Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckingham_Palace "Buckingham Palace") after the funeral—noticing the Rhodesian's absence, the Queen sent a royal [equerry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equerry "Equerry") to Smith's hotel to retrieve him, reportedly causing Wilson much irritation—the two prime ministers inconclusively debated at 10 Downing Street. They differed on most matters, but agreed on a visit to Rhodesia the next month by Bottomley and the Lord Chancellor, [Lord Gardiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_Gardiner,_Baron_Gardiner "Gerald Gardiner, Baron Gardiner"), to gauge public opinion and meet political and commercial figures.[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-129) Bottomley and Gardiner visited Rhodesia from 22 February to 3 March, collected a wide cross-section of opinions, including some from black Rhodesians, and on returning to Britain reported to the House of Commons that they were "not without hope of finding a way towards a solution that will win the support of all communities and lead to independence and prosperity for all Rhodesians".[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood286-130) Bottomley also condemned black-on-black political violence, and dismissed the idea of introducing majority rule through military force.[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood286-130)

The RF called a new general election for [May 1965](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1965_Rhodesian_general_election "1965 Rhodesian general election") and, campaigning on an [election promise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Election_promise "Election promise") of independence, won all 50 "A"-roll seats (the voters for which were mostly white).[\[n 19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-crossvoting-132) [Josiah Gondo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josiah_Gondo "Josiah Gondo"), leader of the United People's Party, became Rhodesia's first black [Leader of the Opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Opposition_/(Rhodesia/) "Leader of the Opposition (Rhodesia)"). Opening parliament on 9 June, Gibbs told the Legislative Assembly in his [speech from the throne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speech_from_the_throne "Speech from the throne") that the RF's strengthened majority amounted to "a mandate to lead the country to its full independence", and announced that the new government had informed him of its intent to open its own [diplomatic mission in Lisbon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_mission_in_Lisbon "Rhodesian mission in Lisbon"), separate from the British embassy there. The British and Rhodesians argued about this unilateral act by Salisbury, described by the historian J R T Wood as the "veritable straw in the wind",[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood319-100) alongside the independence issue until Portugal accepted the mission in late September, much to Britain's fury and Rhodesia's delight.[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-fedorowichthomas185186-133) Hoping to bring Smith to heel by stonewalling him, Wilson's ministers deliberately delayed and frustrated the Rhodesian government in negotiations.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-134) Rhodesia was again excluded from the Commonwealth Prime Ministers' Conference in 1965. The UK's refusal of aid, the Lisbon mission, the informal arms embargo and other issues combined with this to cause the Rhodesian government's sense of alienation from Britain and the Commonwealth to deepen.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood335-101) In his memoirs, Smith accused the British of "resorting to politics of convenience and appeasement".[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-135) Wilson, meanwhile, became exasperated by what he saw as Rhodesian inflexibility, describing the gap between the two governments as "between different worlds and different centuries".[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood5-136)

> **Wilson**: We are not giving up. Too much is at stake ... I know I speak for everyone in these islands, all parties, all our people, when I say to Mr Smith, 'Prime Minister, think again'.  
> **Smith**: After 43 years of proving our case we are told that we cannot be master in our own house. Is it not incredible that the British government has allowed our case to deteriorate into this fantastic position? ... I believe I should say to Mr Wilson: 'Prime Minister, think again!'

\-- Wilson and Smith called on each other through televised statements to "think again" on 13 October 1965[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-thinkagain-137)

Amid renewed rumours of an impending Rhodesian UDI, Smith travelled to meet Wilson in London at the start of October 1965, telling the press that he intended to resolve the independence issue once and for all.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood360363-138) Both the British and the Rhodesians were surprised by the large numbers of Britons who came out to support Smith during his visit.[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood381383-139) Smith accepted an invitation from the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC") to appear on its _[Twenty-Four Hours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/24_Hours_/(TV_programme/) "24 Hours (TV programme)")_ evening news and current affairs programme, but Downing Street blocked this at the last minute.[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood381383-139) Following largely abortive talks with Wilson, the Rhodesian prime minister flew home on 12 October.[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood387388-140) Desperate to avert UDI, Wilson travelled to Salisbury two weeks later to continue negotiations.[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood411414-141)

During these discussions, Smith referred to the last resort of a UDI on many occasions,[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-young271-142) though he said he hoped to find another way out of the quandary. He offered to increase black legislative representation by expanding the electorate along the lines of "one taxpayer, one vote"—which would enfranchise about half a million, but still leave most of the nation voteless—in return for a grant of independence.[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood411414-141) Wilson said this was insufficient, and countered that future black representation might be better safeguarded by Britain's withdrawal from the colonial government of the power it had held since 1923 to determine the size and makeup of its parliament. The Rhodesians were horrified by this prospect, particularly as Wilson's suggestion of it seemed to them to have removed the failsafe alternative of keeping the _status quo_.[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-143) Before the British prime minister left Rhodesia on 30 October 1965, he proposed a Royal Commission to gauge public opinion in the colony regarding independence under the 1961 constitution, possibly chaired by the Rhodesian Chief Justice Sir [Hugh Beadle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Beadle "Hugh Beadle"), which would report its findings to both the British and Rhodesian Cabinets.[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood441442-144) Wilson confirmed in the House of Commons two days later that he intended to introduce direct British control over the Rhodesian parliamentary structure to ensure that progress was made towards majority rule.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood445-145)

Stalemate drew closer as the Rhodesian Cabinet resolved that since Wilson had ruled out maintenance of the _status quo_, its only remaining options were to trust in the Royal Commission or declare independence.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood443-146) When the terms for the commission's visit were presented to Smith, he found that contrary to what had been discussed during the British prime minister's visit, the Royal Commission would operate on the basis that the 1961 constitution was unacceptable to the British government, and that Britain would not commit itself to accepting the final report. Smith said these conditions amounted to a "vote of no confidence in \[the commission\] before they commenced", and therefore rejected them.[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-147) "The impression you left with us of a determined effort to resolve our constitutional problem has been utterly dissipated", he wrote to Wilson on 5 November. "It would seem that you have now finally closed the door which you publicly claimed to have opened."[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-young271-142)

Amid frantic efforts by Beadle and others on both sides to revive the Royal Commission, the Rhodesian government had Gibbs announce a [state of emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_emergency "State of emergency") the same day on the grounds that black Rhodesian insurgents were reportedly entering the country. Smith denied that this foreshadowed a declaration of independence,[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood453-148) but the publishing of his letter to Wilson in the press provoked a worldwide storm of speculation that UDI was imminent.[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-young271-142) Smith wrote again to Wilson on 8 November, asking him to appoint the Royal Commission under the terms they had agreed in Salisbury and to commit the British government to accepting its ruling, but Wilson did not immediately reply.[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-149) On 9 November, the Rhodesian Cabinet sent a letter to Queen [Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II"), assuring her that Rhodesia would remain loyal to her personally "whatever happens".[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood460461-150)

Draft, adoption and signing
---------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Draft, adoption and signing")\]

[![Image 9: The United States Declaration of Independence](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/United_States_Declaration_of_Independence.jpg/250px-United_States_Declaration_of_Independence.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:United_States_Declaration_of_Independence.jpg)

The [United States Declaration of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Declaration_of_Independence "United States Declaration of Independence") was used by the Rhodesians as the model for their UDI.

The Rhodesian Minister for Justice and Law and Order, [Desmond Lardner-Burke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Lardner-Burke "Desmond Lardner-Burke"), presented the rest of the Cabinet with a draft for the declaration of independence on 5 November 1965. When [Jack Howman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Howman "Jack Howman"), Minister of Tourism and Information, said that he was also preparing a draft, the Cabinet decided to wait to see his version too. The ministers agreed that if an independence proclamation were issued, they would all sign it.[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood453-148) On 9 November, the Cabinet jointly devised an outline for the proclamation document and the accompanying statement to be made by Smith.[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood460461-150) The final version of the declaration of independence was prepared by a sub-committee of civil servants headed by Gerald Clarke, the Cabinet Secretary,[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-smith100103-2) with the [United States Declaration of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Declaration_of_Independence "United States Declaration of Independence") of 1776, the only other such proclamation ever issued by British colonials, used as a model.[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood471-151) Strongly alluding to [Thomas Jefferson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson")'s text throughout, the Rhodesians used one phrase [verbatim](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/verbatim "wikt:verbatim")—"a respect for the opinions of mankind"[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-stpetersburgtimes-152)—but no reference was made to the assertion that "[all men are created equal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_men_are_created_equal "All men are created equal")", nor to the "[consent of the governed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consent_of_the_governed "Consent of the governed")", two omissions later stressed by a number of commentators.[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-153)

Attached to the declaration of independence was a copy of the 1961 constitution amended for the circumstances, which became the 1965[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-154) constitution. In the eyes of the Smith administration, this document removed Whitehall's remaining authority over Rhodesia and made Rhodesia a _de jure_ independent state. However, the Smith government still professed loyalty to Elizabeth II, and accordingly the document reconstituted Rhodesia as a [Commonwealth realm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_realm "Commonwealth realm") with Elizabeth as "[Queen of Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_of_Rhodesia "Queen of Rhodesia")". The new constitution created the concept of allegiance to the "Constitution of Rhodesia", and introduced the post of [Officer Administering the Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrator_of_the_Government "Administrator of the Government"), a viceregal figure empowered to sign passed legislation into law on behalf of the monarch if she did not appoint a [Governor-General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor-General "Governor-General").[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood471-151)

The Rhodesian Cabinet waited in vain for Wilson's reply for the rest of 9 November and the next day. After briefly meeting Smith late on 10 November,[\[136\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-155) Johnston warned Wilson that evening that the Rhodesians seemed poised to declare independence in the morning. The British prime minister tried repeatedly to call Smith, but did not get through until Smith was already chairing a Cabinet meeting on the independence issue around 08:00 [Central Africa Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Africa_Time "Central Africa Time") (06:00 in London) on 11 November. Wilson attempted to talk Smith out of unilateral action by telling him the _status quo_ could continue, and the two argued inconclusively about the proposed Royal Commission. Returning to his Cabinet meeting, Smith reported the conversation to his ministers, and, after debating for a while, the Cabinet came to the conclusion that Wilson was simply attempting to buy more time and that there was no sign of actual progress. Smith asked if Rhodesia should declare its independence, and had each Cabinet minister [answer in turn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consensus_decision-making "Consensus decision-making"). According to Smith's account, "each one, quietly but firmly, without hesitation, said: 'Yes'."[\[137\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood468470-156)

At 11:00 local time on 11 November 1965, [Armistice Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armistice_Day "Armistice Day"), during the traditional [two minutes' silence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two_minute_silence "Two minute silence") to remember the fallen of the two World Wars, Smith declared Rhodesia independent and signed the proclamation document, with Dupont and the other 10 [ministers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signatories_of_Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence "Signatories of Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence") of the Cabinet following. The timing was intended to emphasise the sacrifices Rhodesia had made for Britain in wartime.[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-157) As [Ken Flower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Flower "Ken Flower") later said, "the rebellion was made to appear as though it was not a rebellion".[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood471-151) Smith and his ministers still pledged allegiance to Queen Elizabeth II, whose official portrait hung prominently behind them as they signed; the declaration even ended "God Save The Queen".[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood471-151) Four junior members of the Cabinet—Lance Smith, Ian Dillon, Andrew Dunlop and [P. K. van der Byl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P._K._van_der_Byl "P. K. van der Byl")—did not sign, but were included in the official photograph.[\[139\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-158)

Text of the declaration
-----------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Text of the declaration")\]

> Proclamation
> 
> * * *
> 
> Whereas in the course of human affairs history has shown that it may become necessary for a people to resolve the political affiliations which have connected them with another people and to assume amongst other nations the separate and equal status to which they are entitled:
> 
> And Whereas in such event a respect for the opinions of mankind requires them to declare to other nations the causes which impel them to assume full responsibility for their own affairs:
> 
> Now Therefore, We, The Government of Rhodesia, Do Hereby Declare:
> 
> That it is an indisputable and accepted historic fact that since 1923 the Government of Rhodesia have exercised the powers of self-government and have been responsible for the progress, development and welfare of their people;
> 
> That the people of Rhodesia having demonstrated their loyalty to the Crown and to their kith and kin in the United Kingdom and elsewhere through two world wars, and having been prepared to shed their blood and give of their substance in what they believed to be the mutual interests of freedom-loving people, now see all that they have cherished about to be shattered on the rocks of expediency;
> 
> That the people of Rhodesia have witnessed a process which is destructive of those very precepts upon which civilization in a primitive country has been built, they have seen the principles of Western democracy, responsible government and moral standards crumble elsewhere, nevertheless they have remained steadfast;
> 
> That the people of Rhodesia fully support the requests of their government for sovereign independence but have witnessed the consistent refusal of the Government of the United Kingdom to accede to their entreaties;
> 
> That the Government of the United Kingdom have thus demonstrated that they are not prepared to grant sovereign independence to Rhodesia on terms acceptable to the people of Rhodesia, thereby persisting in maintaining an unwarrantable jurisdiction over Rhodesia, obstructing laws and treaties with other states and the conduct of affairs with other nations and refusing assent to laws necessary for the public good, all this to the detriment of the future peace, prosperity and good government of Rhodesia;
> 
> That the Government of Rhodesia have for a long period patiently and in good faith negotiated with the Government of the United Kingdom for the removal of the remaining limitations placed upon them and for the grant of sovereign independence;
> 
> That in the belief that procrastination and delay strike at and injure the very life of the nation, the Government of Rhodesia consider it essential that Rhodesia should attain, without delay, sovereign independence, the justice of which is beyond question;
> 
> Now Therefore, We The Government of Rhodesia, in humble submission to Almighty God who controls the destinies of nations, conscious that the people of Rhodesia have always shown unswerving loyalty and devotion to Her Majesty the Queen and earnestly praying that we and the people of Rhodesia will not be hindered in our determination to continue exercising our undoubted right to demonstrate the same loyalty and devotion, and seeking to promote the common good so that the dignity and freedom of all men may be assured, Do, By This Proclamation, adopt, enact and give to the people of Rhodesia the Constitution annexed hereto;
> 
> God Save The Queen
> 
> Given under Our Hand at Salisbury, this eleventh day of November in the Year of Our Lord one thousand nine hundred and sixty-five.
> 
> *   _[Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Rhodesia "Prime Minister of Rhodesia"):_ [Ian Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Smith "Ian Smith")
> *   _Deputy Prime Minister:_ [Clifford Dupont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_Dupont "Clifford Dupont")
> *   _Ministers:_ [William Harper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_John_Harper "William John Harper"), [Montrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Graham,_7th_Duke_of_Montrose "James Graham, 7th Duke of Montrose"), [Phillip van Heerden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phillip_van_Heerden "Phillip van Heerden"), [Jack Howman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Howman "Jack Howman"), [Jack Mussett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Mussett "Jack Mussett"), [John Wrathall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Wrathall "John Wrathall"), [Desmond Lardner-Burke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desmond_Lardner-Burke "Desmond Lardner-Burke"), [George Rudland](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=George_Rudland&action=edit&redlink=1 "George Rudland (page does not exist)"), [Ian McLean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Finlay_McLean "Ian Finlay McLean"), [Arthur Philip Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Arthur_Philip_Smith&action=edit&redlink=1 "Arthur Philip Smith (page does not exist)")

Announcement and reactions
--------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Announcement and reactions")\]

Prompted by the government, the [Rhodesian Broadcasting Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_Broadcasting_Corporation "Zimbabwe Broadcasting Corporation") told the public to stand by for an important announcement from the Prime Minister at 13:15 local time. Smith went first to [Government House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_House,_Harare "State House, Harare") to inform Gibbs that his Cabinet had declared independence,[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood471-151) then to Pockets Hill Studios in east Salisbury to announce UDI to the nation. He read the proclamation aloud, then stated that independence had been declared because it had become "abundantly clear that it is the policy of the British government to play us along with no real intention of arriving at a solution which we could possibly accept ... I promised the people of this country that I would continue to negotiate to the bitter end and that I would leave no stone unturned in my endeavours to secure an honourable and mutually accepted settlement; it now falls to me to tell you that negotiations have come to an end".[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood472-159)

Smith said that he believed that he would be remiss in his duty if he allowed Rhodesia to continue to "drift in its present paralysing state of uncertainty", and that following Britain's abandonment of the Federation his government was determined that "the same will never be allowed to happen here". He claimed that UDI did not mark "a diminution in the opportunities which our African people have to advance and prosper in Rhodesia", described "racial harmony in Africa" as part of his agenda and condemned black Rhodesian activities as attempts to "blackmail the British government into ... handing the country over to irresponsible rule". He then attempted to assuage fears that economic sanctions might destroy the economy, and asked Rhodesians to stand firm: "The mantle of the pioneers has fallen on our shoulders ... In the lives of most nations there comes a moment when a stand has to be made for principles, whatever the consequences. This moment has come to Rhodesia ... the first Western nation in the last two decades to say 'so far and no further'." He concluded with an assertion that the declaration of independence was "a blow for the preservation of justice, civilisation and Christianity".[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood472475-160)

[![Image 10: The front page of a newspaper, "The Rhodesia Herald". The main headline is "UDI—Rhodesia goes it alone".](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/1/15/Udinewspaper.jpg/250px-Udinewspaper.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Udinewspaper.jpg)

The front page of _[The Rhodesia Herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Herald_/(Zimbabwe/) "The Herald (Zimbabwe)")_'s 12 November 1965 edition. The blank spaces are where content was removed by state censors.

By the time Smith and Dupont arrived at Government House to see Gibbs, Whitehall had instructed the Governor to formally dismiss Smith and his ministers for treason. Gibbs complied without hesitation. Smith and his ministers ignored this, holding that under the new 1965 constitution Gibbs "no longer ha\[d\] any executive powers in Rhodesia", and his [reserve power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reserve_power "Reserve power") to sack them no longer existed.[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-161) The Rhodesian government hoped that Gibbs might obligingly resign in light of his impotent situation, but he did not; following orders from London, he remained at his post at Government House. Gibbs told the Rhodesian military's senior officers, some of whom were troubled by the perceived choice between Queen and country, to remain at their posts to maintain law and order.[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood0834-162) He also refused some Army officers' requests for a warrant to arrest Smith.[\[144\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-163) Wilson briefly flirted with the idea of sending [Lord Mountbatten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Mountbatten "Lord Mountbatten") to Rhodesia to support Gibbs as a direct representative of the Queen, but this was dropped after Gibbs asked for somebody "higher up" in the royal family instead.[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood1999-164) "Not likely", Wilson retorted.[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood1999-164) [Prince Philip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Philip,_Duke_of_Edinburgh "Prince Philip, Duke of Edinburgh") was suggested by diplomats to be appointed as Governor-General so he could legally sack Smith but this was refused due to the personal risk he would have been in.[\[146\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-165)

The Rhodesian government accompanied UDI with emergency measures that it said were intended to prevent alarm, unrest and the flight of people and capital. Press censorship and petrol rationing were imposed, import licences were cancelled and emigration allowances were cut to £100. News of UDI was generally received calmly by the local citizenry, apart from some isolated incidents of passing cars being stoned in the black townships outside Bulawayo. A few expected dissenters were arrested, most prominently [Leo Baron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Baron "Leo Baron"), Nkomo's lawyer, whose links with black Rhodesians and communists were seen by authorities as "subversive".[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood0834-162) Baron, the younger brother of the scientist [Jacob Bronowski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Bronowski "Jacob Bronowski"), was arrested nine minutes after UDI was made.[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood0834-162)

> What was it that could make a country twice the size of Britain with half the population of London pit itself against the massive weight of world opinion? Rights or wrongs aside, there was something splendid about the gesture.

\-- Rhodesian journalist Phillippa Berlyn on UDI[\[147\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-beleaguered-166)

Welensky, who had opposed UDI, stated that he felt it was nevertheless "the duty of every responsible Rhodesian to support the revolutionary government" as he believed the only alternative was a descent into anarchy.[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood0834-162) [João de Freitas Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jo%C3%A3o_de_Freitas_Cruz&action=edit&redlink=1 "João de Freitas Cruz (page does not exist)") ([pt](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo%C3%A3o_de_Freitas_Cruz "pt:João de Freitas Cruz")), the Portuguese consul-general in Salisbury, reacted to the news with wild excitement; visiting the Smith residence later in the day, he declared "Only Rhodesians could do this!"[\[148\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-berlyn171-167) A statement from ZAPU's [Jason Moyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Moyo "Jason Moyo"), who was in London at the time, denounced UDI as an act of "treason and rebellion" and asserted that "the lives particularly of four million unarmed Africans are in jeopardy".[\[149\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-bbc1965-168) Davis M'Gabe of the [Zimbabwe African National Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_African_National_Union "Zimbabwe African National Union") (ZANU) said that "For all those who cherish freedom and a meaningful life, UDI has set a collision course which cannot be altered. \[It has\] marked the turning point of the struggle for freedom ... from a constitutional and political one to primarily a military struggle."[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-169) Most major Christian denominational leaders in the country publicly rejected UDI and the assertion that it defended Christianity, with the exception of the local [Dutch Reformed Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Reformed_Church_in_South_Africa "Dutch Reformed Church in South Africa"), which stated that it was apolitical and thereafter refrained from comment.[\[151\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-170)

A week after UDI, Smith's government announced that Dupont, the Deputy Prime Minister, had resigned from the Cabinet to accept the post of Officer Administering the Government created by the 1965 constitution.[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood1999-164) Attempting to assert his claimed prerogatives as Her Majesty's Rhodesian Prime Minister, Smith advised the Queen by letter to appoint Dupont as Governor-General to supersede Gibbs. The letter was ignored, with [Buckingham Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckingham_Palace "Buckingham Palace") characterising Smith's request as "purported advice".[\[152\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-171) Whitehall maintained that Gibbs was the Queen's only legitimate representative in what it still reckoned as the colony of Southern Rhodesia–and hence, the only lawful authority in the area.[\[153\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-172) Dupont nevertheless effectively replaced the Governor. The Smith administration assigned him the Governor's official residence at Government House, but no attempt was made to forcibly remove Gibbs and his entourage; the post-UDI government stated that the Officer Administering the Government would live at Governor's Lodge instead "until Government House, at present temporarily occupied by Sir Humphrey Gibbs in a private capacity, becomes available".[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood1999-164)

The [Speaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_/(politics/) "Speaker (politics)") of the Rhodesian parliament, [A. R. W. Stumbles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubidge_Stumbles "Rubidge Stumbles"), reconvened the Legislative Assembly on 25 November, resolving that if he did not there would be chaos. He feared that Gibbs might dramatically walk into the chamber in an attempt to stop the proceedings, but Gibbs did no such thing. The parliamentary opposition opened the meeting by asking whether the assembly was legal.[\[154\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood200821-173) [Ahrn Palley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahrn_Palley "Ahrn Palley"), the lone white opposition MP, announced that as he saw it, "certain Honourable Members in collusion have torn up the constitution under which this House meets. The proceedings have no legal validity whatsoever".[\[155\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-time65-174) Stumbles overruled this objection and two more interruptions from Palley, and suggested that any members with reservations might leave.[\[154\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood200821-173) Palley continued his loud protests until he was forcibly ejected by the [Sergeant-at-Arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serjeant-at-Arms "Serjeant-at-Arms"), shouting "This is an illegal assembly! God save the Queen!"[\[155\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-time65-174) Gondo and eight other opposition MPs followed Palley out;[\[154\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood200821-173) all ten of them rejoined the Legislative Assembly in February 1966.[\[n 20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-outoforder-176)

Gibbs received threatening letters from the Rhodesian public, and on 26 November 1965 Smith's government cut off the telephones at Government House, and removed the ceremonial guard, the official cars "and even the typewriters", Wood records.[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood1999-164) Gibbs nevertheless refused to step down or to leave Government House, issuing a statement that he would remain there "as the lawful Governor of Rhodesia until such time as constitutional government is restored, which I hope will be soon."[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood1999-164) He stayed at his post, ignored by the post-UDI government, until the declaration of a republic in 1970.[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood1999-164)

### British and international responses; sanctions

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: British and international responses; sanctions")\]

Wilson was astonished by Smith's actions, and found the timing of the declaration to coincide with the Armistice Day silence deeply insulting.[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-thinkagain-137) Describing Salisbury as "hell-bent on illegal self-destroying",[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood5-136) the British prime minister, supported in the Commons by the Liberals and most Conservatives, called on Rhodesians to ignore the post-UDI government.[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood5-136) Within hours of UDI, the [UN General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UN_General_Assembly "UN General Assembly") passed a condemnatory resolution, 107–2—South Africa and Portugal voted against, and France abstained—decrying Rhodesia's actions and calling on Britain to end "the rebellion by the unlawful authorities in Salisbury".[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-177) The [UN Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council") the next day adopted [Resolution 216](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_Resolution_216 "United Nations Security Council Resolution 216"), which denounced the declaration of independence as illegal and racist, and called on all states to refuse recognition and assistance to the Rhodesian government. [Security Council Resolution 217](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_Resolution_217 "United Nations Security Council Resolution 217"), following on 20 November, condemned UDI as an illegitimate "usurpation of power by a racist settler minority", and called on nations neither to recognise what it deemed "this illegal authority" nor to entertain diplomatic or economic relations with it. Both of these measures were adopted by ten votes to none with France abstaining.[\[158\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-gd183-178)

Rhodesian nationalists and their overseas supporters, prominently the OAU, clamoured for Britain to remove Smith's government by force.[\[159\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-Wood_2008_6-179) The [UN Committee on Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Committee_on_Decolonization "Special Committee on Decolonization") also strongly advised military intervention.[\[160\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-FOOTNOTENyamunda20161012-180) The British government dismissed this option because of various logistical issues, the risk of provoking a Rhodesian attack on Zambia and the psychological problems that were likely to accompany any confrontation between British and Rhodesian troops in what Smith said would be a "fratricidal war".[\[159\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-Wood_2008_6-179) British Foreign Secretary [Michael Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Stewart,_Baron_Stewart_of_Fulham "Michael Stewart, Baron Stewart of Fulham") stated that the United Kingdom thought that Rhodesian forces were well-equipped, well-trained and highly motivated and that an invasion would lead to "a medium sized war of uncertain duration".[\[161\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-FOOTNOTENyamunda20161011%E2%80%931012-181) Wilson instead resolved to end the Rhodesian rebellion through economic sanctions; these principally comprised the expulsion of Rhodesia from the [Sterling area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sterling_area "Sterling area"), a ban on the import of Rhodesian sugar, tobacco, chrome and other goods and an oil boycott of Rhodesia.
