When the Rhodesians continued to receive oil, Wilson attempted to directly cut off their main supply lines, namely the Portuguese Mozambican ports at [Beira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beira,_Mozambique "Beira, Mozambique") and [Lourenço Marques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maputo "Maputo"), by posting a [Royal Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Navy "Royal Navy") squadron to the [Mozambique Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozambique_Channel "Mozambique Channel") in March 1966. This blockade, the [Beira Patrol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beira_Patrol "Beira Patrol"), was endorsed the following month by [UN Security Council Resolution 221](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_Resolution_221 "United Nations Security Council Resolution 221").[\[162\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-mobley-182) The United Nations proceeded to institute the first mandatory trade sanctions in its history with [Security Council Resolutions 232](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_Resolution_232 "United Nations Security Council Resolution 232") (December 1966) and [253](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_Resolution_253 "United Nations Security Council Resolution 253") (April 1968), which required member states to cease all trade and economic links with Rhodesia.[\[163\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-183)

Wilson predicted in January 1966 that the various boycotts would force Smith to give in "within a matter of weeks rather than months", but the British and UN sanctions had little effect on Rhodesia, largely because South Africa and Portugal went on trading with the breakaway colony, providing it with oil and other commodities.[\[164\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-184)[\[165\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-185) Clandestine "sanction-busting" trade with other nations also continued, initially at a reduced level and the diminished presence of foreign competitors helped domestic industries to slowly mature and expand. Rhodesia thus avoided the economic collapse predicted by Wilson and gradually became more self-sufficient.[\[166\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-186) The Rhodesian government set up a string of front [holding companies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holding_company "Holding company") in Switzerland, Luxembourg and Liechtenstein to help keep trade open with some success; goods that had been imported from Britain were replaced by Japanese, French and West German equivalents. Even many OAU states, while bombarding Rhodesia with vitriol, continued importing Rhodesian food and other products.[\[167\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-187) The United States created a formal exception in its embargo with the [Byrd Amendment of 1971](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byrd_Amendment_/(1971/) "Byrd Amendment (1971)"),[\[168\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-188) under which the US replaced its import of chrome from the Soviet Union with Rhodesian chrome ore. This breach of the UN sanctions, passed by the [US Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress "United States Congress") on the back of anti-communist Cold War considerations, was warmly welcomed by several [white Southerners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_Southerners "White Southerners") in Congress; it aided the Rhodesian economy until 1977, when the new president, [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter"), successfully pushed Congress to repeal it.[\[169\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-189)

[![Image 11: An Edwardian building with six floors stands on a moderate day, a flag flying atop it.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d4/Zimbabwean_embassy_in_London.jpg/250px-Zimbabwean_embassy_in_London.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Zimbabwean_embassy_in_London.jpg)

[Rhodesia House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embassy_of_Zimbabwe,_London "Embassy of Zimbabwe, London"), the Rhodesian [High Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_commissioner_/(Commonwealth/) "High commissioner (Commonwealth)") in London, represented Smith's government in the UK until 1969, and became a regular target for political activists.

Official diplomatic recognition by other countries was key for Rhodesia as it was the only way it could regain the international legitimacy it had lost through UDI.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-white97-73) Recognition by the UK itself through a bilateral settlement would be the "first prize", in Smith's words, as it would end sanctions and constitutional ambiguity and make foreign acceptance, at least in the West, far more likely.[\[170\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-190) Considering their country a potentially important player in the Cold War as a "bastion against communism" in southern Africa,[\[171\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-191) the RF posited that some Western countries might recognise UDI even without a prior Anglo-Rhodesian rapprochement. Specifically, it expected diplomatic recognition from South Africa and Portugal, and thought that France might recognise Rhodesia to annoy Britain and create a precedent for an [independent Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec_sovereignty_movement "Quebec sovereignty movement").[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-white97-73) But although South Africa and Portugal gave economic, military and limited political support to the post-UDI government (as did France and other nations, to a lesser extent), neither they nor any other country ever recognised Rhodesia as a _de jure_ independent state.[\[172\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-192) Rhodesia's unsuccessful attempts to win Western support and recognition included offers to the US government in 1966 and 1967, ignored by [Lyndon B. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson "Lyndon B. Johnson")'s administration, to provide Rhodesian troops to fight alongside the Americans and other anti-communist forces [in Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War").[\[173\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-193)

Britain withdrew most of its [High Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Commission "High Commission") staff from Salisbury in the days following UDI, leaving a small skeleton staff to man a "residual mission" intended to help Gibbs keep the British government informed of local happenings.[\[148\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-berlyn171-167) Several countries followed Britain's lead and closed their [consulates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consul_/(representative/) "Consul (representative)") in Salisbury, with one prominent exception to this being the United States, which retained its consulate-general in post-UDI Rhodesia, relabelling it a "US Contacts Office" to circumvent the problem of diplomatic recognition.[\[n 21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-embassies-195) South Africa and Portugal maintained "Accredited Diplomatic Representative" offices in Salisbury, which were embassies in all but name, while Rhodesia kept its pre-UDI overseas missions in Pretoria, Lisbon and Lourenço Marques. Unofficial representative offices of the Rhodesian government also existed in the US, Japan and West Germany, while a citizen of Belgium was employed to represent Rhodesian interests there with the [Rhodesia Information Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia_Information_Centre "Rhodesia Information Centre") being in Australia to represent Rhodesia. The Rhodesian High Commission in London, located at [Rhodesia House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embassy_of_Zimbabwe,_London "Embassy of Zimbabwe, London") on the [Strand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strand,_London "Strand, London"), remained under the control of the post-UDI government and effectively became its representative office in the UK.[\[174\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-strack5152-194) Like the [South African Embassy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Commission_of_South_Africa,_London "High Commission of South Africa, London") on [Trafalgar Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trafalgar_Square "Trafalgar Square"), Rhodesia House became a regular target for political demonstrations. These continued even after Britain forced the office to close in 1969.[\[175\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-brownell-196)

Because UDI claimed to make Rhodesia independent under the Queen as an effective dominion, many countries justified their retention of missions in Rhodesia concurrently with their non-recognition of the state by pointing out that the envoys' accreditation was to the Queen and not to Smith's government _per se_. But Rhodesia moved away from its original line of independence as a [constitutional monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_monarchy "Constitutional monarchy") and towards republicanism during the late 1960s, hoping to end ambiguity regarding its claimed constitutional status and elicit official foreign recognition. In March 1970, after the electorate had voted "yes" in a [referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1969_Rhodesian_constitutional_referendum "1969 Rhodesian constitutional referendum") the previous year both to a new constitution and to the abandoning of symbolic ties to the Queen, Smith's government declared Rhodesia a republic. Far from prompting recognition, this led all countries apart from Portugal and South Africa to withdraw their consulates and missions, as the justification of royal accreditation could no longer be used.[\[174\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-strack5152-194) After Portugal's [Carnation Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnation_Revolution "Carnation Revolution") in 1974, the Rhodesian mission in Lisbon was closed in May 1975, with its counterpart in Lourenço Marques following a month later on Mozambican independence. Portugal also withdrew its own remaining officials from Rhodesia, leaving South Africa as the only country with links to Salisbury. Rhodesia's diplomatic activities were thereafter greatly diminished.[\[176\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-strack53-197)

The [Rhodesian High Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Court_of_Southern_Rhodesia "High Court of Southern Rhodesia")'s nine Appellate and General Division judges initially neither rejected UDI nor openly supported it. The Chief Justice Sir Hugh Beadle, of the Appellate Division, announced simply that the judges would go on carrying out their duties "according to the law".[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood1999-164) This originally noncommittal stance evolved over time, largely pivoting around legal cases argued at the High Court in Salisbury between 1966 and 1968. The first of these, _[Madzimbamuto v. Lardner-Burke N. O. and Others](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madzimbamuto_v._Lardner-Burke "Madzimbamuto v. Lardner-Burke")_, concerned Daniel Madzimbamuto, a black Rhodesian who was detained without trial by the Rhodesian government on 6 November 1965, the day after the declaration of a state of emergency and five days before UDI, on the grounds that he might pose a danger to the public. Desmond Lardner-Burke, the Rhodesian Minister of Justice and Law and Order, prolonged the state of emergency in February 1966, prompting Madzimbamuto's wife to appeal for his release, arguing that since the United Kingdom had declared UDI illegal and outlawed the Rhodesian government with the Southern Rhodesia Act 1965, the state of emergency (and, by extension, Madzimbamuto's imprisonment) had no legal basis.[\[177\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-gowllanddebbas7576-198)

The General Division of the Rhodesian High Court ruled on 9 September 1966 that legal sovereignty lay with the British government, but that to "avoid chaos and a vacuum in the law" the Rhodesian government should be considered to be in control of law and order to the same extent as before UDI. In February 1968, ruling on Madzimbamuto's appeal, Beadle concluded that the Smith administration would be recognised by the local judiciary as the _de facto_ government by virtue of its "effective control over the state's territory", but that _de jure_ recognition would be withheld as this was not "firmly established".[\[177\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-gowllanddebbas7576-198) Madzimbamuto applied for the right to appeal to the British [Privy Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privy_Council_of_the_United_Kingdom "Privy Council of the United Kingdom"); the Rhodesian Appellate Division promptly ruled that he had no right to do so,[\[178\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-199) but the Privy Council [considered his case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madzimbamuto_v._Lardner-Burke "Madzimbamuto v. Lardner-Burke") anyway.[\[179\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood487488-200)

In late February 1968, considering the fate of James Dhlamini, Victor Mlambo and Duly Shadreck, three black Rhodesians convicted of murder and terrorist offences before UDI, Beadle ruled that Salisbury retained its pre-UDI powers regarding executions and could carry out death sentences. Whitehall announced on 1 March that at the request of the UK government, the Queen had exercised the [royal prerogative of mercy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_prerogative_of_mercy "Royal prerogative of mercy") and commuted the three death sentences to life imprisonment. Dhlamini and the others applied for a permanent [stay of execution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stay_of_execution "Stay of execution") on this basis. At the hearing for Dhlamini and Mlambo on 4 March 1968, Beadle argued that he saw the statement from London as a decision by the UK government and not the Queen herself, and that in any case the 1961 constitution had transferred the prerogative of mercy from Britain to the Rhodesian Executive Council. "The present government is the fully _de facto_ government and as such is the only power that can exercise the prerogative", he concluded. "It would be strange indeed if the United Kingdom government, exercising no internal power in Rhodesia, were given the right to exercise the prerogative of clemency."[\[180\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood423424-201) The Judge President Sir [Vincent Quénet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Qu%C3%A9net "Vincent Quénet") and Justice [Hector Macdonald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hector_Macdonald_/(judge/) "Hector Macdonald (judge)") agreed, and the application was dismissed. Justice [John Fieldsend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Fieldsend "John Fieldsend") of the High Court's General Division resigned in protest, writing to Gibbs that he no longer believed the High Court to be defending the rights of Rhodesian citizens. Dhlamini, Mlambo and Shadreck were hanged on 6 March.[\[180\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood423424-201)

On 23 July 1968, the Privy Council in London ruled in Madzimbamuto's favour, deciding that orders for detention made by the Rhodesian government were invalid regardless of whether the 1961 or 1965 constitution was considered effective. It declared the latter, "revolutionary" constitution illegal, and ruled that the former was overridden by the [Southern Rhodesia Act 1965](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_Act_1965 "Southern Rhodesia Act 1965"), which had effectively outlawed the Rhodesian legislative, administrative and legal authorities in British law. [Lord Reid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Reid,_Baron_Reid "James Reid, Baron Reid"), delivering the majority opinion ([Lord Pearce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Pearce,_Baron_Pearce "Edward Pearce, Baron Pearce") dissented), argued that the "usurper" government, though the effective master of Rhodesia, could not be considered lawful as the UK government was still attempting to regain control and it was impossible to say whether or not it would succeed. He ruled that only Whitehall could determine what constituted the maintenance of "law and order" in Rhodesia, and that the Rhodesian emergency measures were unlawful as they had been formalised by the Officer Administering the Government, a post-UDI figure who was, in British eyes, unconstitutional. Reid concluded that Madzimbamuto was illegally detained.[\[179\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood487488-200) Harry Davies, one of the Rhodesian judges, announced on 8 August that the Rhodesian courts would not consider this ruling binding as they no longer accepted the Privy Council as part of the Rhodesian judicial hierarchy. Justice [J. R. Dendy Young](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dendy_Young "Dendy Young") resigned in protest at Davies' ruling on 12 August and four days later was sworn in as Chief Justice of Botswana.[\[181\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood499-202)

The Rhodesian High Court granted full _de jure_ recognition to the post-UDI government on 13 September 1968, while rejecting the appeals of 32 black Rhodesians who had been a month earlier convicted of terrorist offences and sentenced to death. Beadle declared that while he believed the Rhodesian judiciary should respect rulings of the Privy Council "so far as possible", the judgement of 23 July had made it legally impossible for Rhodesian judges to continue under the 1961 constitution. He asserted that the court therefore faced a choice between the 1965 constitution and a legal vacuum, the latter of which he felt he could not endorse.[\[182\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood513-203) Referring to the Privy Council's decision that the UK might yet remove the post-UDI government, he said that "on the facts as they exist today, the only prediction which this court can make is that sanctions will not succeed in overthrowing the present government ... and that there are no other factors which might succeed in doing so".[\[177\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-gowllanddebbas7576-198)

Macdonald, a member of Beadle's ruling panel, argued that since UDI, the British government had acted unconstitutionally and illegally regarding Rhodesia by involving the United Nations in what should have been legally considered a domestic problem, and had concurrently abdicated its right to the allegiance of the Rhodesian people by waging economic war against the country and encouraging other nations to do the same. To support this argument, Macdonald referred to the assertion by the 17th-century Dutch jurist [Hugo Grotius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugo_Grotius "Hugo Grotius") that "the purpose of governing and the purpose of destroying cannot subsist together".[\[183\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-young538541-204) Since Britain was in a state of economic war against Rhodesia, the court concluded, it could not at the same time be regarded as governing it.[\[183\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-young538541-204) UDI, the associated 1965 constitution and the government were thereafter considered _de jure_ by the Rhodesian legal system.[\[177\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-gowllanddebbas7576-198)

The British Commonwealth Secretary, [George Thomson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Thomson,_Baron_Thomson_of_Monifieth "George Thomson, Baron Thomson of Monifieth"), promptly accused the Rhodesian judges of breaching "the fundamental laws of the land",[\[182\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood513-203) while Gibbs announced that since his position as Governor existed under the 1961 constitution, which allowed appeals to the Privy Council, he could only reject the Rhodesian court ruling.[\[182\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood513-203) The Rhodesian judges continued regardless. Their recognition of the post-UDI order carried over to the [1969 republican constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1969_Rhodesian_constitutional_referendum "1969 Rhodesian constitutional referendum"), adopted in 1970.[\[177\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-gowllanddebbas7576-198)

Replacement of national symbols
-------------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Replacement of national symbols")\]

[![Image 12: A sky blue flag with the Union Jack in the upper-left-hand corner, and a coat of arms on the right.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/Flag_of_Rhodesia_%281964%E2%80%931968%29.svg/250px-Flag_of_Rhodesia_%281964%E2%80%931968%29.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flag_of_Rhodesia_/(1964%E2%80%931968/).svg)

[![Image 13: A flag with vertical green, white and green stripes, with a coat of arms on the central white stripe.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/02/Flag_of_Rhodesia_%281968%E2%80%931979%29.svg/250px-Flag_of_Rhodesia_%281968%E2%80%931979%29.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flag_of_Rhodesia_/(1968%E2%80%931979/).svg)

Rhodesian green-and-white [triband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triband_/(flag/) "Triband (flag)"), adopted in 1968

Vestiges of British ties were removed piecemeal by the government over the decade following UDI, and replaced with symbols and terminology intended to be more uniquely Rhodesian.[\[185\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-nyoka-207) A silver "[Liberty Bell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Independence_Bell "Rhodesian Independence Bell")", based on the bell of the [same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_Bell "Liberty Bell") in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia"), was cast during 1966 and rung by the Prime Minister 12 times each year on [Independence Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_holidays_in_Rhodesia "Public holidays in Rhodesia") (the anniversary of UDI), with some in the press erroneously believing the number of chimes signifying the number of years since the declaration of independence.[\[186\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-208) The [Union Jack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_Jack "Union Jack") and [Rhodesia's Commonwealth-style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_of_Southern_Rhodesia "Flag of Southern Rhodesia") [national flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_of_Rhodesia "Flag of Rhodesia")—a [defaced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defacement_/(flag/) "Defacement (flag)") [Sky Blue Ensign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Ensign "Blue Ensign") with the Union Jack in the canton—continued to fly over government buildings, military bases and other official locations until 11 November 1968, the third anniversary of UDI, when they were superseded by a new national flag: a green-white-green vertical [triband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triband_/(flag/) "Triband (flag)"), [charged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charge_/(heraldry/) "Charge (heraldry)") centrally with the [Rhodesian coat of arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coat_of_arms_of_Rhodesia "Coat of arms of Rhodesia").[\[187\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-young585-209) The Union Jack continued to be ceremonially raised at Cecil Square in Salisbury on 12 September each year as part of the [Pioneers' Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_holidays_in_Rhodesia "Public holidays in Rhodesia") holiday, which marked the anniversary of the establishment of Salisbury (and, by extension, Rhodesia) in 1890.[\[188\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-210)

Since Elizabeth II was still the Rhodesian head of state in the eyes of Smith's administration until 1970, "[God Save the Queen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God_Save_the_Queen "God Save the Queen")" remained the Rhodesian national anthem, and continued to accompany official occasions such as the opening of the Rhodesian parliament. This was intended to demonstrate Rhodesia's continued loyalty to the Queen, but the use of the unmistakably British song at Rhodesian state occasions soon seemed "fairly ironic", as _[The Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Times "The Times")_ put it.[\[189\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-buch243-211) Salisbury started looking for a replacement anthem around the same time as its introduction of the new flag,[\[190\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-212) and in 1974, after four years without an anthem ("God Save the Queen" was formally dropped in 1970), republican Rhodesia adopted "[Rise, O Voices of Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rise,_O_Voices_of_Rhodesia "Rise, O Voices of Rhodesia")", an anthem coupling original lyrics with the tune of [Beethoven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_van_Beethoven "Ludwig van Beethoven")'s "[Ode to Joy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symphony_No._9_/(Beethoven/) "Symphony No. 9 (Beethoven)")".[\[191\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-buch247248-213) The country's head of state under the republican constitution was the [President of Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Rhodesia "President of Rhodesia"), the first of whom was Dupont.[\[192\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-pb162-214)

State press censorship, which had been introduced on UDI, was lifted in early April 1968.[\[193\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-215) [Decimalisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decimalisation "Decimalisation") occurred on 17 February 1970, two weeks before Rhodesia's reconstitution as a republic, with the new [Rhodesian dollar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_dollar "Rhodesian dollar") replacing the [pound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_pound "Rhodesian pound") at a rate of two dollars to each pound.[\[194\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-216) Following the republic's formal declaration the next month, the Rhodesian military removed nomenclatural and symbolic references to the Crown—the Royal [Rhodesian Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Air_Force "Rhodesian Air Force") and Royal [Rhodesia Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia_Regiment "Rhodesia Regiment") dropped their "Royal" prefixes after the Queen formally revoked them because of the declaration,[\[195\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-217) new branch and regimental flags were designed, and the [St Edward's Crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Edward%27s_Crown "St Edward's Crown") surmounting many regimental emblems was expunged in favour of the "[Lion and Tusk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lion_and_Tusk "Lion and Tusk")", a motif from the coat of arms of the British South Africa Company that had been used in Rhodesian military symbolism since the 1890s. The air force's new [roundel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundel "Roundel") was a green ring with the lion and tusk on a white centre.[\[192\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-pb162-214) Later that year, a system of new [Rhodesian honours and decorations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orders,_decorations,_and_medals_of_Rhodesia "Orders, decorations, and medals of Rhodesia") was created to replace the old British honours. Rhodesia's police force, the [British South Africa Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_South_Africa_Police "British South Africa Police"), was not renamed.[\[196\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-218)

[![Image 14: A portrait photograph of Abel Muzorewa](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/Muzorewa_1978_b.jpg/250px-Muzorewa_1978_b.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Muzorewa_1978_b.jpg)

Bishop [Abel Muzorewa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel_Muzorewa "Abel Muzorewa"), the country's first black prime minister, whose unrecognised government revoked UDI in 1979 as part of the [Lancaster House Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster_House_Agreement "Lancaster House Agreement")

Wilson told the British House of Commons in January 1966 that he would not enter any kind of dialogue with the post-UDI Rhodesian "illegal regime" until it gave up its claim of independence,[\[197\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-219) but by mid-1966 British and Rhodesian civil servants were holding "talks about talks" in London and Salisbury.[\[198\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-220) By November that year, Wilson had agreed to negotiate personally with Smith.[\[199\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-221) The two Prime Ministers unsuccessfully attempted to settle aboard [HMS _Tiger_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Tiger_/(C20/) "HMS Tiger (C20)") in December 1966 and [HMS _Fearless_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Fearless_/(L10/) "HMS Fearless (L10)") in October 1968.

After the Conservatives returned to power in Britain [in 1970](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970_United_Kingdom_general_election "1970 United Kingdom general election"), provisional agreement was reached in November 1971 between the Rhodesian government and a British team headed by Douglas-Home (who was [Foreign Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Foreign_and_Commonwealth_Affairs "Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs") under Prime Minister [Edward Heath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Heath "Edward Heath")), and in early 1972 a Royal Commission chaired by Lord Pearce travelled to Rhodesia to investigate how acceptable the proposals were to majority opinion. After extensive consultation, the commission reported that while whites, [coloureds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloured "Coloured") and Asians were largely in favour of the presented terms, most blacks rejected them. The deal was therefore shelved by the British government.[\[200\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-222)

The [Rhodesian Bush War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Bush_War "Rhodesian Bush War"), a guerrilla conflict pitting the [Rhodesian Security Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Security_Forces "Rhodesian Security Forces") against the [Zimbabwe African National Liberation Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_African_National_Liberation_Army "Zimbabwe African National Liberation Army") (ZANLA) and the [Zimbabwe People's Revolutionary Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_People%27s_Revolutionary_Army "Zimbabwe People's Revolutionary Army") (ZIPRA), the respective armed wings of ZANU and ZAPU, began in earnest in December 1972, when ZANLA [attacked Altena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_on_Altena_Farm "Attack on Altena Farm") and Whistlefield Farms in north-eastern Rhodesia.[\[201\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-binda133136-223) The 1974 [Carnation Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnation_Revolution "Carnation Revolution") in Portugal, which over the next year replaced Portuguese support for Smith with an independent, [Marxist–Leninist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marxism%E2%80%93Leninism "Marxism–Leninism") Mozambique on Rhodesia's eastern frontier, greatly swung the war's momentum in favour of the nationalists (particularly ZANU, which was allied with Mozambique's governing [FRELIMO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FRELIMO "FRELIMO") party), and caused the sanctions on Rhodesia to finally begin having a noticeable effect.[\[202\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-224) Diplomatic isolation, the sanctions, guerrilla activities and pressure from South Africa to find a settlement led the Rhodesian government to hold talks with the various black Rhodesian factions. Abortive conferences were held at [Victoria Falls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Falls_Conference_/(1975/) "Victoria Falls Conference (1975)") (in 1975) and [Geneva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva_Conference_/(1976/) "Geneva Conference (1976)") (1976).[\[203\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-225) Despite ideological and tribal rifts, ZANU and ZAPU nominally united as the "Patriotic Front" (PF) in late 1976 in a successful attempt to augment overseas support for the black Rhodesian cause.[\[204\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-226)

By the mid-1970s, it was apparent that white minority rule could not continue forever. Even South Africa's prime minister [John Vorster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Vorster "John Vorster") realized that white rule in a country where blacks outnumbered whites 22:1 was not a realistic option.[\[205\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-impression-227) Smith, who was decisively re-elected three times during the 1970s, eventually came to this conclusion as well. He announced his acceptance in principle of [one man, one vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_man,_one_vote "One man, one vote") during [Henry Kissinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Kissinger "Henry Kissinger")'s Anglo-American initiative in September 1976, and in March 1978 concluded the [Internal Settlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_Settlement "Internal Settlement") with non-militant nationalist groups headed by Bishop [Abel Muzorewa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel_Muzorewa "Abel Muzorewa"), the Reverend [Ndabaningi Sithole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ndabaningi_Sithole "Ndabaningi Sithole") and Chief [Jeremiah Chirau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremiah_Chirau "Jeremiah Chirau"). This settlement, boycotted by the PF and rejected internationally,[\[206\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-228) led to [multiracial elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1979_Rhodesian_general_election "1979 Rhodesian general election") and Rhodesia's reconstitution under majority rule as [Zimbabwe Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_Rhodesia "Zimbabwe Rhodesia") in June 1979. Muzorewa, the electoral victor, took office as the country's first black prime minister at the head of a coalition cabinet comprising 12 blacks and five whites,[\[207\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-229) including Smith as [minister without portfolio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minister_without_portfolio "Minister without portfolio").[\[208\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-230) Dismissing Muzorewa as a "neocolonial puppet",[\[209\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-231) ZANLA and ZIPRA continued their armed struggle until December 1979, when Whitehall, Salisbury and the Patriotic Front [settled at Lancaster House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster_House_Agreement "Lancaster House Agreement"). Muzorewa's government revoked UDI, thereby ending the country's claim to be independent after 14 years, and dissolved itself. The UK suspended the constitution and vested full executive and legislative powers in a new Governor, [Lord Soames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Soames "Christopher Soames"), who oversaw a ceasefire and [fresh elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Southern_Rhodesian_general_election "1980 Southern Rhodesian general election") during February and March 1980. These were won by ZANU, whose leader [Robert Mugabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe "Robert Mugabe") became Prime Minister when the UK granted independence to Zimbabwe as a republic within the Commonwealth in April 1980.[\[210\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-232) African nationalist politicians continued to cite their opposition to the UDI as a means of legitimising their rule of Zimbabwe into the 21st century.[\[211\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-FOOTNOTENyamunda20161006-233) Since it was issued, the UDI has been recounted in scholarly literature, autobiographies of those involved in its creation, and works of fiction.[\[212\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-FOOTNOTENyamunda20161008-234)

1.  ^ [_**a**_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_ref-name_1-0) [_**b**_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_ref-name_1-1) [_**c**_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_ref-name_1-2) Renamed Zimbabwe in 1980.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-4) The official name of the colony under British law was [Southern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia "Southern Rhodesia"), but the colonial government switched to using the name [Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia_/(name/) "Rhodesia (name)") in October 1964, when [Northern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Rhodesia "Northern Rhodesia") changed its name to Zambia concurrently with its independence from Britain.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-palley742743-5)
2.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_ref-selfgoverning_9-0)** Powers reserved to the British government at Whitehall under the 1923 constitution concerned foreign affairs, alterations to the constitution, the British-appointed [Governor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Southern_Rhodesia "Governor of Southern Rhodesia")'s salary, and bills regarding native administration, mining revenues and railways. Laws relevant to these subjects had to receive assent from the Governor (and, by extension, Whitehall), but all other bills could be passed by Salisbury without interference.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-rowland247248-6)
3.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_ref-fed_23-0)** The original vision shared by Huggins and his Northern Rhodesian counterpart Sir [Roy Welensky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Welensky "Roy Welensky") was a [unitary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_state "Unitary state") amalgamation of the two Rhodesias that would eventually become a dominion. British politicians rejected this idea, asserting that black Northern Rhodesians would never accept it, but agreed to consider a Federation on the condition that neighbouring Nyasaland was also included.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-22)
4.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_ref-by1955_27-0)** Southern Rhodesian politicians from various parties later claimed that had Federation not occurred, Southern Rhodesia would have been a dominion by 1955.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-26)
5.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_ref-federaludi_33-0)** With Northern Rhodesia and Nyasaland under direct British control, a Federal UDI would have been far more complicated and difficult to execute than one by Southern Rhodesia alone. Indeed, it was partly because of this that Welensky deemed it infeasible.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood3-32)
6.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_ref-nationalists_47-0)** Zimbabwe, derived from the name applied by the [Shona people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shona_people "Shona people") to the ancient ruined city today referred to as [Great Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Zimbabwe "Great Zimbabwe"), was adopted by the black Rhodesian movement between 1960 and 1962 as their preferred name for a majority-ruled Southern Rhodesia.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-42) ZAPU was banned by the Whitehead administration in 1962 because of its violent activities,[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-43) but it continued operating nevertheless, publicly calling itself the People's Caretaker Council (PCC). Several prominent members left to form the rival [Zimbabwe African National Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_African_National_Union "Zimbabwe African National Union") (ZANU) in 1963. ZANU and ZAPU were respectively backed by China and the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union"), and influenced to various degrees by Chinese [Maoism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maoism "Maoism") and Soviet [Marxism–Leninism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marxism%E2%80%93Leninism "Marxism–Leninism").[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood173175-44) Following an escalation in internecine political violence between the two movements, a spate of industrial sabotage and civil disobedience and the politically motivated killing of a white man, Petrus Oberholzer, by ZANU insurgents, both PCC and ZANU were banned by Smith's government in August 1964, with most of each party's leaders concurrently jailed for criminal offences or otherwise restricted.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-45) Both movements thereafter based themselves overseas.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-46)

[Lord Alport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuthbert_Alport,_Baron_Alport "Cuthbert Alport, Baron Alport"), the UK's High Commissioner to the Federation, reportedly left the meeting and vomited.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood99-54)
8.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_ref-promise_59-0)** In particular, Field and Smith claimed that Butler told them at [Victoria Falls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Falls,_Zimbabwe "Victoria Falls, Zimbabwe") on 27 June 1963 that in return for their help in winding up the Federation, Southern Rhodesia would be granted "independence no later than, if not before, the other two territories ... in view of your country's wonderful record of Responsible Government over the past forty years ... and above all the great loyalty you have always given to Britain in time of war".[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-butlerpromise-58)

10.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_ref-lobby_74-0)** In particular, a small but vocal phalanx of stridently pro-Salisbury Conservative peers emerged in the [House of Lords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Lords "House of Lords"), including [Robert Gascoyne-Cecil, 5th Marquess of Salisbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Gascoyne-Cecil,_5th_Marquess_of_Salisbury "Robert Gascoyne-Cecil, 5th Marquess of Salisbury") (after whose grandfather the Southern Rhodesian capital was named), [Richard Law, 1st Baron Coleraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Law,_1st_Baron_Coleraine "Richard Law, 1st Baron Coleraine") and [Robert Grimston, 1st Baron Grimston of Westbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Grimston,_1st_Baron_Grimston_of_Westbury "Robert Grimston, 1st Baron Grimston of Westbury").[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-72) Together with an ancillary group of similarly minded Conservative MPs in the Commons, headed by Major [Patrick Wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Wall "Patrick Wall"), these became referred to as the "Rhodesia Lobby".[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-white97-73)
11.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_ref-harper_87-0)** The Lardner-Burke bill proposed that a two-thirds majority in the Legislative Assembly would prompt automatic consent for alterations from the Governor, who would then sign them into law on behalf of the Queen.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood200202-85) [William Harper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_John_Harper "William John Harper"), the Minister of Water Development and Roads, posited that if this passed, Salisbury would be able to proclaim an independent republic outside the Commonwealth with a two-thirds majority in parliament.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood204207-86)
12.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_ref-nativeborn_94-0)** [Roy Welensky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Welensky "Roy Welensky"), who held the Federal premiership from 1956 to dissolution in 1963, was also born in Southern Rhodesia. Before Smith, Southern Rhodesia had had seven Prime Ministers, three of whom (including Field) had been born in Britain. The country's first two Prime Ministers, [Charles Coghlan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Coghlan_/(politician/) "Charles Coghlan (politician)") (1923–27) and [Howard Moffat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Unwin_Moffat "Howard Unwin Moffat") (1927–33), were respectively born in South Africa and [Bechuanaland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bechuanaland_Protectorate "Bechuanaland Protectorate"),[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-91) while [Garfield Todd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garfield_Todd "Garfield Todd") (1953–58) was originally from New Zealand.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-92) [Edgar Whitehead](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Whitehead "Edgar Whitehead") (1958–62) was born at the British Embassy in Germany, where his father was a diplomat.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-93)
13.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_ref-102)** Britain told Southern Rhodesia that this was because the British economy was in trouble. When Salisbury pointed out that the UK was still giving aid to other countries, Whitehall implied that financial assistance might resume if progress was made towards an independence settlement acceptable to Britain.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood335-101)
14.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_ref-conference_104-0)** Salisbury attended under the Federal flag from 1953 to 1963.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-welenskyspeech-103)
15.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_ref-campaign64_111-0)** During the bitterly fought campaign,[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-byelection-108) Welensky was falsely personified by his opponents as representing appeasement of Britain and black extremists, and heckled at public concourses with cries of "communist", "traitor" and "coward";[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-109) one man even screamed "you bloody Jew" at Welensky during a debate.[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-110)
16.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_ref-observers_115-0)** Official observers came from Australia, Austria, France, Greece, New Zealand, Norway, Portugal, South Africa and Sweden.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood242243-114)
17.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_ref-name2_117-0)** Salisbury passed legislation to shorten the name, but Britain ruled this _[ultra vires](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultra_vires "Ultra vires")_ as the laws naming the country were British acts passed at Westminster. Salisbury went on using the shortened name in an official manner anyway,[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-palley742743-5) while the British government, the United Nations and other overseas bodies continued referring to the country as Southern Rhodesia. This situation continued throughout the UDI period.[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-rowland251-116)
18.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_ref-vote_125-0)** Turnout was 61% of the 105,444 registered voters (89,886 whites, 12,729 blacks and 2,829 [coloureds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloured "Coloured") and Asians). There were 58,091 ballots in favour, 6,096 against and 944 spoilt papers. Most eligible non-whites reportedly abstained.[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-wood249-124)
19.  **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_ref-crossvoting_132-0)** The electoral system devised in the 1961 constitution replaced the common voters' roll with two rolls, the "A" roll and the "B" roll, the latter of which had lower qualifications intended to make it easier for prospective voters to enter the political system. There were 50 "A"-roll constituencies and 15 larger "B"-roll districts, with a complicated mechanism of "cross-voting" allowing "B"-roll voters to slightly influence "A"-roll elections and _vice versa_. This system was theoretically non-racial, but in practice the "A" roll was largely white and the "B" roll was almost all black.[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence#cite_note-131)
