In 1970, the United States declared it would not recognise UDI "under \[any\] circumstances".[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-a-60) South Africa and Portugal, Rhodesia's largest trading partners, also refused to extend diplomatic recognition, and did not open embassies in the Rhodesian capital, [Salisbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harare "Harare"), preferring to conduct diplomatic activities through "accredited representatives".[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-google13-61) This allowed the South African and Portuguese governments to maintain they were continuing to respect British sovereignty while also accepting the practical authority of the Smith administration.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-google257-62) Initially, the Rhodesian state retained its pledged loyalty to Queen [Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II"), recognising her as Queen of Rhodesia.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) When Smith and Deputy Prime Minister [Clifford Dupont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_Dupont "Clifford Dupont") visited Sir [Humphrey Gibbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humphrey_Gibbs "Humphrey Gibbs"), the [Governor of Southern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Southern_Rhodesia "Governor of Southern Rhodesia"), to formally notify him of the UDI, Gibbs condemned it as an act of treason. After Smith formally announced the UDI on the radio, Governor Gibbs used his [reserve power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reserve_power "Reserve power") to dismiss Smith and his entire cabinet from office, on orders from the [Colonial Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonial_Office "Colonial Office") in [Whitehall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehall "Whitehall"). However, Gibbs was unable to take any concrete actions to bring about a return to lawful colonial government. Rhodesian ministers simply ignored his notices, contending that UDI had made his office obsolete. Even so, Gibbs continued to occupy his [official residence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_residence "Official residence"), [Government House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_House,_Harare "State House, Harare"), in Salisbury until 1970, when he finally left Rhodesia, following the declaration of a republic.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Age-63) He had effectively been superseded before then; the Smith government stated that if the Queen did not appoint a Governor-General, it would name Dupont as "[Officer Administering the Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Officer_Administering_the_Government "Officer Administering the Government")".[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-strips-64) Smith had intended to have Dupont named Governor-General, but Queen Elizabeth II would not even consider this advice.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-65) With few exceptions, the international community backed Whitehall's assertion that Gibbs was the Queen's only legitimate representative, and hence the only lawful authority in Rhodesia. In September 1968, the [Appellate Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appellate_court "Appellate court") of the [High Court of Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Court_of_Rhodesia "High Court of Rhodesia") ruled that Ian Smith's administration had become the _de jure_ government of the country, not merely the _de facto_ one.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Beadle-66) To support his decision, Chief Justice Sir [Hugh Beadle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Beadle "Hugh Beadle") used several statements made by [Hugo Grotius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugo_Grotius "Hugo Grotius"), who maintained that there was no way that a nation could rightly claim to be governing a particular territory – if it was waging a war against that territory. Beadle argued that due to Britain's economic war against Rhodesia, she could not (at the same point) be described as _governing_ Rhodesia.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-67)[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-68) The ruling set the precedent that despite the UDI, the incumbent Smith government "could lawfully do anything its predecessors could lawfully have done".[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-legalitylaw-69) A Salisbury commission chaired by prominent lawyer W.R. Waley was appointed to study constitutional options open to the Rhodesian authorities as of April 1968, including on the topic of majority rule, but reopening negotiations with the British on a settlement was ruled out early on.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-weitzer1990-25)[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-70) The Waley Commission found that in practical as well as legal terms, "Europeans must surrender any belief in permanent European domination", pointing out that minority rule was not permanently sustainable.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) However, Waley also testified that majority rule was not desirable immediately.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) Talks aimed at easing the differences between Rhodesia and the United Kingdom were carried out aboard Royal Navy vessels once in December 1966 and again in October 1968.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-71)[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-72)[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-73) Both efforts failed to achieve agreement, although Harold Wilson added a sixth principle to the five he had previously enunciated: "it would be necessary to ensure that, regardless of race, there was no oppression of the majority by the minority or of \[any\] minority by the majority." Rhodesian resolve stiffened following a failure to reach a new settlement, with more radical elements of the Rhodesian Front calling for a republican constitution.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) During a [two-proposition referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_constitutional_referendum,_1969 "Rhodesian constitutional referendum, 1969") held in 1969, the proposal for severing all remaining ties to the British Crown passed by a majority of 61,130 votes to 14,327.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) Rhodesia declared itself a republic on 2 March 1970. Under the new constitution, a president served as ceremonial head of state, with the prime minister nominally reporting to him.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-74) Some in the Rhodesian government had hoped in vain that the declaration of a republic would finally prompt other nations to grant recognition.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-75) The years following Rhodesia's UDI saw an unfolding series of economic, military, and political pressures placed on the country that eventually brought about majority rule, a totality of these factors rather than any one the reason for introducing change.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-frontiersmen-76) In 2005, a conference at the [London School of Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_School_of_Economics "London School of Economics") that discussed Rhodesia's independence concluded that UDI was sparked by an existing racial conflict complicated by [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War") intrigues.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-b-77) Critics of UDI maintained that Ian Smith intended to safeguard the privileges of an entrenched colonial ruling class at the expense of the impoverished black population.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-c-78) Smith defended his actions by claiming that the black Rhodesian majority was too inexperienced at the time to participate in the complex administrative process of what was, by contemporary African standards, a reasonably industrialised state.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-SmithGB-32) At large, UDI further hardened the white population's attitudes towards majority rule and relations with the UK.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-raft-47) A significant majority of white Rhodesian residents were either British immigrants or of British ancestry, and many held a special affection for the British Empire.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-raft-47) However, the UK's refusal to grant them independence on their terms further confirmed their opposition to a political settlement on British terms, and fed their negative attitudes towards British interference in Rhodesian politics at large.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-raft-47) In the years prior to UDI, white Rhodesians increasingly saw themselves as beleaguered and threatened, perpetually insecure and undermined by the metropole, unable to rely on anybody but themselves.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-SmithGB-32) The policy of "No independence before majority rule" transformed the white community's relationship with the UK and increased its suspicions of the British government's untrustworthiness and duplicity in colonial affairs, especially since the latter had adopted NIBMR as a formal policy - the very circumstance UDI was carried out to avoid, and which white Rhodesians had struggled to resist since the onset of decolonisation.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-SmithGB-32) Black nationalist parties reacted with outrage at UDI, with one ZANU official stating, "for all those who cherish freedom and a meaningful life, UDI has set a collision course that cannot be altered. 11 November 1965 \[has\] marked the turning point of the struggle for freedom in that land from a constitutional and political one to primarily a military struggle."[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) It would, however, be several years before the nationalists adopted armed struggle as their primary strategy for obtaining political power.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) Violent tactics at this time were intended to create opportunities for [external intervention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interventionism_/(politics/) "Interventionism (politics)"), either by the international community or the British government, rather than seriously undermine the Rhodesian security forces.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) Because Rhodesian exports were generally competitive and had previously been entitled to preferential treatment on the British market, the former colony did not recognise the need for escalating the pace of [diversification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diversification_/(marketing_strategy/) "Diversification (marketing strategy)") before independence. Following the UDI, however, Rhodesia began to demonstrate that it had the potential to develop a greater degree of economic [self-sufficiency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-sufficiency "Self-sufficiency").[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-SmithGB-32)[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-79) After the Rhodesian Front began introducing incentives accorded to domestic production, industrial output expanded dramatically. A rigid system of countermeasures enacted to combat sanctions succeeded in blunting their impact for at least a decade.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) Over the next nine years, Rhodesian companies, spiting the [freezing of their assets and blocking of overseas accounts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_asset_recovery "International asset recovery"), also perfected cunning techniques of sanctions evasion through both local and foreign subsidiaries, which operated on a clandestine trade network.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) From 1968 until 1970, there was virtually no further dialogue between Rhodesia and the UK. In a [referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_constitutional_referendum,_1969 "Rhodesian constitutional referendum, 1969") in 1969, white voters approved a new constitution and the establishment of a republic, thereby severing Rhodesia's last links with the British Crown, duly declared in March 1970. This changed immediately after the election of [Edward Heath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Heath "Edward Heath"), who reopened negotiations.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-racewar-80) Smith remained optimistic that Heath would do his utmost to remedy Anglo-Rhodesian relations, although disappointed that he continued to adhere publicly to the original "five principles" proposed by Alec Douglas-Home, now [foreign secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secretary_of_State_for_Foreign_and_Commonwealth_Affairs "Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs"). In November 1971, Douglas-Home renewed contacts with Salisbury and announced a proposed agreement that would be satisfactory to both sides – it recognised Rhodesia's 1969 constitution as the legal frame of government, while agreeing that gradual legislative representation was an acceptable formula for unhindered advance to majority rule.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) Nevertheless, the new settlement, if approved, would also implement an immediate improvement in black political status, offer a means to terminate racial discrimination, and provide a solid guarantee against retrogressive constitutional amendments.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-81) Implementation of the proposed settlement hinged on popular acceptance, but the Rhodesian government consistently refused to submit it to a universal referendum.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) A twenty four-member commission headed by an eminent jurist, [Lord Pearce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Pearce,_Baron_Pearce "Edward Pearce, Baron Pearce"), was therefore tasked with ascertaining [public opinion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_opinion "Public opinion") on the subject.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-historyps-82) In 1972, the commission began interviewing interest groups and sampling opinions – although concern was expressed over the widespread [apathy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_apathy "Political apathy") encountered.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-SmithGB-32) According to the commission, whites were in favour of the settlement, and Rhodesians of [Coloured](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coloured "Coloured") or Asian ancestry generally pleased, while the black response to the settlement's terms was resoundingly negative.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-racewar-80)[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-83) As many as thirty black Rhodesian chiefs and politicians voiced their opposition, prompting Britain to withdraw from the proposals on the grounds of the commission's report.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-historyps-82) #### Early militant activity \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia&action=edit§ion=7 "Edit section: Early militant activity")\] As early as 1960, [minority rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_rule "Minority rule") in Southern Rhodesia was already being challenged by a rising tide of [political violence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_violence "Political violence") led by black African nationalists such as [Joshua Nkomo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Nkomo "Joshua Nkomo") and [Ndabaningi Sithole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ndabaningi_Sithole "Ndabaningi Sithole"). A sustained period of civil unrest between 1960 and 1965 further polarised relations between the government and the increasingly militant black nationalists.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) After their public campaigns were initially suppressed, many black nationalists believed that negotiation was completely incapable of meeting their aspirations. Petrol bombings by politicised radicals became increasingly common, with the _Zimbabwe Review_ observing in 1961, "for the first time home-made petrol bombs were used by freedom fighters in Salisbury against settler establishments."[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-84) Between January and September 1962, nationalists detonated 33 bombs and were implicated in 28 acts of arson, and 27 acts of sabotage against communications infrastructure.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) The nationalists also murdered a number of black Rhodesians who were accused of collaboration with the security forces.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) Nkomo's party, the [Zimbabwe African People's Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_African_People%27s_Union "Zimbabwe African People's Union") (ZAPU) announced that year that it had formed a military wing, the [Zimbabwe People's Revolutionary Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_People%27s_Revolutionary_Army "Zimbabwe People's Revolutionary Army") (ZIPRA) and "the decision to start bringing in arms and ammunition and to send young men away for sabotage training" had already been implemented.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) As early as 1960, ZAPU's predecessor, the National Democratic Party (NDP), had established informal contacts with the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") and [Czechoslovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czechoslovak_Socialist_Republic "Czechoslovak Socialist Republic"), and discussed the possibility of obtaining military training in Eastern Europe for its members.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Hot-85) In July 1962, Nkomo visited Moscow and discussed plans for a ZAPU-led armed uprising in Rhodesia.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Hot-85) He made formal requests for Soviet funding and arms for ZIPRA, explaining that "for these purposes ZAPU needs arms, explosives, revolvers...the party also needs money to bribe persons who guard important installations, to carry out sabotage".[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Hot-85) The Soviets agreed to supply ZAPU with limited funds beginning in 1963, and increased its level of financial support after UDI.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Hot-85) In 1963, ZIPRA also made its first formal request to the Soviet Union for military training.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Hot-85) The Soviets began training ZIPRA militants in guerrilla warfare in early 1964.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Hot-85) Nkomo's public endorsement of a violent strategy confirmed white politicians' opposition to ZAPU and fed their negative attitudes towards black nationalists at large.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) In response to the formation of ZIPRA, the Rhodesian government [banned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ban_/(law/) "Ban (law)") ZAPU, driving that party's supporters underground.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-crisis-86) It also passed draconian security legislation restricting the right to assembly and granting the security forces broad powers to crack down on suspected political subversives.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) For the first time, the [death sentence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment "Capital punishment") was also introduced for any act of politically inspired terrorism which involved arson or the use of explosives.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) The emergence of guerrilla warfare and acts of urban insurrection by the black nationalist parties in Rhodesia allowed racial politics to be elevated into an issue of law and order in white Rhodesian public discourse. To Smith and his government, black nationalists were stateless dissidents whose primary motives were not political, but crime and perpetuating lawlessness; for example, Smith preferred to describe the insurgents as "gangsters" in his commentary.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-SmithGB-32) The use of weapons and explosives sourced from communist states by the black nationalists also disguised the racial dynamics of the conflict, allowing white Rhodesians to claim that they were targets of Soviet-directed communist agitators rather than a domestic political movement.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-frontiersmen-76) Smith and his supporters perceived themselves as collective defenders of the traditional values of the [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire") against the twin threats of international communism, manifested through the Soviet Union's support for black nationalist militants, and the social and political decadence of the West.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-raft-47) Often repeated appeals to the Christian heritage of their pioneer ancestors in "defending the [free world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_world "Free world")" and sustaining "Western civilisation" reflected these beliefs.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-raft-47) This was hardly an unusual opinion among white minorities in Southern Africa at the time; a dossier compiled by United States intelligence officials on the topic found that: > many \[southern African\] whites....believe that the current social and political ferment throughout the continent is communist inspired and managed; that it would be no problem without communist instigation. They point to materiel and training provided by communist countries to insurgency groups operating against white minority governments in southern Africa. They see foreign-based black liberation groups operating against the Portuguese, Rhodesians, and South Africans as the spearhead of a communist thrust into southern Africa.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Volk-87) ZAPU's attempts to implement its armed struggle were hamstrung by a factional split within the party between 1962 and 1963. A number of ZAPU dissidents rejected Nkomo's authority and formed their own organisation, the [Zimbabwe African National Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_African_National_Union "Zimbabwe African National Union") (ZANU), with Ndabaningi Sithole as its president and [Robert Mugabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe "Robert Mugabe") as its general secretary.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Hot-85) By August 1964, ZANU was banned by the Rhodesian government as well, which cited widespread acts of violent intimidation attributed to its members.[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-88) ZANU's agenda was left-wing and [pan-Africanist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan-Africanism "Pan-Africanism"); it demanded a one-party state with majority rule and the abolition of private property.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) Ethnic tensions also exacerbated the split: ZANU recruited almost solely from the [Shona-speaking peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shona_people "Shona people") of Rhodesia.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Hot-85) Its chief support base was the rural peasantry in the [Mashonaland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mashonaland "Mashonaland") countryside.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-areahandbook-9) ZAPU did retain Shona members, even among its senior leadership following the split.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Hot-85) However, thereafter it recruited predominantly from the [Ndebele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ndebele_people "Northern Ndebele people") ethnic group.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-frontiersmen-76) Due to ZAPU's close relationship with the Soviet Union, ZANU found itself ostracised by the Soviet bloc but soon found a new ally in the [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China").[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Hot-85) Its political ideology was somewhat more influenced by the principles of [Maoism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maoism "Maoism") than ZAPU, and a sympathetic Chinese government soon agreed to furnish weapons and training for ZANU's own war effort.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-MWM-89) After UDI, ZANU formed its own military wing, the [Zimbabwe African National Liberation Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_African_National_Liberation_Army "Zimbabwe African National Liberation Army") (ZANLA).[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-frontiersmen-76) While ZANLA and ZIPRA both planned for an armed struggle against the Rhodesian government, their respective leadership disagreed on the means of conducting the insurgency. ZIPRA favoured Soviet thinking, placing an emphasis on acquiring sophisticated weaponry in the hopes of winning a conventional battle like the [Viet Minh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viet_Minh "Viet Minh") at [Dien Bien Phu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Dien_Bien_Phu "Battle of Dien Bien Phu").[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-frontiersmen-76) ZANLA placed greater emphasis on the politicisation of the local populace in the areas it operated, and favoured a more irregular style of warfare.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-frontiersmen-76) [![Image 7](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a6/Scoutwithgun.jpg/250px-Scoutwithgun.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Scoutwithgun.jpg) Rhodesian soldier interrogating villagers in late 1977 at gunpoint. This photograph would become one of the most enduring images of the [Bush War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Bush_War "Rhodesian Bush War"). In early April 1966, two groups of ZANLA insurgents recently trained at a Chinese military facility in [Nanjing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanjing "Nanjing") crossed into Rhodesia from Zambia, having been issued vague instructions to sabotage important installations and kill white farmers.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) Five were arrested by the Rhodesian security forces almost immediately.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) Another seven initially evaded capture and planned to destroy an [electric pylon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electricity_pylon "Electricity pylon") near [Sinoia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinhoyi "Chinhoyi").[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) Their explosive charges failed to detonate and were discovered by the [Rhodesian Security Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Security_Forces "Rhodesian Security Forces"), who tracked the insurgents to a nearby ranch on 28 April.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-blackfire-48) All seven were cornered and killed after a brief firefight; this event is considered to be the first engagement of the [Rhodesian Bush War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Bush_War "Rhodesian Bush War").[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-military-90)[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-91) The action at Sinoia has been commemorated by supporters of the guerrillas since as "_Chimurenga Day_", and occupies a place of pride in ZANU hagiography.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-MWM-89) In August 1967, a large and better-equipped column of almost seventy ZIPRA insurgents infiltrated Rhodesia from Zambia, bolstered by recruits from an allied South African militant organisation, [uMkhonto we Sizwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UMkhonto_we_Sizwe "UMkhonto we Sizwe") (MK).[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-MWM-89) The insurgents failed to cultivate prior contacts with the local populace, which immediately informed on their presence to Rhodesian officials. Within the month, the [Rhodesian police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_South_Africa_Police "British South Africa Police") and army had launched a counteroffensive codenamed [Operation Nickel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Nickel "Operation Nickel"), killing forty-seven insurgents, capturing another twenty, and driving the survivors across the border into Botswana. An even larger ZIPRA column of over a hundred insurgents was intercepted in early 1968 and annihilated by the security forces.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-frontiersmen-76) A third ZIPRA incursion attempt in July 1969 met with similarly catastrophic results.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-frontiersmen-76) Thereafter, ZIPRA abandoned the notion of attempting to infiltrate the country with large groups of insurgents equipped only with small arms; it limited itself to more irregular forms of warfare until it could stockpile enough heavy weaponry to mount a major conventional invasion.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-MWM-89) For its part, the ZANLA leadership criticised ZIPRA's continued fixation with winning a major conventional engagement, arguing that the failed incursions demonstrated the futility of engaging the Rhodesian military in the type of pitched battles in which it held an indisputable advantage.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-MWM-89) ZIPRA's failure to obtain support from the locals was also noted, and ZANLA began implementing a long-term covert politicisation programme to cultivate civilian support throughout its future area of operations.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-MWM-89) ### Military and political escalation (1972–1976) \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: Military and political escalation (1972–1976)")\] By December 1972, ZANLA had cached arms and established a vast underground network of informants and supporters in northeastern Rhodesia.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-MWM-89) As a result of the erosion of Portuguese authority in Mozambique's border provinces due to the [Mozambican War of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozambican_War_of_Independence "Mozambican War of Independence"), ZANLA was also able to establish external sanctuaries there.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-MWM-89) It was also in the process of cultivating a military alliance with the leading black nationalist movement in Mozambique, the [Front for the Liberation of Mozambique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Front_for_the_Liberation_of_Mozambique "Front for the Liberation of Mozambique") (FRELIMO).[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-MWM-89) On 21 December, a group of ZANLA insurgents under [Rex Nhongo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rex_Nhongo "Rex Nhongo") crossed into Rhodesia from Mozambique and [raided an isolated commercial farm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_on_Altena_Farm "Attack on Altena Farm").[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-frontiersmen-76) In the successive months, this attack was followed by a succession of raids on white farmers throughout the northeastern districts of the country and resulted in several casualties among the security forces.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-frontiersmen-76) The propaganda value of these raids, coupled with the success of ZANLA's politicisation campaign, denied intelligence to the security forces and furnished more recruits for the insurgents.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-frontiersmen-76) In response, the Rhodesian security forces began coordinating operations in Mozambique with the [Portuguese Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Army "Portuguese Army") to intercept ZANLA insurgents before they could cross the border.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Minter-92) The practical alliances between ZIPRA and MK, and later ZANLA and FRELIMO, prompted Rhodesia to look increasingly towards South Africa and Portugal for active assistance.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Volk-87) Rhodesian politicians frequently reminded officials in the other two nations of common security interests based on the similarity of their restive internal situations.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Volk-87) They saw strong parallels between their nation's position of being threatened by black nationalist insurgencies and the Portuguese predicament with FRELIMO in Mozambique, as well as to a lesser extent the insurgencies in South Africa and [South West Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_West_Africa "South West Africa").[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Volk-87) Under the auspices of the [Alcora Exercise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcora_Exercise "Alcora Exercise"), the three countries' bureaucracies began routinely sharing information and seeking common diplomatic positions.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Volk-87) Lieutenant General [Alan Fraser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_%27Pop%27_Fraser "Charles 'Pop' Fraser"), a senior strategist in the [South African Defence Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_African_Defence_Force "South African Defence Force") wrote in 1970, "there can be no doubt in any of our minds that we have a common enemy: we, i.e. Portugal, the RSA and Rhodesia. Unless we are to lay ourselves open to the possibility of defeat in detail, we must fight this enemy jointly—if not simultaneously."[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Volk-87) Nevertheless, aside from intelligence-sharing and some limited coordination on the operational level in Mozambique, the Portuguese could offer Rhodesia little decisive assistance. Portuguese military resources in Mozambique were preoccupied with FRELIMO and somewhat depleted by a decade of war, and little could be spared to assist a foreign ally.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Volk-87) Rhodesia expected far more from South Africa, which possessed far greater military resources and infinitely more diplomatic influence abroad.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Volk-87) After the [Carnation Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnation_Revolution "Carnation Revolution") and the end of Portuguese rule in Mozambique in 1975, it was no longer viable for the Smith regime to sustain white [minority rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_rule "Minority rule") indefinitely. By this time, even South Africa's [John Vorster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Vorster "John Vorster") had come to this view. While Vorster was unwilling to make concessions to his own country's black people, he concluded that white minority rule was not sustainable in a country where black people outnumbered white people 22:1.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-impression-93) In 1976, there were 270,000 Rhodesians of European descent and six million Africans.[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-94) International business groups involved in the country (e.g. [Lonrho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonrho "Lonrho")) transferred their support from the Rhodesian government to black nationalist parties. Business leaders and politicians feted Nkomo on his visits to Europe. ZANU also attracted business supporters who saw the course that future events were likely to take.[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-95) Funding and arms support provided by supporters, particularly from the Soviet Union and its allies in the latter 1970s, allowed both ZIPRA and the ZANLA to acquire more sophisticated weaponry, thereby increasing the military pressure that the guerrillas were able to place on Rhodesia. Until 1972, containing the guerrillas was little more than a police action. Even as late as August 1975 when Rhodesian government and black nationalist leaders met [at Victoria Falls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Falls_Conference_/(1975/) "Victoria Falls Conference (1975)") for negotiations brokered by South Africa and Zambia, the talks never got beyond the procedural phase.[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-96) Rhodesian representatives made it clear they were prepared to fight an all out war to prevent majority rule.[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-97) However, the situation changed dramatically after the end of Portuguese colonial rule in Mozambique in 1975. Rhodesia now found itself almost entirely surrounded by hostile states and even South Africa, its only real ally, pressed for a settlement. > Having let slip one chance after another of reaching an accommodation with more moderate black leaders, Rhodesia's whites seem to have made the tragic choice of facing black nationalism over the barrel of a gun rather than the conference table. The downhill road toward a race war in Rhodesia is becoming increasingly slippery with blood. At this point, ZANU's alliance with FRELIMO and the porous border between Mozambique and eastern Rhodesia enabled large-scale training and infiltration of ZANU/ZANLA fighters. The governments of Zambia and Botswana were also emboldened sufficiently to allow resistance movement bases to be set up in their territories. Guerrillas began to launch operations deep inside Rhodesia, attacking roads, railways, economic targets and isolated security force positions, in 1976.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-99) [![Image 8](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/0/0c/Rhodesian_Army_recruitment_Bush_War_1976.png/250px-Rhodesian_Army_recruitment_Bush_War_1976.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rhodesian_Army_recruitment_Bush_War_1976.png) A Rhodesian servicewoman taking aim with her [Browning Hi-Power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Browning_Hi-Power "Browning Hi-Power") [9×19mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9%C3%9719mm "9×19mm") [semi-automatic pistol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-automatic_pistol "Semi-automatic pistol"); from a 1976 army recruitment poster The government adopted a [strategic hamlets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_hamlet "Strategic hamlet") policy of the kind used in [Malaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malayan_Emergency#Comparisons_with_Vietnam "Malayan Emergency") and [Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War") to restrict the influence of insurgents over the population of rural areas. Local people were forced to relocate to protected villages (PVs) which were strictly controlled and guarded by the government against rebel atrocities. The protected villages were compared by the guerrillas to [concentration camps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concentration_camps "Concentration camps"). Some contemporary accounts claim that this interference in the lives of local residents induced many of them who had previously been neutral to support the guerrillas.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-100) The war degenerated into rounds of increasing brutality from all three parties involved (ZANU and ZAPU, and the Rhodesian Army). Mike Subritzky, a former [New Zealand Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Army "New Zealand Army") ceasefire monitor in Rhodesia, in 1980 described the war as "both bloody and brutal and brought out the very worst in the opposing combatants on all three sides."[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-101) A major problem for the Rhodesian state in fighting the Bush War was always a shortage of manpower.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Brownell-102): 601  Of the 3,000 white men [liable for conscription](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscription_in_Rhodesia "Conscription in Rhodesia") in 1973, only about 1,000 reported when called-up.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Brownell-102): 601  In February 1978, the Rhodesian Army stated it needed a minimum of 1,041 men to continue combat operations, and of those called up, only 570 reported for duty while the rest chose to move to South Africa.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Brownell-102): 601  White emigration increased as the state called up more and more men to fight in the war, creating a vicious circle, which gradually limited the capacity of the Rhodesian state to continue the war.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Brownell-102): 602  In order to stop white emigration, the Smith government brought in a law in 1975 forbidding Rhodesian citizens from holding foreign currency, but the law was widely flouted.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Brownell-102): 604  In order to encourage white emigration, the guerrillas of ZANU and ZAPU followed a strategy of attacking anything and everything that was of economic value across the country in order to force the state to call up more men, and of killing white civilians.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Brownell-102): 606  Killing Rhodesian white citizens tended to have an "echo effect" as the ZANU and ZAPU had each estimated that for one white citizen killed, it caused about 20 to leave Rhodesia.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Brownell-102): 606 ### End of the Bush War \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia&action=edit§ion=9 "Edit section: End of the Bush War")\] [![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/RhodesiaAllies1965.png/250px-RhodesiaAllies1965.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:RhodesiaAllies1965.png) [![Image 10](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/RhodesiaAllies1975-en.svg/250px-RhodesiaAllies1975-en.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:RhodesiaAllies1975-en.svg) The geographical situation in 1965 (left, on UDI) and 1975 (right, after the independence of Mozambique and Angola from Portugal). Green: Rhodesia; purple: friendly nations; orange: hostile states; grey: neutral countries Rhodesia began to lose vital economic and military support from South Africa, which, while sympathetic to the white minority government, never accorded it diplomatic recognition. The South African government placed limits on the fuel and munitions they supplied to the Rhodesian military. They also withdrew the personnel and equipment that they had previously provided to aid the war effort, though covert military support continued.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-news.bbc.co.uk-103) In 1976, the South African government and [United States governments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_government "United States government") worked together to place pressure on Smith to agree to a form of majority rule. In response to the initiative of [United States Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_State "United States Secretary of State") [Henry Kissinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Kissinger "Henry Kissinger"), in 1976 Ian Smith accepted the principle of black majority rule within two years.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-news.bbc.co.uk-103) The Rhodesians now offered more concessions, but those concessions, focused on reaching an "internal settlement" with moderate black leaders, were insufficient to end the war. At the time, some Rhodesians said the still embittered history between the British-dominated Rhodesia and the [Afrikaner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrikaner "Afrikaner")\-dominated South Africa partly led the South African government to withdraw its aid to Rhodesia. Ian Smith said in his memoirs that even though many white South Africans supported Rhodesia, South African Prime Minister [John Vorster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Vorster "John Vorster")'s policy of [détente](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%A9tente "Détente") with the black African states ended up with Rhodesia being offered as the "sacrificial lamb" to buy more time for South Africa. Other observers perceived South Africa's distancing itself from Rhodesia as being an early move in the process that led to majority rule in South Africa itself.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-104) > In 1976 South Africa saw settlement of the Rhodesian question as vital on several fronts: to cauterise the wound of the psychological blow … caused by her defeat in the Angolan conflict; to pre-empt possible Cuban intervention in Rhodesia and the possibility of South Africa being sucked into another [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War") regional conflict without the support and endorsement of the western powers In the latter 1970s, the militants had successfully put the economy of Rhodesia under significant pressure while the numbers of guerrillas in the country were steadily increasing.[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-106)[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-107) The government abandoned its early strategy of trying to defend the borders in favour of trying to defend key economic areas and lines of communication with South Africa, while the rest of the countryside became a patchwork of "[no-go areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No-go_area "No-go area")". By the late 1970s, Rhodesia's front-line forces contained about 25,000 regular troops and police – backed up by relatively strong army and police reserves.[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-108) Its mechanised contingent consisted of light armoured cars and improvised [mine-protected](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MRAP "MRAP") armoured personnel carriers, complemented by eight tanks (Polish built [T-55LD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-54/T-55_Operators_and_variants#Poland "T-54/T-55 Operators and variants") tanks), delivered in the last year of the war. The [Rhodesian Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Air_Force "Rhodesian Air Force") operated an assortment of both [Canberra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Electric_Canberra "English Electric Canberra") light bombers, [Hawker Hunter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawker_Hunter "Hawker Hunter") fighter bombers, older [de Havilland Vampire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Havilland_Vampire "De Havilland Vampire") jets as well as a somewhat antiquated, but still potent, helicopter arm. These forces, including highly trained special operations units, were capable of launching devastating raids on resistance movement camps outside the country, as in [Operation Dingo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Dingo "Operation Dingo") in 1977 and other similar operations.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] Nevertheless, guerrilla pressure inside the country itself was steadily increasing in the latter 1970s. By 1978–1979, the war had become a contest between the guerrilla warfare placing ever increasing pressure on the Rhodesian regime and civil population, and the Rhodesian government's strategy of trying to hold off the militants until external recognition for a compromise political settlement with moderate black leaders could be secured. By this time, the need to cut a deal was apparent to most Rhodesians, but not to all. Ian Smith had dismissed his intransigent Defence Minister, [P. K. van der Byl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P._K._van_der_Byl "P. K. van der Byl"), as early as 1976.[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-109) Van der Byl was a hard-line opponent of any form of compromise with domestic opposition or the international community since before UDI. > ...it is better to fight to the last man and the last cartridge and die with some honour. Because, what is being presented to us here is a degree of humiliation... — P. K. van der Byl in 1977, commenting on a British peace plan.[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-110) Van der Byl eventually retired to his country estate outside [Cape Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Town "Cape Town"), but there were elements in Rhodesia, mainly embittered former security force personnel, who forcibly opposed majority rule up to and well beyond the establishment of majority rule.[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-111) New white immigrants continued to arrive in Rhodesia right up to the eve of majority rule.[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-112) #### Intensification of the Bush War \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia&action=edit§ion=11 "Edit section: Intensification of the Bush War")\] The work of journalists such as [Lord Richard Cecil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Richard_Cecil "Lord Richard Cecil"), son of [Robert Gascoyne-Cecil, 6th Marquess of Salisbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Gascoyne-Cecil,_6th_Marquess_of_Salisbury "Robert Gascoyne-Cecil, 6th Marquess of Salisbury"), stiffened the morale of Rhodesians and their overseas supporters.[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-113) Lord Richard produced news reports for [ITN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITN "ITN") which typically contrasted the "incompetent" insurgents with the "superbly professional" government troops.[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-114) A group of ZANLA fighters killed Lord Richard on 20 April 1978 when he was accompanying a Rhodesian airborne unit employed in [Fire Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_Force_/(Rhodesia/) "Fire Force (Rhodesia)") Operations.[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-115) The shooting down on 3 September 1978 of the civilian [Air Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Rhodesia "Air Rhodesia") airliner, a [Vickers Viscount](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vickers_Viscount "Vickers Viscount") named the _[Hunyani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Rhodesia_Flight_825 "Air Rhodesia Flight 825")_, in the [Kariba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kariba,_Zimbabwe "Kariba, Zimbabwe") area by ZIPRA fighters using a [surface-to-air missile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surface-to-air_missile "Surface-to-air missile"), with the subsequent massacre of 10 of its 18 survivors, is widely considered to be the event that finally destroyed the Rhodesians' will to continue the war. Although militarily insignificant, the loss of this aircraft (and a second Viscount, named the _[Umniati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Rhodesia_Flight_827 "Air Rhodesia Flight 827")_, in 1979) demonstrated the reach of resistance movements extended to Rhodesian civil society.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-116) The Rhodesians' means to continue the war were also eroding fast. In December 1978, a ZANLA unit penetrated the outskirts of Salisbury and fired a volley of rockets and [incendiary device](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incendiary_device "Incendiary device") rounds into the main oil storage depot – the most heavily defended economic asset in the country. The storage tanks burned for five days, giving off a column of smoke that could be seen 130 kilometres (80 mi) away. Five hundred thousand barrels (79,000 m3) of petroleum product (comprising Rhodesia's strategic oil reserve) were lost.[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-117) The government's defence spending increased from R$30 million, 8.5% of the national budget in 1971 to 1972, to R$400 m in 1978 to 1979, 47% of the national budget. In 1980, the post-independence government of Zimbabwe inherited a US$500 million national debt.[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-118) [![Image 11](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/Internal_Settlement.jpg/250px-Internal_Settlement.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Internal_Settlement.jpg) Signing of the Rhodesian Internal Settlement (from left: Bishop Abel Muzorewa, [Ian Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Smith "Ian Smith"), [Jeremiah Chirau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremiah_Chirau "Jeremiah Chirau") and [Ndabaningi Sithole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ndabaningi_Sithole "Ndabaningi Sithole")) The Rhodesian army continued its "mobile counter-offensive" strategy of holding key positions ("vital asset ground") while carrying out raids into the no-go areas and into neighbouring countries. While often extraordinarily successful in inflicting heavy guerrilla casualties, such raids also on occasion failed to achieve their objectives. In April 1979 special forces carried out a raid on [Joshua Nkomo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Nkomo "Joshua Nkomo")'s residence in [Lusaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lusaka "Lusaka"), [Zambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambia "Zambia"), with the stated intention of assassinating him.[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-119) Nkomo and his family left hastily a few hours before the raid – having clearly been warned that the raid was coming. In 1979, some special forces units were accused of using counterinsurgent operations as cover for ivory poaching and smuggling. Colonel [Reid-Daly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reid-Daly "Reid-Daly") (commander of the [Selous Scouts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selous_Scouts "Selous Scouts")) discovered that his phone was bugged and after challenging a superior officer on this issue was court martialled for insubordination. He received the lightest sentence possible, a caution, but he continued to fight his conviction and eventually resigned his commission and left the Army. By 1978–1979, up to 70% of the regular army was composed of black soldiers (though both the army and police reserves remained overwhelmingly white). By 1979 there were also 30 black commissioned officers in the regular army. While there was never any suggestion of disloyalty among the soldiers from predominantly black units (in particular within the Selous Scouts or the [Rhodesian African Rifles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_African_Rifles "Rhodesian African Rifles") – RAR), some argue that, by the time of the 1980 election, many of the RAR soldiers voted for Robert Mugabe.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-120) As the result of an [Internal Settlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_Settlement "Internal Settlement") signed on 3 March 1978 between the Rhodesian government and the moderate African nationalist parties, which were not in exile and not involved in the war, elections were held in April 1979. The [United African National Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_African_National_Council "United African National Council") (UANC) party won a majority in this election, and its leader, [Abel Muzorewa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abel_Muzorewa "Abel Muzorewa") (a [United Methodist Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Methodist_Church "United Methodist Church") bishop), became the country's first black prime minister on 1 June 1979. The country's name was changed to [Zimbabwe Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_Rhodesia "Zimbabwe Rhodesia"). The internal settlement left control of the country's police, security forces, civil service and judiciary in white hands, for the moment. It assured whites of about one-third of the seats in parliament. It was essentially a power-sharing arrangement between white people and black people which, in the eyes of many, particularly the insurgents, did not amount to majority rule.[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-121) However, the [United States Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") voted to end economic sanctions against Zimbabwe Rhodesia on 12 June.[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-endsanctions-122) While the 1979 election was described by the Rhodesian government as non-racial and democratic, it did not include the main nationalist parties ZANU and ZAPU. In spite of offers from Ian Smith, the latter parties declined to participate in an election in which their political position would be insecure and under a proposed constitution which they had played no part in drafting and which was perceived as retaining strong white minority privilege. Bishop Muzorewa's government did not receive international recognition. The Bush War continued unabated and sanctions were not lifted. The international community refused to accept the validity of any agreement which did not incorporate the main nationalist parties. The British government (then led by the recently elected [Margaret Thatcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Thatcher "Margaret Thatcher")) issued invitations to all parties to attend a peace conference at [Lancaster House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster_House "Lancaster House"). These negotiations took place in London in late 1979. The three-month-long conference almost failed to reach conclusion, due to disagreements on [land reform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_reform_in_Zimbabwe "Land reform in Zimbabwe"), but resulted in the [Lancaster House Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster_House_Agreement "Lancaster House Agreement"). UDI ended, and Rhodesia temporarily reverted to the status of a British colony (the 'Colony of Southern Rhodesia').[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-123) As per the agreement, [Lord Soames](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Soames "Christopher Soames") became governor with full legislative and executive powers. The Lancaster House Agreement further provided for a ceasefire which was followed by an internationally supervised general election, held in [February 1980](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesian_general_election,_1980 "Southern Rhodesian general election, 1980"). ZANU led by [Robert Mugabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe "Robert Mugabe") won this election, some alleged,\[_[who?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Words_to_watch#Unsupported_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_\] by terrorising its political opposition, including supporters of ZAPU, through former insurgents that had not confined themselves to the designated guerrilla assembly points, as stipulated by the Lancaster House Agreement. The observers and Soames were accused of looking the other way, and Mugabe's victory was certified. Nevertheless, few could doubt that Mugabe's support within his majority Shona tribal group was extremely strong. The Rhodesian military seriously considered mounting a coup against a perceived stolen election ("[Operation Quartz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Quartz "Operation Quartz")") to prevent ZANU from taking over the country.[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-124) The alleged coup was to include the assassination of Mugabe and coordinated assaults on guerrilla assembly points throughout the country. The plan was eventually scuttled, as it was obvious that Mugabe enjoyed widespread support from the black majority despite voter intimidation, as well as the fact that the coup would gain no external support, and a conflagration which would engulf the country was seen as inevitable. ### Republic of Zimbabwe (1980) \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia&action=edit§ion=13 "Edit section: Republic of Zimbabwe (1980)")\] On 18 April 1980, the country became independent within the [Commonwealth of Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations "Commonwealth of Nations") as the Republic of Zimbabwe, and its capital, Salisbury, was renamed [Harare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harare "Harare") two years later. Rhodesia is equivalent in territory to modern [Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe "Zimbabwe"). It was a [landlocked country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landlocked_country "Landlocked country") in [southern Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Africa "Southern Africa"), lying between latitudes [15°](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15th_parallel_south "15th parallel south") and [23°S](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/23rd_parallel_south "23rd parallel south"), and longitudes [25°](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/25th_meridian_east "25th meridian east") and [34°E](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/34th_meridian_east "34th meridian east"). It was bordered by [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") to the south, the [Bechuanaland Protectorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bechuanaland_Protectorate "Bechuanaland Protectorate") (later [Botswana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botswana "Botswana")) to the west and southwest, [Zambia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambia "Zambia") to the northwest, and [Mozambique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozambique "Mozambique") to the east and northeast. Its northwest corner was roughly 150 metres (500 feet) from [South West Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_West_Africa "South West Africa") (present-day [Namibia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Namibia "Namibia")), South Africa, nearly forming a four-nation [quadripoint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadripoint "Quadripoint"). Most of the country was elevated, consisting of a central plateau (high veld) stretching from the southwest northwards with altitudes between 1,000 and 1,600 m (3,300 and 5,200 ft). The country's extreme east was mountainous, this area being known as the [Eastern Highlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Highlands "Eastern Highlands"), with [Mount Inyangani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Nyangani "Mount Nyangani") as the highest point at 2,592 m (8,504 ft).\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] Rhodesia had a [tropical climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tropical_climate "Tropical climate") with many local variations. The southern areas were known for their heat and aridity, parts of the central plateau received frost in winter, the [Zambezi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zambezi "Zambezi") valley was also known for its extreme heat and the Eastern Highlands usually experienced cool temperatures and the highest rainfall in the country. The country's rainy season was from late October to March and the hot climate was moderated by increasing altitude. The country was faced with recurring droughts, and severe storms were rare.[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Baughan,_M._2005-125) The country was mostly savannah, although the moist and mountainous eastern highlands supported areas of tropical evergreen and hardwood forests. Trees found in these Eastern Highlands included [teak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teak "Teak"), [mahogany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahogany "Mahogany"), enormous specimens of [strangling fig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strangler_fig "Strangler fig"), [forest newtonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newtonia_buchananii "Newtonia buchananii"), big leaf, [white stinkwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celtis_africana "Celtis africana"), [chirinda stinkwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celtis_mildbraedii "Celtis mildbraedii"), [knobthorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senegalia_nigrescens "Senegalia nigrescens") and many others. In the low-lying parts of the country, [fever trees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vachellia_xanthophloea "Vachellia xanthophloea"), [mopane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mopane "Mopane"), [combretum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combretum "Combretum") and [baobabs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adansonia "Adansonia") abound. Much of the country was covered by [miombo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miombo "Miombo") woodland, dominated by [brachystegia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brachystegia "Brachystegia") species and others. Among the numerous flowers and shrubs were [hibiscus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hibiscus "Hibiscus"), [flame lily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flame_lily "Flame lily"), [snake lily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scadoxus_puniceus "Scadoxus puniceus"), [spider lily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spider_lily "Spider lily"), [leonotus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonotis "Leonotis"), [cassia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassia_/(genus/) "Cassia (genus)"), [tree wisteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wisteria "Wisteria") and [dombeya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dombeya "Dombeya"). There were around 350 species of mammals that can be found in Rhodesia. There were also many snakes and lizards, over 500 bird species, and 131 fish species. Government and politics ----------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia&action=edit§ion=17 "Edit section: Government and politics")\] [![Image 12](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/Flag_of_the_President_of_Rhodesia_%281970%E2%80%931979%29.svg/330px-Flag_of_the_President_of_Rhodesia_%281970%E2%80%931979%29.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flag_of_the_President_of_Rhodesia_/(1970%E2%80%931979/).svg) The presidential flag of Rhodesia Although Southern Rhodesia never gained full [Dominion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominion "Dominion") status within the [Commonwealth of Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations "Commonwealth of Nations"), Southern Rhodesians ruled themselves from the attainment of '[Responsible Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Responsible_government "Responsible government")' in 1923. Its electoral register had property and education qualifications. Over the years various electoral arrangements made at a national and municipal level upheld these standards. For example, the franchise for the first [Southern Rhodesian Legislative Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesian_Legislative_Council "Southern Rhodesian Legislative Council") election in 1899 contained the following requirement: > voters to be British subjects, male, 21 years of age and older, able to write their address and occupation, and then to fulfil the following financial requirements: (a) ownership of a registered mining claim in Southern Rhodesia, or (b) occupying immovable property worth £75, or (c) receiving wages or salary of £50 per annum in Southern Rhodesia. Six months' continuous residence was also required for qualifications (b) and (c). Following [Cecil Rhodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecil_Rhodes "Cecil Rhodes")'s dictum of "equal rights for all civilised men", there was an implicit, albeit not an overt, racial component to the franchise, which effectively excluded a majority of native black people from the electorate via such means as [property qualifications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Property_qualification "Property qualification").[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-126) Up until the 1950s, Southern Rhodesia had a vibrant political life with right and left wing parties competing for power. The [Rhodesian Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Labour_Party "Rhodesian Labour Party") held seats in the Assembly and in municipal councils throughout the 1920s and 1930s. From 1953 to 1958, the prime minister was [Garfield Todd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garfield_Todd "Garfield Todd"), a liberal who did much to promote the development of the black community through investment in education, housing and healthcare. However, the government forced Todd from office because his proposed reforms were seen by many whites as too radical. From 1958 onwards, white settler politics consolidated and ossified around resistance to majority rule, setting the stage for UDI. The 1961 Constitution governed Southern Rhodesia and independent Rhodesia up until 1969, using the Westminster Parliamentary System modified by a system of separate voter rolls with differing property and education qualifications, without regard to race. Whites ended up with the majority of Assembly seats with Whites attaining 50 out of 66 seats. Blacks would only attain 16 out of the 66 seats in the Rhodesian Parliament. The 1969 republican constitution established a [bicameral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicameral "Bicameral") Parliament consisting of an indirectly elected [Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_Rhodesia "Senate of Rhodesia") and a directly elected [House of Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Assembly_of_Rhodesia "House of Assembly of Rhodesia"), effectively reserving the majority of seats for whites. The office of [president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Rhodesia "President of Rhodesia") had only ceremonial significance with the prime minister holding executive power. The Constitution of the short-lived [Zimbabwe Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_Rhodesia "Zimbabwe Rhodesia"), which saw a black-led government elected for the first time, reserved 28 of the 100 parliamentary seats for whites. The independence constitution agreed at [Lancaster House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster_House_Agreement "Lancaster House Agreement") watered those provisions down and reserved 20 out of 100 seats for whites in the House of Assembly and 8 out of 40 seats in the Senate. The constitution prohibited Zimbabwe authorities from altering the Constitution for seven years without unanimous consent and required a three-quarters vote in Parliament for a further three years. The government amended the Constitution in 1987 to abolish the seats reserved for whites, and replace the office of [prime minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Zimbabwe "Prime Minister of Zimbabwe") with an executive president.
