were black volunteers.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Good-127) In the tradition of many colonial armies, it was primarily organised into light infantry battalions trained and equipped for counter-insurgency warfare or internal security actions,[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Arnold-128) and possessed little artillery or armour.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Good-127) The [Royal Rhodesian Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Rhodesian_Air_Force "Royal Rhodesian Air Force") (RRAF) had 1,000 personnel and six squadrons of aircraft, including forty to fifty [Hawker Hunter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawker_Hunter "Hawker Hunter") and [de Havilland Vampire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_Havilland_Vampire "De Havilland Vampire") strike aircraft and [English Electric Canberra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Electric_Canberra "English Electric Canberra") light bombers.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Good-127) It also possessed a helicopter squadron, a transport squadron, and a light reconnaissance squadron.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Good-127) The Rhodesian military was backed by the [British South Africa Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_South_Africa_Police "British South Africa Police") (BSAP), a well-equipped police force whose title was derived from the law enforcement division of the British South Africa Company.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Good-127) The BSAP had armoured vehicles of its own and a potent paramilitary capability.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Good-127) Domestic and external intelligence gathering were vested in the [Central Intelligence Organisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Intelligence_Organisation "Central Intelligence Organisation") (CIO).[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-COIN-129) As a result of the escalating rural insurgency, the Rhodesian Security Forces began to depend more heavily on white conscripts and reservists of the Territorial Force and Territorial reserves.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Arnold-128) Regular units remained small throughout the Rhodesian Bush War but became increasingly specialised and were often able to have an effect utterly disproportionate to their size.[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-mcnab2002-130) The security forces included a disproportionate number of personnel who had seen action during the [First Malayan Emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Malayan_Emergency "First Malayan Emergency") as well as the [Aden Emergency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aden_Emergency "Aden Emergency"), and their experience gave Rhodesia's defence establishment a solid grounding in counter-insurgency warfare and small unit tactics in particular.[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-COIN-129) Nevertheless, the vastness of the operational area and Rhodesia's limited manpower pool left the army, air force, and BSAP constantly overstretched.[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-COIN-129) Budgetary and resource restraints, coupled with manpower shortages, meant the security forces could not expand quickly enough to match the guerrilla movements, and were almost always outnumbered.[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-COIN-129) Rhodesian units compensated for their disadvantage in this regard by pursuing an aggressive preemptive and counterstrike strategy, raiding neighbouring states to destroy guerrilla forces in their external sanctuaries.[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-COIN-129) All white, male residents aged eighteen to twenty-three were obligated to fulfill four and a half months (later extended to nine months) of full-time [national service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_service "National service").[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Good-127) This was followed by a three-year reservist obligation.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Good-127) By 1974, the national service intakes had been doubled, and white men over twenty-three were also conscripted.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Arnold-128) In 1978, the Rhodesian Army had about 14,000 white national servicemen, but continued manpower shortages forced it to recruit black volunteers in larger numbers and extend compulsory military service to all white males up to sixty years of age.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Arnold-128) By the end of the Rhodesian Bush War virtually all male white residents were either serving in the military or police in a full-time or part-time capacity.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Arnold-128) The size of the Rhodesian Army had swelled to about 20,000 personnel, and the BSAP to over 40,000, including reservists.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Arnold-128) ### Biological and chemical warfare \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia&action=edit§ion=20 "Edit section: Biological and chemical warfare")\] From 1975 to 1980, the Rhodesian government made several attempts to weaponise chemical and biological agents.[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Glenn_Cross_1980-131) Members of the security forces contaminated supplies before replacing them in guerrilla caches or planted them in rural stores to be stolen by the guerrillas during raids.[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-132) They also poisoned water sources along known infiltration routes along the Rhodesian border, forcing their opponents to travel through more arid regions or carry more water during their treks.[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-133) The chemical agents most used in the Rhodesian chemical and biological warfare (CBW) programme were [parathion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parathion "Parathion") (an organophosphate insecticide) and [thallium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thallium "Thallium") (a heavy metal commonly found in rodenticide).[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-134) The weapons the Rhodesians selected for use also included _Vibrio cholerae_ (causative agent of [cholera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cholera "Cholera")) and possibly _Bacillus anthracis_ (causative agent of [anthrax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthrax "Anthrax")). They also looked at using _Rickettsia prowazekii_ (causative agent of epidemic [typhus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typhus "Typhus")), and _Salmonella typhi_ (causative agent of [typhoid fever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typhoid_fever "Typhoid fever")), and toxins such as [ricin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricin "Ricin") and [botulinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Botulinum "Botulinum") toxin.[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Glenn_Cross_1980-131) Biological agents, namely _Vibrio cholerae_, had some impact on the fighting capability of ZANLA.[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-the_plague_wars-135) Some former officers of the Rhodesian Security Forces alleged that anthrax was used covertly during the late 1970s, but this has been disputed.[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Glenn_Cross_1980-131) Use of _anthracis_, ricin, or botulinum toxin was favoured during assassination attempts of prominent guerrilla commanders.[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Glenn_Cross_1980-131) Economically, [Southern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia "Southern Rhodesia") developed an economy that was narrowly based on the production of a few [primary products](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primary_products "Primary products"), notably, [chromium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromium "Chromium") and [tobacco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobacco "Tobacco"). It was therefore vulnerable to the economic cycle. The deep [recession of the 1930s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Great_Depression "The Great Depression") gave way to a post-war boom. This boom prompted the immigration of about 200,000 whites between 1945 and 1970, taking the white population up to 307,000. A large number of these immigrants were of British working-class origin, with others coming from the [Belgian Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgian_Congo "Belgian Congo"), [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Kenya "British Kenya"), [Tanzania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanzania "Tanzania"), and later [Angola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Angola "Portuguese Angola") and [Mozambique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Mozambique "Portuguese Mozambique"). They established a relatively balanced economy, transforming what was once a primary producer dependent on backwoods farming into an modest industrial power which spawned a strong manufacturing sector, [iron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron "Iron") and [steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steel "Steel") industries, and modern mining ventures. These economic successes owed a lot to the immigration of skilled labour and backing from South Africa. The economy of the state of Rhodesia sustained international sanctions for a decade following the declaration of its independence, a resistance which waned as more southern African states declared independence and majority rule as well as the destruction caused by the [Rhodesian Bush War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Bush_War "Rhodesian Bush War"). A central feature of the white community in Rhodesia was its transience, as white settlers were just as likely to leave Rhodesia after a few years as permanently settle; for example, of the 700 Britons who were the first white settlers, arriving in 1890, only 15 were still living in Rhodesia in 1924.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Brownell-102): 6593  As the white population of Rhodesia had a low birth rate (18 per 1,000 compared to the African rate of 48 per 1,000[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Paxton-136)), maintaining white population growth was largely dependent upon taking in new white immigrants with immigration accounting for 60% of the growth of the white Rhodesian population between 1955 and 1972.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Brownell-102) In the ten years after the nation's declaration of independence from Britain, around 70,000 from the white population of Rhodesia emigrated from the nation. 45% of the emigration was to South Africa, as it was geographically adjacent and shared similarities in climate, topography, economic standards, and social customs. The remaining 55% chiefly headed to other mainly white, English-speaking nations at the time: the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada, and New Zealand.[\[136\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-137) However, the American historian Josiah Brownell noted that the turnover rate for white residents in Rhodesia was very high, as Rhodesia took in a total of 255,692 white immigrants between 1955 and 1979 while the same period a total of 246,583 whites emigrated. Even during the boom years of the late 1950s, when Rhodesia took in an average of 13,666 white immigrants per year, mostly from the United Kingdom and South Africa, an average of about 7,666 whites emigrated annually. Between 1961 and 1965, Rhodesia took in an average of 8,225 white immigrants per year while also having an average white emigration of 12,912 per year. Many prospective white immigrants in Rhodesia arrived seeking economic opportunities and departed with fluctuations in the security situation as the Bush War intensified. A substantial number were uninterested in settling there permanently and did not apply for Rhodesian citizenship, despite a much-publicised 1967 campaign urging them to do so.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Brownell-102) Brownell asserted that patriotism in the white community was "shallow" due to its essentially expatriate character. He also claimed that the majority of white immigrants in the late 1960s and early 1970s were unskilled laborers who competed with the country's black African workforce and did not contribute badly needed technical or professional skills to the country, arguing that this was due to government policy aimed at making white immigration as "unselective as possible" and guaranteeing every white immigrant a job. The population of Rhodesia boomed during the late 1960s due to immigration and an exceptional rate of natural increase among its black citizens, the highest in sub-Saharan Africa at the time.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Brownell-102)

White Rhodesians mostly spoke English, with a minority that spoke [Afrikaans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrikaans "Afrikaans"). Approximately 70% of black Rhodesians spoke [Shona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shona_language "Shona language"), and around 20% spoke [Ndebele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ndebele_language "Northern Ndebele language").[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-139) A majority of [Rhodesia's Indian community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indians_in_Zimbabwe "Indians in Zimbabwe") spoke [Gujarati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gujarati_language "Gujarati language") and a minority spoke [Hindi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindi "Hindi"). Rhodesia predominantly adhered to [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity"), with [Protestantism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestantism "Protestantism") being the largest denomination. However, many native Africans still adhered to [traditional African religions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_African_religions "Traditional African religions"). Throughout the period of its [Unilateral Declaration of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence_/(Rhodesia/) "Unilateral Declaration of Independence (Rhodesia)") (1965 to 1979), Rhodesia pursued a foreign policy of attempting to secure recognition as an independent country, and insisting that its political system would include 'gradual steps to majority rule.' Ardently anti-communist, Rhodesia tried to present itself to the West as a front-line state against communist expansion in Africa, to little avail. Rhodesia received little international recognition during its existence; recognition only occurred after elections in 1980 and a transition to majority rule. Rhodesia wished to retain its economic prosperity and also feared communist elements in the rebel forces, and thus felt their policy of a gradual progression to black majority rule was justified. However, the international community refused to accept this rationale, believing that their policies were perpetuating racism. This attitude was part of the larger [decolonisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decolonisation "Decolonisation") context, during which Western powers such as the United Kingdom, France, and Belgium hastened to grant independence to their colonies in Africa. Rhodesia was originally a [British colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_colony "British colony"). Although [decolonisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decolonisation "Decolonisation") in Africa had begun after World War II, it began accelerating in the early 1960s, causing Britain to negotiate independence rapidly with several of its colonies. During this period, it adopted a foreign policy called [NIBMAR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NIBMAR "NIBMAR"), or No Independence Before Majority African Rule, mandating democratic reforms that placed governance in the hands of the majority black Africans. The governing white minority of Rhodesia, led by Ian Smith, opposed the policy and its implications. On 11 November 1965, Rhodesia's minority white government made a [unilateral declaration of independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence "Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence") (UDI) from the United Kingdom, as it became apparent that negotiations would not lead to independence under the white regime. The United Kingdom government immediately brought in legislation ([Southern Rhodesia Act 1965](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_Act_1965 "Southern Rhodesia Act 1965")) which formally abolished all Rhodesian government institutions. This move made life difficult for Rhodesian citizens who wished to travel internationally as passports issued by Rhodesia's UDI administration were not recognised as valid;[\[139\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-Passports_invalidated-140) in January 1966, the British issued a statement accepting as valid any passport issued before the declaration of independence and allowing six-month United Kingdom passports to be granted when they expired – provided that the bearer declared they did not intend to aid the UDI Rhodesian government.[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-1966_statement-141) Developments in Britain helped to alienate the white Rhodesian population from the former mother country, namely Queen [Elizabeth II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_II "Elizabeth II")'s 1966 speech to the [Parliament of Jamaica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_Jamaica "Parliament of Jamaica") where she endorsed majority rule and her attempt in 1968 to block the hanging of what Rhodesians perceived as Zimbabwean nationalist terrorists.[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-142) Until late 1969, Rhodesia still recognised Queen Elizabeth II as head of state, even though it opposed the British government itself for hindering its goals of independence. However she refused to accept the title _Queen of Rhodesia_ and eventually the Smith government abandoned their attempts to remain loyal to the British Crown. In a 1969 referendum, a majority of the electorate voted to declare Rhodesia an independent republic. The hope being that this move would facilitate recognition as an independent state by the international community, but the issue of white minority rule remained and continued to hinder this effort, and like the UDI before it, the proclamation of a republic lacked international recognition. The British public overall viewed the issue of Rhodesia and UDI as a distant and anachronistic one that they cared relatively little about and saw any expedient response to it by their government as satisfactory. Most Britons saw the end of Rhodesia's [white supremacist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_supremacy "White supremacy") [timocracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timocracy "Timocracy") as inevitable and justified. Although the majority Britons opposed military intervention against the renegade Rhodesian state, this opinion was not uniformly held.[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-143) After the declaration of independence, and indeed for the entire duration of its existence, Rhodesia did not receive official recognition from any state, although it did maintain diplomatic relations with South Africa, which was then under [apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartheid "Apartheid"). South Africa did not recognise Rhodesia to preserve its fragile positions with other nations, but frequently assisted the Rhodesian state. [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estado_Novo_/(Portugal/) "Estado Novo (Portugal)") maintained informal relations until the [Carnation Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnation_Revolution "Carnation Revolution") of 1974. The day following the declaration of independence, the [United Nations Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council") passed a resolution ([S/RES/216](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_Resolution_216 "United Nations Security Council Resolution 216")) calling upon all states not to accord Rhodesia recognition, and to refrain from any assistance. The Security Council also imposed selective mandatory economic sanctions, which were later made comprehensive. The US, despite voting in favour of the sanctions at the UNSC, violated them to buy chromium ore from Rhodesia.[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-144) Kenneth Kaunda, president of Zambia, also accused western oil companies of violating the sanctions and selling oil to Rhodesia.[\[144\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-145) ### International perspective \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesia&action=edit§ion=29 "Edit section: International perspective")\] Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence from the United Kingdom on 11 November 1965 was promptly condemned by the international community. The United Nations Security Council Resolution 216 of 12 November 1965 called "upon all States not to recognise this illegal racist minority regime in Southern Rhodesia."[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-146) Rhodesia campaigned for international acceptance and invoked the doctrine of [non-intervention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-intervention "Non-intervention") in internal affairs as justification for rebuking external criticism of its internal policies. However, the emerging doctrine of [self-determination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-determination "Self-determination") in colonial situations meant that most nations regarded Rhodesia's self-declared independence as illegitimate. Zambia, formerly [Northern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Rhodesia "Northern Rhodesia"), took a pragmatic approach towards Rhodesia. [Kenneth Kaunda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Kaunda "Kenneth Kaunda"), heavily dependent on access through Rhodesia for his nation's copper ore exports, fuel, and power imports unofficially worked with the Rhodesian government. Rhodesia still allowed Zambia to export and import its goods through its territory to Mozambique ports, despite the Zambian government's official policy of hostility and non-recognition of the post-UDI Smith Administration. The United States, like all other Western nations, refused to recognise Rhodesia, but unlike others allowed its [Consulate-General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consulate-General "Consulate-General") to function as a communications conduit between the US government in Washington, DC and the Rhodesian government in Salisbury. When Rhodesia set up the [Rhodesian Information Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rhodesian_Information_Office&action=edit&redlink=1 "Rhodesian Information Office (page does not exist)") in Washington, DC, [OAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organization_of_American_States "Organization of American States") nations loudly protested. The US government responded by saying the Rhodesian mission and its staff had no official diplomatic status and violated no US laws. Portugal pursued a middle path with Rhodesia. While not officially recognising Rhodesia under Ian Smith, the government of [António Salazar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ant%C3%B3nio_Salazar "António Salazar") did permit Rhodesia to establish a [representative mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_mission_in_Lisbon "Rhodesian mission in Lisbon") in Lisbon, and permitted Rhodesian exports and imports through their colony of Mozambique. The Portuguese government in power at that time, authoritarian and ardently anti-communist, gave active behind-the-scenes support in Rhodesia's fight against the guerrilla groups. South Africa, itself under international pressure as a white minority government, pursued a policy of [détente](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%A9tente "Détente") with the black African states at the time. These states wanted South Africa to pressure Ian Smith to accept a faster transition to majority rule in Rhodesia, in return for pledges of non-interference in South Africa's internal affairs. Prime Minister [John Vorster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Vorster "John Vorster"), believing majority rule in Rhodesia would lead to international acceptance for South Africa, used a number of tactics to pressure Smith. The South African government held up shipments of fuel and ammunition and pulled out friendly South African forces from Rhodesia. The combined loss of Mozambique and the loss of support from South Africa dealt critical blows to the Rhodesian government. ### Diplomatic relations This led to internationally supervised elections, won by [Zimbabwe African National Union – Patriotic Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_African_National_Union_%E2%80%93_Patriotic_Front "Zimbabwe African National Union – Patriotic Front") and Robert Mugabe, establishing the internationally recognised [Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe "Zimbabwe"). The most influential newspapers in the country were the _[Rhodesia Herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia_Herald "Rhodesia Herald")_ in [Salisbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harare "Harare") and _[The Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Chronicle_/(Zimbabwe/) "The Chronicle (Zimbabwe)")_ in [Bulawayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulawayo "Bulawayo"). Following UDI, in 1976, the state-run [Rhodesian Broadcasting Corporation (RBC)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe_Broadcasting_Corporation "Zimbabwe Broadcasting Corporation") took over the privately owned [Rhodesia Television (RTV)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia_Television "Rhodesia Television") service, in which it had previously acquired a 51 percent stake.[\[170\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-171) Among the news magazines published in Rhodesia under UDI were the _[Illustrated Life Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illustrated_Life_Rhodesia "Illustrated Life Rhodesia")_, while _The Valiant Years_ by Beryl Salt told the history of Rhodesia from 1890 to 1978 entirely through the medium of facsimile reproduction of articles and headlines from Rhodesian newspapers.[\[171\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-172) As Rhodesia was a former colony of the United Kingdom, all of the sports that were born in the United Kingdom enjoyed considerable popularity in Rhodesia; especially [cricket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cricket "Cricket"), [rugby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_football "Rugby football"), [water polo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Water_polo "Water polo"), [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football"), [netball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netball "Netball"), [golf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf "Golf"), [tennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis "Tennis") (including the [Rhodesian Open Tennis Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesian_Open_Tennis_Championships "Rhodesian Open Tennis Championships")), [lawn bowls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawn_bowls "Lawn bowls"), [field hockey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_hockey "Field hockey"), etc. Just like neighbouring South Africa, Rhodesia was barred from both competing against and participating with [Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_Nations "Commonwealth of Nations") member countries.[\[172\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia#cite_note-173) One of the biggest triumphs in Rhodesia sports history was when the team defeated the New Zealand national rugby team 10-8 while the All Blacks were touring South Africa. They are 1 of 8 nations to ever defeat the All Blacks and the only non-test nation to have ever beaten them. As this was the only game the two nations ever played they also have the unique honour of having a 100% win record against the All Blacks.\[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] In the ten years after transforming into [Zimbabwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zimbabwe "Zimbabwe"), around 60% of the white population emigrated, most to [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") and to other mainly white, English-speaking countries where they formed immigrant communities. Politically within Zimbabwe, the consolidation of power by [Robert Mugabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Mugabe "Robert Mugabe") continued through the 1980s. Following amendments to the country's [constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Zimbabwe "Constitution of Zimbabwe") in 1987, parliamentary seats reserved for whites were abolished, and an executive presidency was created, held by [Mugabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mugabe "Mugabe"). These individuals are known as "[Rhodies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodie "Rhodie")". 15.content:
[![Image 1: A formative photograph of soldiers in First World War British uniforms, standing and sitting in six rows. A gentleman in civilian clothes sits in the centre of the second row from the front.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Rhodesian_Platoon_of_the_KRRC_at_Sheerness%2C_1914.png/330px-Rhodesian_Platoon_of_the_KRRC_at_Sheerness%2C_1914.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rhodesian_Platoon_of_the_KRRC_at_Sheerness,_1914.png)

The original [King's Royal Rifle Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King%27s_Royal_Rifle_Corps "King's Royal Rifle Corps") Rhodesian Platoon, [Sheerness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheerness "Sheerness"), England, November 1914. Capt. J. B. Brady (third from right, second row) and the [Marquess of Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Paulet,_16th_Marquess_of_Winchester "Henry Paulet, 16th Marquess of Winchester") (fourth) sponsored the unit. Most pictured were later killed or seriously wounded.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-1)

In August 1914, the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom") declared war on the [German Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Empire "German Empire") at the start of [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I"). The settler society in [Southern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia "Southern Rhodesia"),[\[n 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-since1980-2) which was [administered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Company_rule_in_Rhodesia "Company rule in Rhodesia") by the [British South Africa Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_South_Africa_Company "British South Africa Company"), received the news with great patriotic enthusiasm. The Company [administrator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrator_of_Southern_Rhodesia "Administrator of Southern Rhodesia"), [Sir William Milton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Henry_Milton "William Henry Milton"), wired the British government, saying, "All Rhodesia... ready to do its duty".[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl2-3) Although it supported the British Empire, the company was concerned about the possible financial implications for its chartered territory to make direct commitments to the war effort, particularly at first. As a result, most of the colony's contributions to the war were made by Southern Rhodesians individually—not only those who volunteered to fight abroad but also those who remained at home and raised funds to donate food, equipment, and other supplies.

Starting immediately after the outbreak of war, parties of white Southern Rhodesians paid their own way to England to join the [British Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Army "British Army"). Most Southern Rhodesians who served in the war enlisted in this way and fought on the [Western Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Front_/(World_War_I/) "Western Front (World War I)"), taking part in many of the major battles. They fought alongside an assortment of British, South African, and other colonial units, most commonly the [King's Royal Rifle Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King%27s_Royal_Rifle_Corps "King's Royal Rifle Corps"), which recruited hundreds of men from the colony and created homogeneous Rhodesian platoons. Troopers from Southern Rhodesia became renowned on the Western Front for their marksmanship, a result of their frontier lifestyle. Some of the colony's men served in the [Royal Flying Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Flying_Corps "Royal Flying Corps"), one of the two predecessors of the [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force"). The [Rhodesia Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia_Regiment "Rhodesia Regiment"), the [Rhodesia Native Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia_Native_Regiment "Rhodesia Native Regiment"), and the [British South Africa Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_South_Africa_Police "British South Africa Police") served in the [African theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_theatre_of_World_War_I "African theatre of World War I") of the conflict, contributing to the [South-West African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South-West_Africa_Campaign "South-West Africa Campaign") and [East African campaigns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_African_Campaign_/(World_War_I/) "East African Campaign (World War I)").

Though it was one of the few combatant territories not to raise fighting men through [conscription](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscription "Conscription"), proportional to the white population, Southern Rhodesia contributed more manpower to the British war effort than any other dominion or colony and more than Britain itself. White troops numbered 5,716, about 40% of white men in the colony, with 1,720 of these serving as [commissioned officers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Officer_/(armed_forces/) "Officer (armed forces)"). The Rhodesia Native Regiment recruited 2,507 black soldiers; approximately 30 black recruits served as scouts for the Rhodesia Regiment, and approximately 350 black soldiers were assigned to British and South African units. Over 800 Southern Rhodesians of all races died on operational service during the war, with many more seriously wounded.

The territory's contributions during the First World War became a major entry in many histories of the colony and a great source of pride for the white community, as well as for some black Rhodesians. It played a part in the UK government's decision to grant [self-government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Responsible_government "Responsible government") in 1923. The contribution remained prominent in the national consciousness for decades to come. When the colonial government [unilaterally declared independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia%27s_Unilateral_Declaration_of_Independence "Rhodesia's Unilateral Declaration of Independence") from Britain in 1965, it deliberately did so on [Armistice Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armistice_Day "Armistice Day"), 11 November, and signed the proclamation at 11:00 local time. After the territory's reconstitution and recognized independence as Zimbabwe in 1980, the government removed many references to the war, such as memorial monuments and plaques from public view, regarding them as unwelcome vestiges of white minority rule and colonialism. The Zimbabwean cultural memory largely forgot the First World War. Some monuments remain, including the Bulawayo Cenotaph, which was restored in 2017. A number of memorials are maintained by the [Commonwealth War Graves Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_War_Graves_Commission "Commonwealth War Graves Commission").

[![Image 2: A map. See description](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Southern_Rhodesia_1914.png/250px-Southern_Rhodesia_1914.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Southern_Rhodesia_1914.png)

[Southern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia "Southern Rhodesia"), highlighted in red on a map of Africa in 1914; other [British possessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_possessions "British possessions") in pink

At the time of [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") (also known as the First World War or the Great War), [Southern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia "Southern Rhodesia")[\[n 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-since1980-2) was [administered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Company_rule_in_Rhodesia "Company rule in Rhodesia") by the [British South Africa Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_South_Africa_Company "British South Africa Company"), which had controlled it and [Northern Rhodesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Rhodesia "Northern Rhodesia") since acquiring them through diplomacy and conquest during the 1890s. The [white](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_people_in_Zimbabwe "White people in Zimbabwe") population in Southern Rhodesia stood at 23,606 in 1911 (a minority of 3%),[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-walker664-5) while Northern Rhodesia had about 3,000 white settlers (less than half of 1%).[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-walker669-6)[\[n 2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-names-9) With the company's charter expiring in late 1914, most Southern Rhodesian public attention was focused on this issue before the outbreak of war. The settlers were split between those who backed continued administration by the [Chartered Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chartered_company "Chartered company") and those who advocated [responsible government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Responsible_government "Responsible government"), which would make Southern Rhodesia a [self-governing colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-governing_colony "Self-governing colony") within the [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl1-10) Still, others favored the integration of Southern Rhodesia into the [Union of South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_South_Africa "Union of South Africa"), which had been formed in 1910.[\[n 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-unionofsa-12) Following the intervention of the war, the charter was renewed for 10 years in early 1915.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-britannica-13)

Before 1914, Southern Rhodesia's police force was the [British South Africa Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_South_Africa_Police "British South Africa Police") (BSAP), first raised in 1889 and reconstituted into a more permanent form in 1896.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-keppeljones512-14) This paramilitary, mounted infantry force was theoretically also the country's standing army.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl4-15) Organized along military lines,[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-16) it served in the [First](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Matabele_War "First Matabele War") and [Second Matabele Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Matabele_War "Second Matabele War") of the 1890s, operated on Britain's side in the [Anglo-Boer War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Boer_War "Second Boer War") of 1899–1902 (alongside the specially-raised [Rhodesia Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia_Regiment "Rhodesia Regiment")),[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-keppeljones590599-17) and by 1914, it comprised about 1,150 men (including officers). Reserves existed in the form of the Southern Rhodesia Volunteers, an all-white amateur force with a paper strength of 2,000, intended for mobilization against local uprisings. Few doubted the Volunteers' enthusiasm, but they were not extensively trained or equipped; though perhaps useful in a Rhodesian bush skirmish, most observers agreed they would be no match for professional soldiers in a conventional war. In any case, the Volunteers' enlistment contracts bound them for domestic service only.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl4-15)

### Announcement and reception

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Announcement and reception")\]

[![Image 3: Soldiers in colonial-style military uniforms march past the camera, smiling](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/78/Rhodesia_Regiment_in_Cape_Town_1914.jpg/250px-Rhodesia_Regiment_in_Cape_Town_1914.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rhodesia_Regiment_in_Cape_Town_1914.jpg)

Men of the [1st Rhodesia Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia_Regiment "Rhodesia Regiment") in [Cape Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Town "Cape Town"), December 1914

When Britain declared war on Germany at 23:00 [Greenwich Mean Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich_Mean_Time "Greenwich Mean Time") on 4 August 1914, the British Empire's [dominions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominion "Dominion") and colonies automatically became involved as well. Word of this reached the Southern Rhodesian capital city [Salisbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harare "Harare") during the night. Early on 5 August, the Company [administrator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrator_of_Southern_Rhodesia "Administrator of Southern Rhodesia") [Sir William Milton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Henry_Milton "William Henry Milton") wired [Whitehall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_the_United_Kingdom "Government of the United Kingdom"): "All Rhodesia united in devoted loyalty to King and Empire and ready to do its duty."[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl2-3) A few hours later he officially announced to the populace that Southern Rhodesia was at war.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl2-3) The _[Rhodesia Herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Herald_/(Zimbabwe/) "The Herald (Zimbabwe)")_ and _Bulawayo Chronicle_ newspapers published special editions the same day to spread the news;[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl1-10) it took about half a week for word to reach the whole country, but [jingoistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jingoism "Jingoism") demonstrations began in the major towns almost immediately.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl2-3)

In the words of the historian [Peter McLaughlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_McLaughlin "Peter McLaughlin"), the Southern Rhodesian settlers "seemed to out-British the British" in their patriotic zeal,[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcliv-18) so it was to the frustration of many of them that the Company did not immediately commit to any martial action. While it sent supportive messages to Whitehall, the Company felt it could not raise any kind of expeditionary force without first considering the implications for its administrative operations; as a commercial concern, it was possible for the company to go bankrupt. Who would foot the bill for war expenditure, its hierarchy pondered: the Company itself, the Rhodesian taxpayers or the British government?[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl3-19)

As the local newspapers filled with letters from readers clamouring for Rhodesian troops to be mustered and despatched to Europe post-haste,[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl3-19) the administration limited its initial contribution to posting a section of BSAP troopers to the [Victoria Falls Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Falls_Bridge "Victoria Falls Bridge") to guard against possible German attack from [South-West Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_South-West_Africa "German South-West Africa") though the [Caprivi Strip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caprivi_Strip "Caprivi Strip").[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl4-15) In early September, an indignant letter to the _Rhodesia Herald_ from Colonel [Raleigh Grey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raleigh_Grey "Raleigh Grey"), a major figure in local business, politics and military matters, accused the Company of bringing "a slur on a British country" by doing so little.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl3-19)

A few days after the war began, the Chartered Company formed the Rhodesian Reserves, an amorphous entity intended to accommodate the many white men who were keen to put on uniform, as well as to make a start towards organizing what might eventually become an expeditionary force. Eminent citizens and elected leaders formed their own platoons, each bringing 24 volunteers; three or four of these 25-man troops made a company. Units representing the Caledonian Society, the Lancashire and Yorkshire Society, the [Legion of Frontiersmen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legion_of_Frontiersmen "Legion of Frontiersmen") and other local organizations mirrored the [Pals battalions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pals_battalion "Pals battalion") in Britain. Volunteers could opt to serve overseas, within Rhodesia or only locally; around 1,000 had volunteered in all by 13 August.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl5-20)

The Company suggested to the UK government that it might dispatch 500 troopers from the Rhodesian Reserves to Europe to act as an all-Southern Rhodesian unit on the [Western Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Front_/(World_War_I/) "Western Front (World War I)") (in Belgium and France), but the [War Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_Office "War Office") in London replied that such an expeditionary force would be more practically deployed in Africa, within the South African forces. When the Company relayed this idea south, the South Africans said they were happy to take the Southern Rhodesians, but only if they enlisted independently in existing Union regiments. The Company found itself in the unusual position of having a prospective expeditionary force that nobody wanted.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl8-21) Unwilling to wait, some Southern Rhodesian would-be soldiers made their own way to Britain to join the [British Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Army "British Army") directly, as individuals or in groups. By the end of October 1914, about 300 were on their way.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl5-20)

[![Image 4: Soldiers in British uniforms of First World War vintage pose for a formative shot](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7b/Rhodesians_of_King_Edward%27s_Horse%2C_WW1.png/250px-Rhodesians_of_King_Edward%27s_Horse%2C_WW1.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rhodesians_of_King_Edward%27s_Horse,_WW1.png)

Southern Rhodesian members of [King Edward's Horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Edward%27s_Horse "King Edward's Horse"), a [British Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Army "British Army") cavalry regiment

In terms of fighting manpower, Southern Rhodesia's main contribution to World War I was in the [trenches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trench_warfare "Trench warfare") of the Western Front.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl49-22) As the white Southern Rhodesians in this theatre joined the British Army separately, at different times and under their own steam (or were already connected to specific units as reservists), they were spread across dozens of regiments, including the [Black Watch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Watch "Black Watch"), the [Coldstream Guards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coldstream_Guards "Coldstream Guards"), the [Grenadier Guards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenadier_Guards "Grenadier Guards"), the [Royal Engineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Engineers "Royal Engineers") and the [Royal Marines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Marines "Royal Marines"), as well as many South African units and others.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl147to149-23) During the war's opening months, Southern Rhodesian volunteers who could not afford to travel to England were assisted by a private fund set up by [Ernest Lucas Guest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_Lucas_Guest "Ernest Lucas Guest"), a Salisbury lawyer and Anglo-Boer War veteran who also organized an accompanying recruitment campaign for European service. Guest stopped recruiting at the company's request after it created the [1st Rhodesia Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia_Regiment "Rhodesia Regiment"), an expeditionary force to South and South-West Africa, in October 1914.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-gale739-24)

A link developed during the war with the [King's Royal Rifle Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King%27s_Royal_Rifle_Corps "King's Royal Rifle Corps") (KRRC), whose Southern Rhodesian contingent—numbering a few hundred, chiefly in its 2nd and 3rd Battalions—was the largest on the Western Front.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl49-22) The connection with this particular corps began as the result of a chance conversation aboard the ship that took the first batch of Southern Rhodesians from [Cape Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Town "Cape Town") to [Southampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southampton "Southampton") in late 1914. The [16th Marquess of Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Paulet,_16th_Marquess_of_Winchester "Henry Paulet, 16th Marquess of Winchester"), who had links with Rhodesia dating back to the 1890s, was also aboard the ship, returning from a visit to the colony. Encountering Captain [John Banks Brady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Banks_Brady "John Banks Brady"), the officer of Irish origin who led the volunteers, the Marquess asked where his party was headed. Brady enthusiastically replied that they were going to war together in France. The Marquess suggested to Brady that since it might be difficult to prevent his men from being split up during the enlistment process, it might be a good idea for the Rhodesians to join the KRRC, where he could keep an eye on them through his connections with the [Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winchester "Winchester")\-based regiment. The Southern Rhodesian contingent duly mustered into the KRRC. A designated Rhodesian platoon, widely referred to thereafter as "the Rhodesian Platoon", was formed under Brady at the KRRC training camp at [Sheerness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheerness "Sheerness"), on the [Isle of Sheppey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isle_of_Sheppey "Isle of Sheppey") in [Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kent "Kent").[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-ferris-25)

> They are not only intensely British, but quite intolerably Rhodesian ... they exhibit a tendency to collect together, \[and\] are inclined to vaunt themselves, to be puffed up by the mere fact that they _are_ Rhodesians.

A contemporary South African opinion on Rhodesians abroad[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-26)

As a rule, the white Rhodesians overseas combined stridently pro-British attitudes with an even stronger pride in Rhodesia.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl84-8) Many of them saw participation in the war, particularly in distinct "Rhodesian" formations, as a step towards forging a distinctive national identity, like those of Australia and the other more mature British dominions, and building a case for Southern Rhodesian self-government.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-stapleton19-27) The existence of an explicitly Rhodesian Platoon in the KRRC endeared the regiment to the Southern Rhodesian public, and attracted many of the colony's volunteers who arrived in England later in the war; in time, the KRRC formed further Rhodesian platoons from additional personnel. While the average Rhodesian colonial, living on the frontier of the Empire, was at least casually acquainted with rifles, most Englishmen had never held one. At Sheerness, Brady's Rhodesian Platoon won a reputation for fine sharpshooting, and set a regimental record score at the shooting range.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl50-28)

Once posted to France in December 1914, the Rhodesian Platoon almost immediately began suffering regular heavy casualties. Southern Rhodesian volunteers continued to arrive piecemeal in England throughout the conflict, so Rhodesian formations on the Western Front received regular reinforcements in small batches, but because casualties were usually concentrated in far larger groups it often took a few months for a depleted Southern Rhodesian unit to return to full numerical strength. A cycle developed whereby Rhodesian platoons in Belgium and France were abruptly decimated and then gradually built up again only to suffer the same fate on returning to action.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl50to51-29) When the KRRC's Rhodesian platoons took part in British offensives, they were easily recognized by a distinctive [battle cry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_cry "Battle cry") that their men shouted as they went over the top.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl84-8) Sometimes the British and German positions were so close that troopers on each front line could hear what was said in the opposite trench; one group of Southern Rhodesians avoided being understood in this situation by speaking a mixture of [Shona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shona_language "Shona language") and [Sindebele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ndebele_language "Northern Ndebele language") (two African languages) instead of English.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl57-30)

> The cold is frightfully trying. It is snowing and freezing hard tonight, and it makes me yearn to be back on my farm on the Hunyani ...

Trench warfare was a dreadful ordeal for soldiers, and the Southern Rhodesians, coming from the open [veld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veld "Veld") of southern Africa, had a particularly difficult time getting used to the cold and the mud.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl52and55-32) Brady reported that some of his men had contracted [frostbite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frostbite "Frostbite") within 48 hours of reaching the trenches.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl55-31) Despite this, the KRRC's Rhodesians acquitted themselves well in the eyes of their superiors; Lieutenant-Colonel [Sir Edward Hutton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Hutton_/(British_Army_officer/) "Edward Hutton (British Army officer)"), who wrote a history of the KRRC, commented that the Southern Rhodesian contingent "earned for itself great reputation for valor and good shooting".[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-hutton57-33) Southern Rhodesians became especially valuable to the KRRC as designated [snipers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sniper "Sniper"), [grenadiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenadier "Grenadier"), [Lewis Gunners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Gun "Lewis Gun") and other specialists.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl64to65-34) While discussing a KRRC sniper section, Hutton singles its Southern Rhodesian members out for their fine marksmanship, commenting that "accustomed to [big game shooting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big-game_hunting "Big-game hunting"), \[they\] particularly excelled in this system of 'snipers', and inflicted continual losses upon the enemy".[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-hutton57-33) In their 2008 history of sniping, Pat Farey and Mark Spicer highlight the prowess of South African and Rhodesian sharpshooters on the Western Front, and claim that one group of 24 southern Africans collectively accounted for over 3,000 German casualties and fatalities.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-35)

[![Image 5: A black-and-white sketch of a savage battle scene, where the two sides are fighting hand-to-hand and with bayonets](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Delville_Wood_Battle_July_1916.jpg/250px-Delville_Wood_Battle_July_1916.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Delville_Wood_Battle_July_1916.jpg)

South Africans and Rhodesians fight the Germans hand-to-hand in [Delville Wood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Delville_Wood "Battle of Delville Wood")

So many Southern Rhodesians were withdrawn from the trenches for officer training that in mid-1915, Brady appealed through the Salisbury and [Bulawayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulawayo "Bulawayo") presses for more volunteers to replace those who had been commissioned.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl64to65-34) A platoon of Southern Rhodesians with the 2nd Battalion, KRRC took part in the "big push" of 1 July 1916, the [first day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_day_on_the_Somme "First day on the Somme") of the [Battle of the Somme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Somme "Battle of the Somme"), charging German positions elsewhere on the line early that morning. There were 90 Rhodesians on the eve of the attack and only 10 alive and unwounded afterwards.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl50to51-29) On the Somme battlefield itself, Rhodesians were among those at [Delville Wood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Delville_Wood "Battle of Delville Wood"), which began on 14 July. This was the South African [1st Infantry Brigade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Infantry_Brigade_/(South_Africa/) "1st Infantry Brigade (South Africa)")'s first engagement,[\[n 4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-southafricanbattalion-37) and some of the colonials [blacked up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blackface "Blackface") and imitated [Zulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zulu_Kingdom "Zulu Kingdom") battle cries and war dances.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-38) Despite suffering casualties of catastrophic proportions—about 80% of the brigade's personnel were killed, wounded, or captured—they took the Wood and held it as ordered until they were relieved on 20 July.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-liddellhart324-39) By the time of its withdrawal, the South African Brigade, originally numbering 3,155 (123 officers and 3,032 other ranks), had been reduced to 19 officers and 600 men.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-uys194198-36) Delville Wood was later described by [Sir B H Liddell Hart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B._H._Liddell_Hart "B. H. Liddell Hart") as "the bloodiest battle hell of 1916".[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-liddellhart324-39) "God knows I never wish to see such horrible sights again," a Southern Rhodesian veteran of the battle wrote home; "at times I wished it would come fast, anything to get out of that terrible death-trap and murderous place."[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl62-40)

German [gas attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_weapons_in_World_War_I "Chemical weapons in World War I") were among the most traumatic experiences for the Southern Rhodesians in Europe. One Rhodesian survivor of a gas attack described the sensation as like "suffocation, \[or\] slow drowning".[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl116117-41) The Germans used both disabling agents, such as [tear gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tear_gas "Tear gas") and the more severe [mustard gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sulfur_mustard "Sulfur mustard"), and lethal chemicals like [chlorine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chlorine "Chlorine") and [phosgene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phosgene "Phosgene"). Though generally not fatal, gas attacks caused extreme physical discomfort and pain, often to the point where soldiers lost consciousness. Mustard gas in particular caused blistering of the skin, vomiting and internal and external bleeding. The British Army issued [gas masks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gas_mask "Gas mask"), but according to Brady these did little to help the men. Injuries sustained to the eyes, lungs and nasal passages in gas attacks were often extremely debilitating and lasting, remaining with the men for years after the war.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl116117-41)

In July 1917, a KRRC Rhodesian platoon received lofty praise from a senior British officer, who described the colonials as "absolutely first-class soldiers and great gentlemen, every bit as good as soldiers… as our old [Expeditionary Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Expeditionary_Force_/(World_War_I/) "British Expeditionary Force (World War I)")".[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl63-42) Around the same time, a platoon of Southern Rhodesians in the KRRC took part in an engagement near [Nieuwpoort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nieuwpoort,_Belgium "Nieuwpoort, Belgium") in [Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flanders "Flanders"), where it and the [Northamptonshire Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northamptonshire_Regiment "Northamptonshire Regiment") manned positions on the eastern banks of the river [Yser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yser "Yser"). After a heavy artillery bombardment, German infantry and marines charged the British positions and surrounded the Rhodesian platoon. Brutal hand-to-hand fighting ensued in which most of the Southern Rhodesians were killed and some were taken prisoner. The _Bulawayo Chronicle_ ran a eulogy for them soon after, comparing their [last stand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_stand "Last stand") to that of [Allan Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allan_Wilson_/(army_officer/) "Allan Wilson (army officer)")'s [Shangani Patrol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shangani_Patrol "Shangani Patrol") in 1893.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl63to64-43) Later in 1917, a Rhodesian platoon in the KRRC fought in the [Battle of Passchendaele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Passchendaele "Battle of Passchendaele"), near [Ypres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ypres "Ypres") in western Flanders.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl114-44)

The Western Front continued to receive Southern Rhodesian troops right up to the end of the war, including veterans of the 2nd Rhodesia Regiment's campaign in East Africa.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl98-45) During the conflict's latter stages, the British Army sent some of its Southern Rhodesian officers to the Western Front to promote the colony's benefits, hoping to encourage emigration there by British servicemen after the war.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-gale7436-46)

The KRRC's 3rd Battalion, including a platoon of 70 Rhodesians, was transferred from France to the [Salonika front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macedonian_front "Macedonian front") in 1915. On this comparatively quiet front, they were slowly whittled down over the course of the war: 26 of them remained in January 1917,[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl50to51-29) and by the end of the war so few were left that the platoon no longer existed. Most of the men had been killed in action, while others were prisoners of the Bulgarians.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl70to71-47)

[![Image 6: A portrait photograph of a young white man with dark hair, wearing a British military uniform](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/2/2f/Pat_Judson.jpg/250px-Pat_Judson.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pat_Judson.jpg)

Lieutenant Daniel "Pat" Judson, the first airman born in Rhodesia

Some Southern Rhodesians mustered into the [Royal Flying Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Flying_Corps "Royal Flying Corps") (RFC), which merged with the [Royal Naval Air Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Naval_Air_Service "Royal Naval Air Service") in April 1918 to form the [Royal Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Air_Force "Royal Air Force"). Towards the end of the war, the service of airmen from the dominions and colonies was observed by the issuing of shoulder patches denoting the wearer's country of origin: from October 1918, Southern Rhodesians received labels marked "rhodesia".[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-48) One of the territory's first military aviators was Lieutenant Arthur R H Browne, a fighter pilot from [Umvuma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mvuma "Mvuma") in the Southern Rhodesian [Midlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midlands_Province "Midlands Province"), who was attached to No. 13 Squadron, RFC. He was killed in action in a [dogfight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dogfight "Dogfight") on 5 December 1915;[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-49) his aircraft, donated by the people of [Gatooma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kadoma,_Zimbabwe "Kadoma, Zimbabwe") in western [Mashonaland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mashonaland "Mashonaland"), was Gatooma No. 2,[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl71to72-50) one of five airplanes purchased by Southern Rhodesian public donations.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl92to93-51) From Dryden Farm, near the south-western border town of [Plumtree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plumtree,_Zimbabwe "Plumtree, Zimbabwe"), came Lieutenant Frank W H Thomas, an RFC combat pilot who won the [Military Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_Cross "Military Cross"), as well as the French _[Croix de Guerre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Croix_de_guerre_1914%E2%80%931918_/(France/) "Croix de guerre 1914–1918 (France)")_ (with palms), before he died on 5 January 1918 from wounds attained on operational service.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-52)

Lieutenant Daniel S "Pat" Judson, born in Bulawayo in 1898, became the first Rhodesia-born airman in history when he joined the RFC in April 1916. He was severely wounded while bombing enemy positions in March 1918, but recovered and remained in the unit until April 1919.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-53) The first [flying ace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_ace "Flying ace") born in Rhodesia was Major [George Lloyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Lloyd_/(aviator/) "George Lloyd (aviator)"), nicknamed "Zulu",[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-54) who joined No. 60 Squadron in April 1917, and won four aerial victories before transferring to No. 40 Squadron in July 1917, where he won four more.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-franks2627-55) He received the Military Cross in March 1918 for "conspicuous gallantry and devotion to duty",[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-56) and also won the [Air Force Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_Force_Cross_/(United_Kingdom/) "Air Force Cross (United Kingdom)") later that year.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-franks2627-55) Second Lieutenant David "Tommy" Greswolde-Lewis, a born and bred Bulawayan, was the [80th and final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_victories_of_Manfred_von_Richthofen "List of victories of Manfred von Richthofen") pilot defeated by [Manfred von Richthofen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manfred_von_Richthofen "Manfred von Richthofen"), the German ace widely known as the Red Baron. Richthofen downed Lewis just north-east of [Villers-Bretonneux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villers-Bretonneux "Villers-Bretonneux") on 20 April 1918; the Rhodesian's aircraft caught fire in mid-air, and when it crashed he was thrown from the wreckage. The Baron's bullets had hit Lewis' compass, goggles, coat and trouser leg, but he was practically unhurt, having suffered only minor burns. He spent the rest of the war a German prisoner.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-gibbons344-57)[\[n 5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-richthofen-60)

The Great War airman associated with Southern Rhodesia who ultimately earned the most distinction was [Arthur Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Arthur_Harris,_1st_Baronet "Sir Arthur Harris, 1st Baronet"), originally from England, who joined the Royal Flying Corps in late 1915 after serving as a [bugler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bugle "Bugle") with the 1st Rhodesia Regiment in South-West Africa.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-61) Harris alternated between Britain and France during the latter part of the war. He led [No. 45 Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._45_Squadron_RAF "No. 45 Squadron RAF") over the Western Front in 1917, destroying five German aircraft and winning the Air Force Cross, and afterwards commanded [No. 44 Squadron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No._44_Squadron_RAF "No. 44 Squadron RAF") in Britain.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-62) Intending to return to Southern Rhodesia after the war, he wore a "rhodesia" flash on his uniform during the hostilities,[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-63) but ended up staying with the RAF as a career officer. He finished the war a major,[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-64) rose through the ranks during the interwar period and became famous during World War II as "Bomber Harris", the head of [RAF Bomber Command](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Bomber_Command "RAF Bomber Command").[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-65)

### Maritz Rebellion; formation of 1st Rhodesia Regiment

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Maritz Rebellion; formation of 1st Rhodesia Regiment")\]

[![Image 7: A military unit stands on parade, rifles shouldered, in the middle of a town. Large crowds are gathered around.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/1st_Rhodesia_Regiment_in_Bulawayo%2C_1914.png/250px-1st_Rhodesia_Regiment_in_Bulawayo%2C_1914.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1st_Rhodesia_Regiment_in_Bulawayo,_1914.png)

The [1st Rhodesia Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia_Regiment "Rhodesia Regiment") parades in [Bulawayo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulawayo "Bulawayo") on its way south, 1914

Apart from the capture of [Schuckmannsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luhonono "Luhonono") in the Caprivi Strip by a combined force of BSAP and [Northern Rhodesia Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Rhodesia_Police "Northern Rhodesia Police") on 21 September 1914, the British South Africa Company's own armed forces and police remained almost totally uninvolved in the war until the following month. The South African Prime Minister, the former Boer general [Louis Botha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Botha "Louis Botha"), had told Britain that the Union could both handle its own security during the hostilities and defeat German South-West Africa without help, so the Imperial garrison had been sent to the Western Front. Lieutenant-Colonel [Manie Maritz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manie_Maritz "Manie Maritz")—an ex-Boer commander who now headed a column of [Afrikaans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrikaans "Afrikaans")\-speaking Union troops—defected to the Germans in mid-September, hoping to spark an uprising that would overthrow British supremacy in South Africa and restore the old [Boer Republics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boer_Republic "Boer Republic").[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl7-66) Botha requested the 500-man column that the Chartered Company had raised, hoping to reduce the possibility of further defections by interspersing his own forces with firmly pro-British Rhodesians. The expeditionary force was promptly formed in Salisbury, and named the [1st Rhodesia Regiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodesia_Regiment "Rhodesia Regiment") after the unit of Southern Rhodesian volunteers that had fought in the Anglo-Boer War.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl8-21) Apart from a small contingent of [Matabele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ndebele_people "Northern Ndebele people") (or Ndebele) scouts, the unit was all white.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-binda17-67)

> This is the last time I shall see you all together, and I now take the opportunity to thank you for the way you have played the game, and for the trouble you have taken to get fit for duty and to take the field. Remember, Rhodesia looks to you.

Colonel Alfred Edwards addresses the 1st Rhodesia Regiment at Salisbury railway station, October 1914[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl9-68)

After six weeks' training in the capital, the 1st Rhodesia Regiment travelled south by railway in late October 1914. During its stopover in Bulawayo, it paraded in front of about 90% of the town's population; Plumtree, the last stop before crossing the border, provided the soldiers with a lavish parting banquet. Notwithstanding these grand farewells, the [Maritz Rebellion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritz_Rebellion "Maritz Rebellion") was all but over by the time the Southern Rhodesian contingent reached its destination at [Bloemfontein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloemfontein "Bloemfontein").[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl9to14-69) The vast majority of South African troops, including most of Boer origin, had remained loyal to the Union government, and the uprising had been quashed.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-chanock22-70) The Rhodesians garrisoned Bloemfontein for about a month, then redeployed to Cape Town, where they underwent further training for the [South-West Africa Campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South-West_Africa_Campaign "South-West Africa Campaign") as part of South Africa's Northern Force, which Botha personally commanded.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl9to14-69)

### 1st Rhodesia Regiment in South-West Africa

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: 1st Rhodesia Regiment in South-West Africa")\]

[![Image 8: A map. See description](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ca/S%C3%BCdwestafrika_1915.jpg/250px-S%C3%BCdwestafrika_1915.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:S%C3%BCdwestafrika_1915.jpg)

A map of the [South-West Africa Campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South-West_Africa_Campaign "South-West Africa Campaign"), showing South African troop movements in red. The main South African force advanced on [Windhoek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windhoek "Windhoek") from [Walvis Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walvis_Bay "Walvis Bay"), an [exclave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enclave_and_exclave "Enclave and exclave") of South Africa about halfway up the South-West African coast.

During late December 1914, Northern Force travelled to the South African [exclave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enclave_and_exclave "Enclave and exclave") of [Walvis Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walvis_Bay "Walvis Bay"), about halfway up the coast of German South-West Africa. The 1st Rhodesia Regiment disembarked on 26 December 1914.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl9to14-69)

Northern Force made up the northern prong of a pincer movement designed by Botha to encircle the German forces in South-West Africa. Two smaller South African columns came from the Cape and the Orange Free State (the latter coming over the deserts of [Bechuanaland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bechuanaland "Bechuanaland")). The principal target was Windhoek, the capital of South-West Africa. The field of operations was arid and barren in the extreme; water was a precious commodity, so the South Africans and Southern Rhodesians brought thousands of tons of it with them. In the 100 kilometres (62 mi) of desert between Walvis Bay and Windhoek, temperatures could rise to above 50 °C (122 °F) in the daytime, then drop below freezing at night, all while desert winds blew sand and dust into every bodily and mechanical orifice. Germany based much of its defensive strategy in South-West Africa around the assumption that no enemy commander could feasibly attempt to advance across the desert from Walvis Bay to Windhoek, but Botha resolved to do exactly that.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Rhodesia_in_World_War_I#cite_note-mcl13to15-71)

The South African offensive from Walvis Bay began in February 1915, when Northern Force took [Swakopmund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swakopmund "Swakopmund")—the nearest German coastal settlement, about 20 kilometres (12 mi) north—without facing major resistance. The Germans almost immediately retreated, leaving behind explosive booby traps and other improvised weapons.
